s1-headline|Breakdown.Periodic.breakdown.annotation: Spatially periodic data are obtained by cutting off and correcting the evolving reference on a large torus, not by simply identifying opposite faces. The formal periodic implication gives nonexistence of a global smooth periodic velocity from suitable data. Its hypothesis is the smooth recurrent whole-space profile; the periodic blow-up and tracking estimate (1.7) is the stronger quantitative paper conclusion.

s1-finite-codimension-summary|Breakdown..annotation: The spectral circle $|z|=\Theta$ (Lemma 4.5) lies strictly inside the unit circle. Thus a mode with $\Theta<|z|<1$ must also be accounted for, although its amplitude tends to zero. The number of conditions on the datum is the dimension of the exterior spectral subspace, including generalized eigenvectors.

s1-similarity-time|Breakdown.physicalSca.annotation: The velocity scale and the reciprocal spatial length scale are both $a(t)=(1-t)^{-1/2}$. In `physicalScale` this is the factor applied to both $W$ and its spatial argument. The corresponding dilation parameter in Equation (3.4) is $a(t)^2$, not $a(t)$.

pdf-item-equation-1-2|Breakdown.IsSimila.annotation: `IsSimilarityProfile` is the local equation-and-decay part of the profile hypothesis; neither recurrence nor nonvanishing is included. One constant $C$ controls the velocity and its first two spatial derivatives, with one more inverse power of $1+|y|$ at each differentiation, as well as $\nabla q$. The last bound is additional to Equation (1.3) and Remark 1.2.

pdf-item-equation-1-3|Breakdown.IsSimila.annotation: At radius $r\ge1$, integrating the gradient decay bound (1.3) in spherical coordinates gives $\int_{|y|>r}|\nabla W|^2\lesssim\int_r^\infty\rho^{-2}d\rho=r^{-1}$, uniformly in phase. The corresponding sixth-power velocity tail is $O(r^{-3})$. These are the integrable tails of $X$; the square of the velocity bound has radial integral $\int_r^\infty d\rho$, so (1.3) gives no energy bound. The formal profile also has Hessian and pressure-gradient decay.

pdf-item-equation-1-3|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation:
The additional formal bounds on $
abla^2W$ and $
abla q$ have the same exponent three as $(W\cdot
abla)W$. By Equation (1.2) they imply $|\partial_sW+	frac12W+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The separate terms in this combination may decay only as $|y|^{-1}$. Their cancellation gives a square-integrable bound for the physical time derivative in the proof of Proposition 4.1.

pdf-item-equation-1-4|Breakdown.MildFram.annotation: Write $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. Then `selfSimilar` reads Equation (1.4) at $T=1$ as a curve in $X$: $D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$. Inverting by $D_{1-t}$ recovers the slice $w$ at that phase; no choice of pointwise representative is needed for either operation.

pdf-item-equation-1-5|Breakdown.physical.annotation: To see the inverse isometry in the argument, put $\delta=T-t$. At $t'=T-\lambda\delta$, the reconstruction formula (1.4) evaluates $W(s+S,x/\sqrt{\lambda\delta})$. Replace this by $RW(s,\lambda^{-1/2}R^{-1}x/\sqrt\delta)$ using the profile return law in Equation (1.2), and take out the velocity factor $(\lambda\delta)^{-1/2}$. This gives the stated scaling law.

pdf-item-equation-1-6|Breakdown.Transfer.annotation: Put $U(s)=D_{1-t}u(t)$ with $s=-\log(1-t)$. Since $D_{1-t}u^*(t)=W(s)$, the error is exactly $\|U(s)-W(s)\|_X=(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)-u^*(t)\|_X$. `TransferHolds` bounds the left-hand side by $Ce^{-\kappa s}$ for some $\kappa>0$. The physical error in Equation (1.6) follows on dividing by $(1-t)^{1/4}$.

pdf-item-equation-1-6|Breakdown.orbitNor.annotation: The lower estimate follows from $\big|(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_X-\|W(s)\|_X\big|\le C(1-t)^\kappa$. The positive lower bound supplied by `orbitNorm` is uniform in $s$, so the error can be made smaller than half that bound. The compensated norm of $u$ approaches the periodic function $\|W(s)\|_X$; the two-sided blow-up estimate in Equation (1.6) does not require this function to be constant.

pdf-item-equation-1-6|Breakdown.orbitBou.annotation: Let $M_0=\max_{[0,S]}\|W(s)\|_X$. The norm is periodic even when $W$ returns with a nontrivial isometry, so $M_0$ bounds all phases. Consequently the reference gradient norm is at most $M_0(1-t)^{-1/4}$, to which the smaller gradient error in Equation (1.6) can be added.

pdf-item-equation-1-7|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: With $\delta=T-t$, the ball $B_{1/16}$ becomes $B_{1/(16\sqrt\delta)}$. Both the $L^6$ and gradient norms of the rescaled error acquire the factor $\delta^{1/4}$, so the local tracking estimate in Equation (1.7) bounds them there by $C\delta^\kappa$ (using Sobolev on the fixed physical ball for $L^6$). On each fixed similarity ball Hölder also bounds the $L^2$ error. Thus one obtains local $H^1$ convergence; the entire expanding-ball $L^2$ norm has a different scaling. The linked `TorusBlowup` asserts unboundedness in the full periodic $H^1$ norm, not these comparisons.

s1-symmetry-class|Breakdown.certificate_.annotation: The perturbation is required to have the same space-time symmetries as the approximate field. Consequently the linearized and quadratic terms stay in that class, and the inverse estimate need only hold there. For instance, a rotation after half a period gives a half-period for the gradient energy, even when the velocity itself needs the full period; this improves the slice-gradient estimate (7.55).

s1-outline-base-solution|Breakdown.Trans.annotation: Only the reference is recurrent. For its perturbation, the return map is a compact perturbation of a map of norm at most $e^{-S/4}$ (Lemma 4.4). The desired rate $e^{-\kappa S}$ is chosen strictly above this bound and off the spectrum. The initial correction prescribes the exterior projection for that rate; it does not require spectral stability.

adapted.N1-12.1|Breakdown.Freq.gradSixDe.annotation: For $R\ge1$, the profile decay estimate (1.3) gives $\int_{|y|>R}|W|^6\lesssim C_W^6 R^{-3}$ and $\int_{|y|>R}|\nabla W|^2\lesssim C_W^2 R^{-1}$, uniformly in $s$. Together with the bounds on the unit ball this puts each slice in $X$. The velocity bound $O(|y|^{-1})$ does not alone imply $L^2$ integrability, which is why the whole-space construction in Section 5 cuts off the datum.

s1-outline-similarity-equation|Breakdown.annotation:
On substituting $U=W+V$ in Equation (1.2), the terms containing only $W$ vanish. The linearized convection is $(W\cdot
abla)V+(V\cdot
abla)W$, and the only remaining quadratic term is $(V\cdot
abla)V$. The equations for $V$ have the free drift and diffusion of (1.2), but no prescribed return law. One seeks decay of $V$, not a second periodic orbit.

The difference $v=u-u^*$ is in physical variables, whereas $U-W=D_{1-t}v$ is in similarity variables. Their gradient norms differ by the factor $(1-t)^{1/4}$. This scaling factor is part of the weighted norm (4.5) used to control a physical perturbation through many shrinking periods.

s1-outline-cutoff-error|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The cutoff has two useful properties: it leaves the field unchanged where the singularity forms, and it confines the interaction with a perturbation to the support ball (see Equation (6.9)). In `approxFieldProperties_holds` the two radii are $1/16$ and $1/8$ about $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$; the support is strictly inside the unit cell. Neither property by itself estimates the change in the gradient norm.

s1-outline-kernel-decay|Breakdown.FarFie.annotation: For $x\in Q_L$ and $x\prime\in B_{L/8}$, the distance to the translated source at $x\prime+Lj$ is at least $3L|j|_\infty/8$ for $j\ne0$. Consequently the sum of the noncentral heat responses is bounded by $CL^{-4}\|F\|_1$ and its gradient by $CL^{-5}\|F\|_1$, using Equation (3.9) for derivatives of orders one and two. Taking the $L^6$ and gradient $L^2$ norms over the cell gives $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$ in each case. The linked `lerayKernelBound_holds` supplies the first-derivative bound; the second is also needed for Equation (6.2).

s1-outline-torus-final|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The paper chooses $\kappa$ by the whole-space spectral argument. In the sequence construction let $\lambda=e^{-S/k}$ for $k$ subdivisions of a return, $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $t_n=T-\mu_n$. The selected weight $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ can be written $\theta=\lambda^\kappa$ with $0<\kappa<1/4$. The normalized velocity is $U_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u(t_n+\mu_ns)$, on $0\le s\le1-\lambda$. Writing $U_n=\bar U_n+\theta^n z_n$ with bounded $z_n$, endpoint matching forces $z_{n+1}(0)=(\lambda^{1/4}/\theta)z_n(1-\lambda)$. This ratio is less than one. The physical error is bounded by $C\mu_n^{-1/4}\theta^n=CT^{-\kappa}\mu_n^{\kappa-1/4}$, which has the rate of Equation (4.5) since $\lambda\mu_n\le T-t\le\mu_n$.

s1-outline-certificate-force|Breakdown.c.annotation: For a nonstationary time-periodic solution, translating its phase produces another solution: $\partial_s W$ is then a homogeneous solution of the linearized equation. A phase constraint and a corresponding force direction address this obstruction. Appendix C.4 explains why more such pairs can be useful: one chooses right-hand sides for which the discretized linearized equation has a large response, and constrains the correction in the corresponding response directions. The finite-dimensional computation chooses the fields; the inverse and transfer estimates (7.18)–(7.21) and Proposition 7.8 establish invertibility on the full domain.

s1-background-main-conclusion|Breakdown..annotation: For periodic localization, the cutoff must be made on the evolving field. The equation error it creates is cancelled using the periodic right inverse and a contraction (Subsection 6.4), rather than being retained as a force. The linked theorem is the nonexistence consequence of this construction.

s1-lyapunov-perron-method|Breakdown.Step.annotation: The condition at infinite similarity time is a rate of decay, not an initial condition imposed on the evolution run backwards. Only the exterior projection is propagated backwards, where the period map is invertible. Its initial value must cancel the response to all the future inhomogeneous terms in Equation (4.14).

s1-outline-unforced-correction|Breakdown.annotation: `breakdownOnTorus_of_profile` is the implication from a recurrent nonzero similarity profile to periodic breakdown. Its profile hypotheses include bounds on $\nabla^2 W$ and $\nabla q$ in addition to Equation (1.3). The proof first constructs an unbounded mild trajectory, then uses uniqueness to exclude a global smooth solution with the same periodic datum. The moving-frame reduction allows one to start with a hypothetical global solution whose velocity is periodic without assuming periodic pressure; the breakdown conclusion holds for every positive viscosity. Neither construction here supplies the profile itself; that is the separate certificate problem of Section 7.

s1-stable-convergence|Breakdown.Transfer.annotation: Apply $D_{1-t}$ to the difference in Equation (1.6). Since $D_{1-t}u^*(t)=W(s)$ and $\|D_{1-t}f\|_X=(1-t)^{1/4}\|f\|_X$, this gives $\|D_{1-t}u(t)-W(s)\|_X\lesssim e^{-\kappa s}$. Convergence is to the same phase $s=-\log(1-t)$, not merely to the set of slices of the profile.

s1-formal-space-result|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The original formal torus implication allows arbitrary smooth pressure on the covering space and excludes global periodic velocity. The quantitative smooth trajectory with periodic pressure and the local error in Equation (1.7) is still an open target of the supplied edition wrapper, not the conclusion of this nonexistence theorem.

s1-formal-weak-result|Breakdown.certific.annotation: The weak result gives an exact recurrence and the momentum equation tested against compactly supported solenoidal fields. Passing to the smooth profile satisfying the similarity equation, recurrence and decay conditions (1.2)–(1.3) requires a separate regularity and decay argument. The link uses the earlier rectangular certificate, and neither its premise nor that of the extended theorem is an instantiated numerical certificate.

s2-heat-at-zero|Breakdown.Freq.heat_hold.annotation: At zero lag the heat multiplier is one. For a fixed state $g\in X$, dominated convergence gives $\|G(t)g-g\|_2\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, even though there is no $L^1$ heat kernel at time zero. This is strong continuity on $X$, as needed for the initial value in Equation (2.4).

pdf-item-equation-2-2|Breakdown.Freq.hea.annotation: In the weighted Fourier coordinate of $X$, the expression in Equation (2.2) acquires the factor $2\pi|\xi|$. Thus `heatDivFree` takes a physical $L^2$ force, projects its weighted heat transform onto the solenoidal subspace, and returns an element of $X$. The paper's definition has the larger domain $L^1+L^2$; the $L^{3/2}$ estimate is a further step.

pdf-item-equation-2-3|Breakdown.Freq.bil.annotation: When the first input is a compact smooth solenoidal field $\varphi$, both $\varphi\cdot\nabla v$ and $v\cdot\nabla\varphi$ belong to $L^2$: for the second use local $L^2$ control from $v\in L^6$. The linked identity then realizes Equation (2.3) with the $L^2$ projected heat operator. It is this specialization that is useful in the compactness argument of Lemma 3.2, rather than an identification for every pair in $X$.

s2-bilinear-target|Breakdown.Freq.bilin_.annotation: The important point is not only that $K(\tau)(u,v)\in X$ for positive lag, but that the bound in Equation (3.7) is integrable in $\tau$ near zero. In the formal construction a bounded scalar functional of the third, solenoidal argument is represented by an element of the Hilbert space $X$. The linked theorem gives the resulting bilinear bound, not the full linear assertion of Lemma 3.1.

s2-diagonal|Breakdown.Freq.bilinForm|1.annotation: Putting $v=u$ gives two copies of the same advection term, which cancel the factor $1/2$ in Equation (2.3); the minus sign remains. In the formal dual expression this gives $-\int (u\cdot\nabla)u\cdot(-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}w)$, the pairing against a state with velocity $w$. The definition of the form does not itself establish its boundedness.

s2-mild-convention|Breakdown.MildFramewo.annotation: A mild solution here is a continuous curve in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying Equation (2.4), not a velocity already known to solve the differential equations pointwise. In particular no $L^2$ bound on the curve follows from its definition. The use of smooth compactly supported data in Lemma 2.3 is what permits a return to classical solutions.

s2-every-nearby-datum|Breakdown.Contract.annotation: The heat curve of the prescribed displacement has norm $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa=\|\chi\|_X$: the weighted heat estimate (4.20) gives one inequality, and $t=0$ gives the other. Smallness of the datum is therefore precisely smallness of this particular source in the space on which the inverse acts.

pdf-item-equation-2-5|Breakdown.Transfer.annotation: The relative error in Equation (2.5) is at most $(C/c_*)(1-t)^\kappa$, by the lower bound (4.4) for the reference. Thus the physical gradient of the error can become unbounded while its ratio to the reference gradient tends to zero. Both the tracking and the blow-up rate are expressed in the global $\dot H^1$ norm.

s2-periodic-proposition|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The input of Proposition 2.2 is the whole-space profile; the conclusion is a different solution with periodic data. `TorusBlowup` specifies the existence of an unbounded mild trajectory on the unit torus from smooth periodic solenoidal data. Unlike Equation (2.6), it does not prescribe a two-sided rate or a local comparison with $u_T^*$.

pdf-item-equation-2-6|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The lower bound in Equation (2.6) concerns the gradient over the whole cell. The approximation is stated only on $B_{1/16}$, where the reference is uncut. Changing variables $x=\sqrt{T-t}\,y$ in the latter estimate gives an error $O((T-t)^\kappa)$ in the similarity gradient norm on $B_{1/(16\sqrt{T-t})}$. These balls contain each fixed ball in similarity variables for all sufficiently late times. The conclusion of `TorusBlowup` asserts unboundedness in $H^1$, without these rates or spatial comparisons.

s2-smooth-representative-definition|Brea.annotation: A value of the mild curve is an almost-everywhere class. Smoothness means that one jointly smooth velocity $U(t,x)$ and pressure $P(t,x)$ solve Equation (1.1), with $U(0)$ the specified datum and $U(t)$ representing the mild value for each time. The formal property imposes these conditions on a closed interval and also asks for bounded energy and bounded velocity and spatial gradient there.

s2-energy-nonincrease|Breakdown.EnergyBo.annotation: For the smooth local solution, pairing Equation (1.1) with $u$ and integrating eliminates the transport and pressure terms by zero divergence and yields $\tfrac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_2^2=-2\|\nabla u(t)\|_2^2$. This yields the same bound for every $t<T$, even if the gradient diverges as $t\uparrow T$. `EnergyBoundedOn` only asks for some finite bound on a specified closed interval; it is not the dissipation identity.

adapted.N1-27.1|Breakdown.mildRegular_re.annotation: Fix $b<T$ before constructing the local competitor. Mild uniqueness (Lemma 3.5) transfers the bound $M_b=\max_{[0,b]}\|u\|_X$ to its gradient on any shorter interval. The energy identity on $\mathbb R^3$, or Poincaré on the mean-zero torus, then bounds its full $H^1$ norm independently of the shorter endpoint. Hence it extends through $b$. Lean obtains the whole-space realization by Fourier continuation from compact smooth data.

s2-proof-correction|Breakdown.Contractio.annotation: The cutoff gives a small displacement in $X$, but imposes no conditions on its exterior spectral projection. Inserting its heat evolution into the right inverse of Proposition 4.3 selects the correction needed for the linear problem. The same inverse is then evaluated on the heat curve plus the quadratic Duhamel term, so the corrected datum accounts for the nonlinear interaction as well.

s2-proof-correction|Breakdown.TransferHo.annotation: Take $w_0=\bar u(0)$ with cutoff radius sufficiently large for Equation (5.2). Both $w_0$ and each element of $E$ belong to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$, so $w_0+\gamma$ belongs to the same class. `TransferHolds` supplies the abstract mild tracking conclusion for data from the dense class; the subsequent regularity argument uses the concrete field.

s2-norm-identification|Breakdown.Freq.X|.annotation: The norms in Equation (2.5) are already the physical gradient norms once the representative is recovered. Hence the lower bound gives gradient divergence and the error divided by the reference gradient norm is $O((1-t)^\kappa)$. The definition of the Fourier space explains the norm being tracked; actual gradient norm identification uses `embedNormLinear_holds` and the realization of the smooth curve, not `X` alone.

s2-finite-codimension|Breakdown.Contract.annotation: For $x\in\ker P_{\mathrm u}$, take $w_0=W(0)+x$. The linear right inverse applied to $e^{t\Delta}x$ gives zero datum correction, since the homogeneous solution already has the required decay. Thus $\gamma=(\mathcal R\mathcal B(v,v))_1$ and $\|\gamma\|_X\lesssim\|x\|_X^2$ by Equations (4.8), (4.19), (4.24). Over the interior space the selected data have the form $W(0)+x+O(\|x\|_X^2)$, giving the tangent space of the selected family at $W(0)$.

pdf-item-equation-3-1|Breakdown.Freq.gra.annotation: The bound (3.1) allows a velocity to be estimated using just its gradient, which is what closes the transport estimate in Lemma 3.1. The linked theorem proves this bound for smooth divergence-free fields with velocity and first-derivative decay as in Equation (1.3), with a constant independent of the decay constant. The paper uses the ambient Sobolev inequality without these pointwise hypotheses.

pdf-item-equation-3-1|Breakdown.Freq.vel.annotation: The Sobolev inequality on test fields makes the map $J\varphi\mapsto\varphi$ bounded from the gradient norm to $L^6$. By density it extends to the formal Hilbert space, yielding $\|Vg\|_6\le\|V\|\|g\|_2$. The linked existence theorem concerns this solenoidal reconstruction; Equation (3.1) also applies to nonsolenoidal fields.

pdf-item-equation-3-2|Breakdown.Freq.par.annotation: Writing $g=2\pi|\xi|\hat u$ gives $\widehat{\partial_j u}=i\xi_jg/|\xi|$. This multiplier is bounded, and the squared moduli of the three scalar multipliers sum to one off the origin. The linked result identifies these derivatives for the embedded smooth decay class and bounds the sum of their squared $L^2$ norms for all formal states. The full three-part identity in Equation (3.2) is broader.

pdf-item-equation-3-3|Breakdown.Freq.hea.annotation: The Laplacian has symbol $-4\pi^2|\xi|^2$ with the convention of Subsection 1.4, giving the multiplier in Equation (3.3). The formal scalar factor uses $\max(t,0)$, so negative arguments are assigned the multiplier one; none of the forward heat estimates requires a backward heat operator.

pdf-item-equation-3-4|Breakdown.pushForw.annotation: The argument is pulled back by $R^{-1}$ and the velocity value is pushed forward by $R$. In particular $\nabla(\rho_Ru)(x)=R(\nabla u)(R^{-1}x)R^{-1}$, so its trace and Frobenius norm are preserved. The action includes reflections, as required by the possible isometry in Equation (1.2).

ns-s3-projected-heat-forcing|Breakdown.F.annotation: The exponent in Equation (3.6) combines the loss $\tau^{-1/4}$ for heat smoothing from $L^{3/2}$ to $L^2$ and the loss $\tau^{-1/2}$ for one derivative. In the formal construction `heatDivFree` is the weighted projected heat transform of an $L^2$ force. The bound needed for transport terms with inputs in $X$ is instead proved by duality in `bilin_holds`; the latter does not give (3.6) for arbitrary forcing.

The formal construction proves the consequence of Equation (3.6) needed in the mild equation directly, by estimating the scalar transport pairing and using the Hilbert-space representation theorem. Its conclusion is Equation (3.7) for the symmetrized transport of two states in $X$. It does not estimate the projected heat evolution of an arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ force as in (3.6).

adapted.N2-03.1|Breakdown.Freq.bilin_hol.annotation: The exponent $3/2$ arises from $1/(3/2)=1/6+1/2$: $\|(u\cdot\nabla)v\|_{3/2}\le\|u\|_6\|\nabla v\|_2$. Use the Sobolev inequality (3.1) and apply the projected heat estimate (3.6) to both advection terms in the definition of the bilinear operator (2.3), including their factor $1/2$. This yields the bilinear bound $C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|_X\|v\|_X$. `bilin_holds` establishes existence and that bound for the realized bilinear map, not the full estimate (3.6) on arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ data.

pdf-item-equation-3-8|Breakdown.Freq.bil.annotation: Advection of two dilated velocities scales as $\mu^{3/2}$, since one derivative and two velocity factors are involved: $((D_\mu u)\cdot\nabla)D_\mu v=\mu D_\mu((u\cdot\nabla)v)$. Heat evolution changes its lag from $\tau$ to $\mu\tau$ when moved through the dilation. The factor $\mu$ in Equation (3.8) is also the Jacobian needed when changing the time variable in the Duhamel integral.

The advective derivative transforms as $((\rho_Ru)\cdot\nabla)(\rho_Rv)=\rho_R((u\cdot\nabla)v)$. Orthogonal covariance of the projection and radiality of the heat kernel then give the third identity in Equation (3.8). The formal theorem includes reflections, so the period relation (1.5) may be used without assuming that $R$ preserves orientation.

ns-s3-projection-homogeneity|Breakdown.F.annotation: The longitudinal component at nonzero $\xi$ is $Q_\xi z=\xi(\xi\cdot z)/|\xi|^2$. On replacing $\xi$ by $c\xi$, $c\ne0$, numerator and denominator acquire the same factor $c^2$. Subtracting the unchanged $Q_\xi$ from the identity gives the homogeneity of $\mathbb P_\xi$ needed for the dilation in Equation (3.8).

adapted.N2-04.1|Breakdown.FarField.kerne.annotation: Integrate $(|x|+\sqrt\tau)^{-4}$ in dimension three. The substitution $x=\sqrt\tau z$ gives $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_1\lesssim\tau^{-2+3/2}=\tau^{-1/2}$. This is the estimate used with the bounded tensor in Section 7.10: its integral in time is finite at lag zero.

ns-s3-oseen-decay|Breakdown.FarField.ler.annotation: At the first derivative order the two scales in Equation (3.9) give $|\nabla O_\tau(x)|\lesssim\tau^{-2}$ in the ball of radius $\sqrt\tau$, and $|\nabla O_\tau(x)|\lesssim |x|^{-4}$ outside it. In the Gaussian-integral representation the latter power follows by integrating a third Gaussian derivative in heat time. `lerayKernelBound_holds` proves this first-order estimate componentwise, not all the estimates for $l\ge0$.

adapted.N2-04.2|Breakdown.FarField.leray.annotation: The undifferentiated tensor has an order-three bound, which alone would not give spatial integrability in dimension three. A single derivative gives order four and the radial tail $\int_R^\infty r^{-2}dr$. `lerayKernelBound_holds` concerns this first derivative at positive lag, not the estimate for all orders in Equation (3.9).

ns-s3-derivative-convolution-definition|.annotation: For $u,v\in X$, the tensor $F=u\otimes v$ belongs to $L^3$ by Equation (3.1). At a fixed $\tau>0$, Equation (3.9) gives $\nabla O_\tau\in L^{3/2}$, so the integral defining `kernelConv` is absolutely convergent at each $x$, with bound $C\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{3/2}\|F\|_3$. In particular the second formula of (3.10) does not require $F\in W^{1,1}$ as in the first.

ns-s3-tensor-product|Breakdown.FarField..annotation: The divergence is taken in the second index: $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)_j=\sum_m\partial_m(v_j u_m)=(u\cdot\nabla)v_j+v_j\operatorname{div}u$. Thus the order of the factors is reversed relative to the advection notation. Symmetrization in Equation (3.10) includes both orders.

ns-s3-compact-monodromy|Breakdown.Monodr.annotation: In the period map the initial datum is varied, while the reference $u^*(t')$ in the mixed integral is fixed at each $t'$. Lemma 3.2 gives norm-null integrands for weakly null linearized trajectories, and Equation (3.7) gives an integrable majorant. For the formal short-step proof, fix a test factor $f$ and truncate the last $\epsilon$ units, at cost $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$. At the remaining lags use $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)=G(\tau-\epsilon)K(\epsilon)(f,\cdot)$: the heat images of the compact closure at lag $\epsilon$ have compact closure over the bounded time interval. Approximation of the continuous coefficient curve by finite sums of such factors gives compactness of the mixed endpoint integral. The full return is obtained by composing short steps.

ns-s3-compactness-lemma|Breakdown.Freq.b.annotation: The conclusion concerns the global $X$ norm, even though the proof uses compactness on a ball. The linked `BilinCompact` requires the first factor to belong to `testSpan`, a dense subspace; this already suffices for `HasCompactKernel` in the period-map construction (compare Lemma 4.4). The all-$X$ version follows by the operator-norm approximation in the next paragraph.

ns-3late-abstract-mild|Breakdown.HeatBil.annotation: On $[a,b)$, each integral in Equation (2.4) only involves the compact interval $[a,t]$, $t<b$, on which the two inputs are bounded in $\mathcal X$. Thus the integral is well defined even when $\|u(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$ is unbounded as $t\uparrow b$. There is no initial assumption of a classical velocity or pressure.

pdf-item-theorem-3-5|Breakdown.restrict|.annotation: Evolve the equation at $m$ by $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$. The free term becomes $e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)$ and the integral becomes $\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))dt'$ by Equation (3.12). Subtract these terms from the equation at $t$. The only surviving integral is over $[m,t]$.

pdf-item-equation-3-13|Breakdown.restric.annotation: To move the heat operator through the integral, one uses boundedness of $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ on $\mathcal X$ and Bochner integrability from Lemma 3.3. The upper endpoint $t'=m$ of the earlier integral is a null set, so Equation (3.12) is only needed at positive lag. `restrict` implements the identity when both inputs are the solution.

ns-3late-restart-consequence|Breakdown.r.annotation: The datum after a restart is the value of the same solution, so both uniqueness and estimates can be applied on an interval chosen for the time of interest. In Section 7.10 one takes $m=2t-1$ for an ancient solution, making the heat interval have length $1-t$ and keeping the similarity scale comparable throughout it.

ns-3late-weak-assumptions|Breakdown.Freq.annotation: In the weak equation the pressure drops out against compact solenoidal tests. The paper assumes continuity in $X$ and Equation (3.14). In `IsWeakSolution` one also requires smooth decaying slices and $u(t)-u(t')\in L^2$ for every pair of times, with $\|u(t)-u(t_0)\|_2\to0$ as $t\to t_0$ within the interval. The difference condition permits infinite energy of the slices themselves.

The weak equation gives the derivative of scalar test pairings, while the mild formulation (2.4) gives an equality of velocities in $X$. It is the latter that permits uniqueness against the mild trajectories of Lemma 3.5. `MildOfWeak` has the same type of conclusion on $[a,b]$, under the stronger hypotheses of `IsWeakSolution`.

ns-3late-weak-equation|Breakdown.Freq.Is.annotation:
The linear term in Equation (3.14) is $\int u\cdot\Delta\psi=-\int
abla u:
abla\psi$. For the nonlinear term integrate $\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_i\psi_j$ by parts; since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the result is $-\int (u\cdot
abla)u\cdot\psi$. These are the two negative terms in `IsWeakSolution`, where the scalar derivative is required in the interior and the pairings are continuous up to both endpoints.

ns-3late-weak-to-mild|Breakdown.Freq.Mil.annotation: Once the scalar test identity gives Equation (2.4), the same datum $u(a)$ and the same curve in $X$ can be used in the restart and uniqueness lemmas. No separate existence problem for a mild solution is being solved. The formal `MildOfWeak` makes this identification for the smooth-decay class with continuous $L^2$ differences.

pdf-item-equation-3-15|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The additional $1$ in `weight` gives the velocity contribution $\|u\|_2^2$ to the squared $H^1$ norm. At $n=0$ this is the entire weight. It is for this reason that `V` can include constants whereas Equation (3.15) defines a norm only with the mean-zero condition.

pdf-item-equation-3-16|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: For a nonzero unit-torus frequency $k$, the ratio of the inhomogeneous to the homogeneous squared weight is $1+(4\pi^2|k|^2)^{-1}\le1+(4\pi^2)^{-1}$. This proves Equation (3.16) after removing $k=0$. The linked `weight` takes value one at that frequency; without mean zero the upper bound in (3.16) would fail even for a constant velocity.

pdf-item-equation-3-17|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The coefficient of $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ at $k$ is $\sum_j(2\pi i\,j\cdot\hat u(k-j))\hat v(j)$. At $k=0$ every summand vanishes by solenoidality of $\hat u(-j)$. This gives the mean-zero property directly in the Fourier representation, even though `V` allows constants. `kernel` adds the expression with the inputs reversed and multiplies its projected heat evolution by $-1/2$, as in Equation (3.17).

Because $K_{\mathbb T}$ is symmetric, the cross terms in $K_{\mathbb T}(u^{\mathrm a}+z,u^{\mathrm a}+z)$ combine to $2K_{\mathbb T}(u^{\mathrm a},z)$. The linearized operator in Equation (6.6) contains this term with a minus sign; the term with both inputs $z$ is the quadratic remainder. `kernel_symm` follows directly from the symmetrized convolution.

ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws|Breakdown.Pe.annotation: At $t=a$ in Equation (2.4) the integration interval has length zero. The free evolution must return the datum, which is precisely `heat_zero`: each Fourier multiplier is one, including at frequency zero.

s3-periodic-sobolev-proof-dependency|Bre.annotation: The two factors of the advection have norms in $L^6$ and $L^2$, giving $1/6+1/2=2/3$. To bound their product in $L^{3/2}$ by two gradient norms uniformly in the period one needs precisely the period-independent Sobolev inequality (3.18). A bound in terms of two inhomogeneous norms followed by Poincaré would not give such a uniform constant. The linked formal kernel estimate uses the full $H^1$ norm at unit period.

pdf-item-equation-3-18|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: For Equation (3.18) the exponent $6$ is the one for which scaling the cell and scaling the gradient have the same effect. The formal starting point `TrigHs` is different: it bounds finite complex Fourier sums in $L^6$ using the full weight $1+4\pi^2|k|^2$. In particular it applies without removing the constant coefficient.

pdf-item-theorem-3-7|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: In `sourceOp_threeHalves` the source $A$ is inserted as $A((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$, with no amplitude change. Its $L^{3/2}$ norm is multiplied by $\mu$, and the heat lag $\mu\tau$ costs $(\mu\tau)^{-3/4}$; the resulting factor is $\mu^{1/4}$. The interaction operator used below includes the inverse factor $\mu^{-1/4}$, so its bound is uniform in the scale. The formal estimate takes supported $L^2$ sources and $0<\mu\tau\le1$, unlike the unrestricted positive lags of Equation (3.19).

The nonlinear source has mean zero because it is the divergence of $v\otimes u+u\otimes v$. Its $L^{3/2}$ norm is bounded by $\|u\|_6\|\nabla v\|_2+\|v\|_6\|\nabla u\|_2$. Inserting this into the periodic heat estimate (3.19) and using the uniform Sobolev bound (3.18) gives the bilinear estimate (3.20), including the factor $1/2$ in the bilinear operator definition (3.17). The formal proof uses a Fourier trilinear bound and polarization to give the analogous operator estimate on `V`, for $0<\tau\le1$.

ns-3late-periodic-kernel-bound|Breakdown.annotation: For bounded inputs on an interval of length $h\le1$, integrating Equation (3.20) costs $\int_0^h\tau^{-3/4}d\tau=4h^{1/4}$. The mixed linear term therefore has operator norm at most $8C_{\mathbb T}h^{1/4}$ times the bound of the reference velocity on that interval. The same small-interval factor is available from `KernelSharpBound` after the time normalization in `stepFrame`.

pdf-item-equation-3-21|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The operator $D_\mu$ in Equation (3.21) changes the spatial period to $L/\sqrt\mu$. `stepFrame` does not perform that spatial dilation. It keeps the space `V` fixed, changes the time to $s=(t-t_0)/\mu$, and multiplies the velocity state by $\mu^{1/4}$. The resulting heat operator and bilinear kernel are $e^{\mu s\Delta}$ and $\mu^{3/4}K_{\mathbb T}(\mu\tau)$; the latter has the uniform smoothing estimate for normalized lags at most one. The local spatial change of variables enters separately in `restrictTorus` and `transplantField`.

ns-s4-003|Breakdown.physicalField|1.annotation: In $D_\mu$ the velocity factor is $\sqrt\mu$. For Equation (4.1) the choice $\mu=(T-t)^{-1}$ therefore gives the spatial scale $\mu^{-1/2}=\sqrt{T-t}$ and the correct velocity prefactor $(T-t)^{-1/2}$. The argument of $W$ still uses its own logarithmic time.

pdf-item-equation-4-1|Breakdown.physical.annotation: Scaling the two bounds in Equation (1.3) gives $(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)^{-1}$ for the velocity and $(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)^{-2}$ for its gradient. The inequalities on the right of Equation (4.1) discard $\sqrt{1-t}$ to give bounds uniform in time away from zero. In the next paragraph the full denominators must be kept near zero, where $|x|^{-2}$ is not square integrable.

pdf-item-equation-4-1|Breakdown.IsSimila.annotation: The $j=0,1$ clauses of the profile decay give Equation (4.1) after scaling. The formal premise includes $j=2$ and $\nabla q$ with exponent three as well. For derivatives, the formal operator norm and the paper's square-sum norm are equivalent in fixed dimension; a decay constant may be enlarged when translating the estimates.

pdf-item-equation-4-2|Breakdown.Freq.Dil.annotation: The algebra used twice in iterating Equation (4.2) is $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$ and $D_\mu\rho_R=\rho_R D_\mu$. The norm law gives $\|D_{1/\lambda}f\|_X=\lambda^{-1/4}\|f\|_X$. In particular the isometry introduces no additional norm factor.

ns-s4-018|Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatemen.annotation: For the short-piece version of Equation (4.3), take $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $j=nk+r$ with $0\le r<k$. The $j$th piece samples the phase $jS/k-\log(1-\sigma)$ and its normalized profile equals $\rho_R^n$ of the $r$th piece. The additional $D_{\mu^{-j}}$ restores physical units. `ProfilePieceStatement` also verifies mildness and matching at the endpoints.

ns-s4-018|Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSi.annotation: Since $1-(t_n+\lambda^n\sigma)=\lambda^n(1-\sigma)$, the sampled phase is $nS-\log(1-\sigma)$. The physical dilation splits as $D_{\lambda^{-n}}D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}$. Substitution into `selfSimilar` and $n$ applications of recurrence prove Equation (4.3).

ns-s4-019|Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra.annotation: In Equation (4.3) the isometry has norm one, and $D_{\lambda^{-n}}$ multiplies the gradient norm by $\lambda^{-n/4}$. Therefore $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u^*(t)\|_X=(1-\sigma)^{1/4}\|u^*(\sigma)\|_X$. The factor on the right lies in $[\lambda^{1/4},1]$ for $0\le\sigma<t_1$, giving the two constants in the proof.

ns-s4-019|Breakdown.monodromy|4.annotation: The dilation in Equation (4.3) is undone when defining the return of a linearized perturbation. If $h_\chi$ solves Equation (4.9), then $M\chi=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda h_\chi(t_1)$. Without the interaction with $u^*$ this becomes $M_0\chi=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}\chi$, of norm at most $\lambda^{1/4}$. Lemma 4.4 makes $M-M_0$ compact. The growth rate of the reference itself in Equation (4.4) is not the norm of $M$.

ns-s4-020|Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatemen.annotation: In the induction the normalized variable $\sigma$ is unchanged by the advance: $1-\lambda(1-t)=t_{n+1}+\lambda^{n+1}\sigma$. Every application contributes one $\rho_R$ and one $D_{1/\lambda}$. Their commutation gives the powers in Equation (4.3); the short-piece theorem uses the same endpoint matching with step factor $\mu$.

ns-s4-025|Breakdown.Piece|1.annotation: On $[0,b]$ the weight in Equation (4.5) lies between $(1-b)^{1/4-\kappa}$ and one; thus the ordinary and weighted supremum norms are equivalent there. The equivalence is not uniform as $b\uparrow1$. Subdividing in similarity time gives the same compact normalized interval on each step and puts all the dependence on the physical time into the scaling factors.

ns-s4-026|Breakdown.orbitSeq|4.annotation: An additive source curve acts throughout a period. Its endpoint alone is insufficient to determine the discrete forcing: in Equation (4.13) the relevant quantity is the endpoint of $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$, since the state is $v_n(0)-g_n(0)$. The bounded-sequence recurrence `orbitSeq` is obtained by dividing this state and forcing by $\Theta^n$.

ns-s4-027|Breakdown.PieceOperatorStateme.annotation: In Equation (4.8), $e^{t\Delta}\gamma$ means the entire heat curve. Its evaluation at time zero is $\gamma$, whereas its value at the end of a period is the freely evolved datum. `pieceFree` is the operator $\Gamma:X\to\mathrm{Piece}$ giving this curve on one short interval; it has norm at most one.

ns-s4-029|Breakdown.PiecePerturbationSta.annotation: The error equation retains the two mixed terms as $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)$ and the entire quadratic term as $\mathcal B(v,v)$. Since $u^*$ is an exact solution, its pure term cancels. Solving Equation (4.7) is therefore equivalent to solving the mild equation for $u^*+v$, with its shifted initial value; no approximation is made at this step.

pdf-item-equation-4-7|Breakdown.varConst.annotation: Equation (4.7) makes sense on every $[0,b]$ with $b<1$, since the inputs are bounded there and $(t-t')^{-3/4}$ is integrable. `varConstIntegral` gives this local assertion. Control of the quadratic term in the weighted norm on all of $[0,1)$ is a further estimate, proved in Equations (4.18)–(4.19).

ns-s4-032|Breakdown.exists_section|2.annotation: For a fixed $g$, any two admissible data in Equation (4.12) differ by an element of $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$: their difference evolves homogeneously, and the inverse power bound forces its exterior projection to vanish. Conversely an interior displacement has the required decay. Taking the datum in the complementary space $E$ selects exactly one point of this affine space.

pdf-item-equation-4-8|Breakdown.StepData.annotation: At zero Equation (4.8) gives $v(0)-g(0)=\gamma$. For the later source $g=e^{t\Delta}\chi+\mathcal B(v,v)$, this reads $v(0)=\chi+\gamma$. The two terms should not be confused: the prescribed displacement is part of the source, whereas the correction comes from the first component of the inverse.

pdf-item-equation-4-8|Breakdown.Contract.annotation: The use of Equation (4.8) in the nonlinear problem is to insert $g=e^{t\Delta}\chi+\mathcal B(v,v)$. At a fixed point of its second component, the resulting pair solves Equation (4.7) with $v(0)=\chi+\gamma$. One does not first solve the nonlinear equation and then choose the correction.

pdf-item-equation-4-9|Breakdown.Monodrom.annotation: To recover Equation (4.9) from the short-interval construction, solve the homogeneous linear equation on each successive normalized piece and pass $D_\mu h(L)$ into the next. After $k$ steps, the product has applied total dilation $D_{\mu^k}=D_\lambda$. The remaining operation is $\rho_R^{-1}$, returning the last field to the orientation of the first.

ns-s4-037|Breakdown.MonodromyStatement|2.annotation: The recurrence of the background multiplies it by $\rho_R D_{1/\lambda}$ over one period. Both operations are invertible and commute, so undoing them on the final perturbation gives exactly $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda h_\chi(t_1)$. This is why there is no forward rotation in Equation (4.10).

ns-s4-039|Breakdown.MonodromyStatement|2.annotation: A free step is $B=D_\mu e^{(1-\mu)\Delta}$, with norm at most $\mu^{1/4}$. The Lean proof only needs $\|B^k\|\le\mu^{k/4}$. To identify it with the paper’s free map, use Equation (3.5): $B^2=D_{\mu^2}e^{(1-\mu^2)\Delta}$, since the heat times add as $(1-\mu)+\mu(1-\mu)$. Hence $B^k=D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}$ and $\rho_R^{-1}B^k$ is the desired return.

ns-s4-055|Breakdown.orbitSeq|1.annotation: In the full-endpoint convention, a global heat input $g=e^{t\Delta}\eta$ is accounted for by adding $\eta$ to the initial datum; it supplies no new local source on later intervals. In Equation (4.13) the same heat curve can produce a nonzero $f_n$ because the propagated endpoint is that of $v-g$. The difference is bookkeeping of the heat input, not a different linearized equation.

ns-s4-057|Breakdown.orbitSeq|1.annotation: The key point of the second identity in Equation (4.14) is that $f_n$ is independent of $\chi_0$. Thus the datum can be chosen using the entire sequence of $f_n$, computed from the prescribed $g$. For the nonlinear equation we first fix a trial quadratic source, apply this linear selection, then use the resulting trajectory to update the source.

ns-s4-059|Breakdown.PeriodicInverseState.annotation: Splitting the integral at $t_n$ and using Equation (3.12), the part before $t_n$ is the heat evolution of $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)(t_n)$. Adding the original heat term yields the heat evolution of $v(t_n)-g(t_n)$. The remaining integral begins at $t_n$; this is the exact restart identity even when $g$ has no time derivative.

ns-s4-061|Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp.annotation: Upon setting $t'=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma'$, the factor $dt'=\lambda^n d\sigma'$ cancels the inverse time-scaling factor of $K$. In formulas, for $\mu=\lambda^n$, $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(a,b)=K(\tau)(D_\mu a,D_\mu b)$. Isometry equivariance and Equation (4.3) then return the mixed kernel to $K(\sigma-\sigma')(u^*(\sigma'),v_n(\sigma'))$.

ns-s4-063|Breakdown.orbitSeq|1.annotation: At the common physical endpoint of periods $n$ and $n+1$ the two normalized values differ by $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda$. Applying this map to $v_n(t_1)-g_n(t_1)$ gives $\chi_{n+1}$. With $v_n=h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal U g_n$, its homogeneous term is $\mathcal M\chi_n$ and its source is precisely the difference in Equation (4.13).

ns-s4-074|Breakdown.HeatBilinear|1.annotation: The construction of the torus inverse is postponed to Section 6; the contraction uses only its trajectory estimate, as in Equation (4.22). Neither compactness of the kernel nor the spectral splitting is required again here. This separation allows the same lemma to correct an approximate field that is not recurrent on the torus.

ns-s4-075|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: The residual is the difference between the proposed curve and the mild formula with its own initial value. It is zero at the left endpoint whether or not the curve solves the equation. The sign in Equation (4.17) is negative because the error must cancel this defect; in the piece version this also makes the residual contribution zero at each restart.

ns-s4-076|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: The defect in Equation (4.16) is a mild-equation residual, so its norm is measured after the heat evolution and time integration, in the same space as the velocity error. This is the norm estimated in Lemma 6.2. In the formal sequence setting the analogous local defect is divided by $\theta^n$; its smallness is a bound uniform in $n$.

ns-s4-083|Breakdown.varConstIntegral|1.annotation: The two products have different time dependence: the quadratic product has exponent $2\kappa-1/2$, and the interaction of a bounded field with a $C_0$ field has exponent $-1/4$. On $0<1-t'\le1$ both are bounded by $(1-t')^{\kappa-1/2}$. The common integral (4.18) therefore controls both Equation (4.19) and the cutoff estimate (4.21).

ns-s4-083|Breakdown.PieceOperatorStateme.annotation: On a compact interval the kernel estimate gives the factor $4C_KL^{1/4}$ times two ordinary supremum norms. These norms need not be bounded as the interval approaches time one. Substitution in Equation (4.18) keeps the pointwise time-dependent input powers inside the integral and gives an output bound uniform in the weighted norm.

pdf-item-equation-4-19|Breakdown.PieceOp.annotation: The estimate loses some of the decay of a product of two errors: their product has the power $(1-t')^{2\kappa-1/2}$. In fact Equation (4.18) with $\eta$ in place of $\kappa$ bounds $\mathcal B(v,v')$ in $C_\eta$ whenever $\eta\le2\kappa$ and $0<\eta<1/4$. For the fixed point it is enough to take $\eta=\kappa$, without changing the spectral circle used for the inverse.

ns-s4-086|Breakdown.varConstIntegral|1.annotation: The bounded input in Equation (4.21) need not decay in physical time. In Section 6 it is the difference $\bar u-u^*$, whose ordinary supremum norm is $O(L^{-1/2})$ by Equation (6.4). The other factor is allowed the reference rate in $C_0$. This estimate makes their mixed Duhamel term small in the stronger $C_\kappa$ norm required by the inverse.

ns-s4-088|Breakdown.HeatBilinear|1.annotation: The lag $t-t'$ controls smoothing, while the time to the singularity $1-t'$ controls the size of the inputs. Their relation is $1-t'=(1-t)+(t-t')$. The substitution in Equation (4.18) separates out the current remaining time $1-t$ and leaves a dimensionless integral, whose finiteness is what makes the bound uniform in $t$.

ns-s4-090|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: The lemma assumes a right inverse of the mixed equation about the chosen reference, whether or not the reference is exact. It does not need that reference to be small. In `SeqPerturbation` the analogous given inverse acts on divided pieces, and the residual and prescribed heat input are small together. The hard part on the torus is constructing that inverse (the approximate inverse is built in Lemma 6.3), not proving a second contraction principle.

pdf-item-equation-4-22|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The inverse is applied to trial right-hand sides, and only its second component is iterated. The parameter space $E$ therefore needs no norm in Lemma 4.8. A bound for the parameter is available if the inverse has one, as in Equation (4.8) or the bounded sequence inverse, and is needed for the Lipschitz estimate of the selected datum in Section 5.2.

ns-s4-092|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: Let $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. The radius is $\delta=2C_{\mathcal R}a$, and on this ball the Lipschitz constant of the inverse applied to the quadratic term is at most $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta=4CC_{\mathcal R}^2a$. The square in Equation (4.23) thus comes once from the size of the solution and once from applying the inverse to a difference.

ns-s4-093|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: With $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$, Equation (4.24) gives a trajectory of size at most $2C_{\mathcal R}a$. If the known input vanishes then the selected fixed point is zero. In the formal sequence estimate the bound is $2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$ on the divided pieces; the actual normalized error has the additional factor $\theta^n$.

ns-s4-095|Breakdown.ContractionInternal..annotation: For the generic fixed-point lemma take $b=C_{\mathcal R}a$ and $K=CC_{\mathcal R}$, with $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. Its hypothesis $8Kb\le1$ is exactly Equation (4.23) for $\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$. It gives a fixed point in the closed ball of radius $2b$.

ns-s4-098|Breakdown.ContractionInternal..annotation: Bilinearity gives $\mathcal B(v',v')-\mathcal B(v'',v'')=\mathcal B(v'-v'',v')+\mathcal B(v'',v'-v'')$. Each term contains the difference once and an unchanged factor of norm at most $\delta$. With Equation (4.19) and the bound for the inverse this gives Lipschitz constant $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta\le1/2$.

pdf-item-equation-5-1|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: In Equation (5.1) the product rule gives $\bar u=\chi u^*+\nabla\chi\times A$, with $\chi=\eta(\cdot/r)$; this is the formula of `cutoffField`. Since $|A|\lesssim1$ and $|\nabla\chi|\lesssim r^{-1}$, the correction has the same order $r^{-1}$ as the velocity in the transition annulus. This is why enforcing zero divergence does not increase the order of the mass estimate.

ns5.cutoff.parameter|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The radius is held fixed during each evolution. On $\mathbb R^3$ the cutoff changes only the datum; on the torus it changes the reference at every time. In the latter case $r=L/8$ makes the support a fixed ball, which is why the entire mixed advection in Equation (6.9) is determined by the perturbation restricted to that ball.

pdf-item-equation-5-2|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The paper gives an explicit physical norm estimate for every $r>0$. With remaining time $\ell$ and fixed physical $r$, squaring and changing to similarity variables gives $\|\nabla(f-W)\|_2^2\lesssim\sqrt\ell/r$. `cutoffGradientClose` proves the needed smallness of the squared similarity gradient by an integrable majorant, with a weaker power of $\ell$ in its proof and a fixed physical radius. Its tolerance is a squared norm, not the norm in Equation (5.2).

ns5.correction.error|Breakdown.Contracti.annotation: By Equation (4.24), $\|v\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0$. Undoing the norm weight gives the first bound. The second uses the independently chosen inequality $4C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0\le c_*$, not any improvement of the contraction estimate.

pdf-item-equation-6-2|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The right-hand side in Equation (6.2) is the mass of the tensor, so the local response comparison (6.11) will not need to estimate a derivative of its factors. The formal local comparison uses a supported $L^2$ vector source $A$ and its $L^{3/2}$ norm; there is no need for $A$ itself to be divergence-free. The projection is part of the response being compared.

pdf-item-equation-6-3|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The factor $L$ lost from Equation (6.2) bounds the first moment $\|x\otimes f\|_1$. For the cutoff datum $\bar u(0)$ this estimate gives $L^{-5/2}O(L^2)=O(L^{-1/2})$, while for $\gamma\in E$ it gives $O(L^{-5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1})$ by the common support of $E$. The fixed-datum formal comparison is closer to the latter use.

ns6.cutoff-properties|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: Formula (5.1) also ensures that every mixed convection term involving $\bar u(t)$ is confined to the same ball, even when the perturbation is not compactly supported. The inner equality is used again at the end, for the comparison in Equation (2.6). `approxFieldProperties_holds` gives the corresponding support, inner equality and solenoidality on a centered unit cell.

pdf-item-equation-6-4|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The cutoff error is uniformly bounded in the unweighted gradient norm: on the annulus its squared gradient integral is $O(L^{-4}L^3)$ and beyond it the tail is $O(L^{-1})$. In the comparison of the linearized equations this lets us use Equation (4.21) with one bounded factor. `cutoffGradientClose` instead estimates the squared difference after pulling back to similarity coordinates, uniformly as the remaining time tends to zero.

pdf-item-theorem-6-2|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The equality of gradient norms in Equation (6.5) is exact, since $u^{\mathrm a}$ is one copy of the cutoff in each cell. The formal normalized $H^1$ identity contains a further nonnegative mass term. It can be dropped for the lower bound; the upper bound also needs the separate mass estimate.

pdf-item-equation-6-5|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: After multiplying Equation (6.4) by $(1-t)^{1/4}$, the cutoff contributes at most $CL^{-1/2}(1-t)^{1/4}$ to the error in the normalized profile norm. The estimate (6.5) replaces this by its maximum over time. In `ApproxSizes` the analogous bound is uniform over all normalized pieces.

No heat comparison is used for Equation (6.5). It is an identity of instantaneous gradient norms before and after periodization, followed by comparison with $u^*$. `TransplantNorm` is the identity at scale $\mu$ on the unit torus, with the additional mass term $\mu\|f\|_2^2$ in the normalized squared norm.

ns6.residual-definition|Breakdown.Period.annotation: With two factors of size $(1-t)^{-1/4}$ the convolution in Equation (4.18) would have the same singular order as the background. The subtraction here puts the bounded difference $\bar u-u^*$ into each bilinear term; this gives the gain in Equation (4.21). `ApproxResidualSmall` obtains a gain separately by integrating the differential error over each shrinking interval.

ns6.residual-route|Breakdown.Periodic.Ap.annotation: One cannot periodize $\bar F$ using the compact-support construction of Section 6.1: the heat terms have spread outside the ball. The paper compares their compact inputs. In the formal differential route, `ApproxResidualBound` uses $\bar p=\eta(p^*-p^*(a_*))$ with a fixed annular point $a_*$. The subtraction makes the pressure term in the annulus controllable by the given pressure-gradient decay, regardless of the gauge of $p^*$.

ns6.candidate-inverse|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The local space lets us use the whole-space inverse of Proposition 4.3 without extending the periodic right-hand side to a decaying field. The part of $g$ outside the support ball remains in the periodic equation. `ShellInverseTransfer` makes this separation after summing the free propagation between intervals.

pdf-item-equation-6-7|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: Restriction decreases the gradient integral, and $\|v\|_{L^6(B)}\le\|v\|_{L^6(\mathbb R^3)}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_2$ by Equation (3.1). Both constants are independent of the size of $B$. `RestrictR3Bound` gives the analogous uniform bound for the local values and derivatives.

ns6.forcing-continuity|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: To prove continuity, subtract the two product expressions at times $t$ and $t_0$ and put the difference on one factor at a time. Hölder as in Equation (6.8), with both remaining factors bounded near $t_0<1$, gives convergence in $L^{3/2}$. The local curve need not be differentiable in time. `advectShell` supplies the spatial linear map for a fixed background.

ns6.integral-continuity|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The same endpoint estimate applies in the periodic norm because the heat bound is uniform in $L$. In particular the response is continuous in the full space on the torus, before restricting to $B$. This is needed when $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$ is used to reconstruct $z$ in Equation (6.12).

ns6.weighted-local-integral|Breakdown.Pe.annotation: From Equation (6.8) the source size is bounded by $(1-t\prime)^{\kappa-1/2}\|\zeta\|_\kappa$. Substitution $t-t\prime=(1-t)r$ produces $(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}$ times an integral of $r^{-3/4}(1+r)^{\kappa-1/2}$. Its integrability at infinity requires $\kappa<1/4$. The upper bound on the normalized response in the formal interval construction is obtained using the integrable short-lag kernel and the uniform bound for the background pieces.

pdf-item-equation-6-11|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The integral of $(1-t\prime)^{\kappa-1/4}$ up to time one is finite, so the displayed estimate is actually unweighted in time. Its uniformity over the entire local input space is needed because the input in Equation (6.12) depends on $g$ and on $L$. `ComparisonSmall` compares the propagated response maps for fixed compact approximants as $T$ decreases.

ns6.local-agreement|Breakdown.Periodic.c.annotation: The two local values agree at zero for every input: $v(0)=\gamma$ since $\mathcal A(g|_B)(0)=0$, and $z(0)=g(0)+\Pi_L\gamma$. Hence the defect in Equation (6.13) has zero initial value. The remaining issue is the equality of the local values at positive time, not the matching of the prescribed datum.

pdf-item-equation-6-13|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: In $\mathcal L(\gamma,z)-g$ the two heat curves of $\Pi_L\gamma$ cancel, leaving $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}\zeta-\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}(z|_B)$. In particular Equation (6.10) will give a global operator defect from a local estimate for $\zeta-z|_B$. In `chainOp` the interaction factors as $BR_r$ and the free shift and seed are separate linear maps.

pdf-item-equation-6-14|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Equation (4.8) uses $u^*$ in the mixed term, whereas Equation (6.9) uses $\bar u$. The identity $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)=\mathcal A(v|_B)-2\mathcal B(\bar u-u^*,v)$ gives Equation (6.14) by linearity of $\mathcal A$. The last term is the sole error in the whole-space equation from changing the background; the periodic heat comparison has not yet entered.

ns6.lemma-6-3|Breakdown.Periodic.shellIn.annotation: In `chainOp`, denote the free shift by $S$, the datum response by $G$, the local interaction response by $B$ and restriction by $R_r$. Put $D=(I-S)^{-1}$. If $(e,v)=R_f(Bw)$ for a local source $w$, then $v=D(Ge+B(w+R_rv))$. Thus $\zeta=w+R_rv$ solves $\zeta-R_rDB\zeta-R_rDGe=w$. After changing these two response maps to their periodic counterparts, take $w=R_t(I-S_t)^{-1}g$ and reconstruct $(I-S_t)^{-1}(g+G_te+B_t\zeta)$. This is the reduced equation implicit in Equation (6.12), with the propagation included.

pdf-item-equation-6-15|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Writing $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}g=(\gamma,z)$, Equation (6.15) gives $\|\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\|\le C$ and $\|I-\mathcal L\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\|\le CL^{-1/2}$. These are estimates on different maps. The second gives a series on the right-hand-side space with norm at most two once $L$ is large; the first controls the reconstructed pair. `ShellInverseTransfer` includes this cost and the bounds $(1-q)^{-1}$, where $q=\lambda^{1/4}/\theta$, for eliminating the free shifts.

ns6.defect-local-term|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: In the paper Equation (6.11) applies to the output $\zeta$ of the candidate inverse, although it varies with $L$. In the sequence proof the comparison must be uniform also over the number of intervals. A contribution from piece $m$ to piece $m+j$ has a bound $Cq^j\|\zeta\|$, with $q=\lambda^{1/4}/\theta<1$. The terms with large $j$ have a uniformly small geometric sum. For bounded $j$ one compares the heat responses on bounded lag windows, with the short-lag part estimated separately. This gives the operator norm bound in `ComparisonSmall`.

ns6.defect-free-term|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The support of every $\gamma\in E$ is inside the fixed ball $\bar B_{r_E}$. Therefore the right-hand side in Equation (6.3) is $O(L^{-5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1})$, unlike the cutoff datum in Lemma 6.2. In the formal seed comparison, the fixed-datum heat estimate is applied to a basis of the correction space; the finite basis and the geometric decay of the later propagated seeds give a uniform operator estimate.

pdf-item-equation-6-16|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Put $a=\|F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$ and $K=2C_2$. The quadratic map after applying the exact inverse has Lipschitz constant at most $4CK^2a$ on the ball of radius $2Ka$ by Equation (4.19). The bound $K^2a\le\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$ therefore gives a contraction; the square of the inverse bound comes from the radius and from applying the inverse to a difference. `SeqPerturbation` uses a corresponding sufficient condition including the prescribed datum discrepancy $\xi$.

The last inequality in Equation (6.16) reserves half the normalized lower bound $c_*$: $C_1L^{-1/2}$ is the loss from the cutoff and $4C_1C_2L^{-1/2}$ bounds the correction. This inequality is not used to solve the equation. The formal proof obtains a lower bound for the normalized leading field and needs only the decay of the normalized correction at late joining times to prove unboundedness.

ns6.proposition-2-2-conclusion|Breakdown.annotation: The unit-period datum is smooth and the mild equation is established. The remaining estimates below use the lower and upper bounds in Equation (6.18) and the exact inner-ball agreement of the approximate field. `TorusBlowup` concludes existence of smooth solenoidal data and an unbounded mild $H^1$ curve; the quantitative conclusions are additional in the paper.

ns7-data-s009|Breakdown.Cert.IsPeriodicF.annotation: The Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ is for the terms of the equation, not for the velocity. A velocity with a tail of order $|y|^{-1}$ may belong to $X$ without being in spatial $L^2$. Its Laplacian, linearized convection and the square-integrable combination of time and drift derivatives can nevertheless be elements of $\mathcal H$. This separation is used in the domain defined in Equation (7.4).

ns7-data-s017|Breakdown.IsPerturbation|1.annotation: For a field with a nonzero angular tail $r^{-1}A(y/r)$, the radial integrals for its sixth and second powers at infinity are proportional to $\int_1^\infty r^{-4}\,dr$ and $\int_1^\infty 1\,dr$, respectively. Thus a smooth cutoff of such a tail may have finite homogeneous $H^1$ norm without being in $L^2$. To belong to $\mathcal D_S$ it must in addition satisfy the transport condition in Equation (7.4), as the following example illustrates.

ns7-data-s019|Breakdown.Cert.Internal.Fr.annotation: The energy identity requires values at individual phases, whereas $v\in L^2((0,1);X)$ initially determines a field only almost everywhere in time. The paper obtains a continuous representative by passing to Eulerian variables defined in Equation (7.40) and applying the Hilbert-space energy lemma there. In `exists_energyCurve` Lean instead approximates the free right-hand side $f$ by fields from a dense linear space: the estimate $\sup_\theta\|c_n(\theta)-c_m(\theta)\|_X\le\sqrt{4+6S}\,\|f_n-f_m\|_{\mathcal H}$ gives uniform convergence of the continuous periodic gradient states. The limit is an $X$-valued curve, not merely a continuous scalar energy.

ns7-data-s022|Breakdown.IsPerturbation.i.annotation: In Lean the relation is written with spatial argument $Ry$, so it becomes $v(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=Rv(\theta,y)$. This is Equation (7.5) after changing variables. For the weak perturbation the equality is almost everywhere.

ns7-data-s023|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: When $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$, the field at the next half-period may be different, but the gradient norm is unchanged under the orthogonal change of variables. It is the energy, not the velocity or the supplied residual representative, that can be followed for half a period in Proposition 7.9. Summing the energy increment over two translated intervals gives the improvement by $1/2$ in Equation (7.55). Lean also allows the conservative choice $m=1$ in this case.

ns7-data-s024|Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH.annotation: Writing the time shift with a minus sign in the operator $\rho_{R,\theta_0}$ makes Equation (7.5) precisely the fixed-point condition $\rho_{R,\theta_0}F=F$. Orthogonality of $R$ and translation invariance of the time-circle measure make this an isometry on $\mathcal H$.

ns7-data-s026|Breakdown.Cert.extendedInv.annotation: The residual need not itself be invariant. Nevertheless the other terms in Equation (7.10) are invariant distributions and therefore have invariant pairings with solenoidal tests. Since (7.10) fixes the Leray projection of the residual, $\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ belongs to $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma$. This is what allows the constrained solve to use the given residual.

ns7-data-s027|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The geometry of $K$ will be needed only to make the final parameter update admissible. At a fixed parameter the constrained inverse is constructed without using that geometry. The formal `params` already incorporates the scaled ball and intervals of Equation (7.29).

ns7-data-s028|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The family is chosen to make the eventual force cancellation possible, not merely to interpolate between numerical profiles. In Appendix C.4 the directions $W^i$, with changes in period and in forcing coefficients, are obtained by approximately solving linearized equations with prescribed constraint values. In Equation (B.9) the family is affine in $\alpha$ inside the ball where the radial phase is fixed; outside it, a change of the period also changes the phase. This explains why the construction is not globally affine.

For fixed $\alpha$, $1/S(\alpha)$ is a given coefficient of $\partial_\theta$. A single normalized time circle therefore suffices for the family. The choice following Equation (B.9) makes $1/S(\alpha)$, rather than $S(\alpha)$, affine in $\alpha$; the same variation in the far-field radial phase is needed to cancel the leading transport term in the oscillatory tail in Appendix C.4. No derivative of the unknown exact period is needed in the trial equation.

ns7-data-s029|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: In Equation (7.55) the factors $2S(\alpha)/m$ bound the growth of the slice energy over a period. Using the uniform $S_{\max}$ instead makes Equation (7.27) a single sufficient inequality for all trial parameters.

ns7-data-s030|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: In the limit of the equations (7.57), the two terms in $\mathcal C_\alpha v$ involve $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$. Joint continuity makes these coefficients converge uniformly on the support of each test; the weak gradient and local strong velocity convergence then suffice. In Equation (7.58) integration by parts similarly removes the need for continuity of the Hessian. Lean assumes a $C^1$ extension jointly in the ambient parameter, time and space, stronger than the stated continuity hypotheses.

ns7-data-s031|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Both convection and the free operator preserve the prescribed symmetry. Applied to Equation (7.10), this makes the projected residual invariant, even if the chosen residual representative is not. Later, the same symmetry of the correction and approximate field gives Equation (7.39) for their sum.

The map $\beta\mapsto\sum_i\beta_i b_i$ has operator norm from Euclidean space to $\mathcal H$ at most $(\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}\le b_*$. This estimate does not require orthogonality. In the energy estimate (7.55) the force therefore contributes at most $b_*|\beta|\|v\|_w$. Injectivity of the projected forcing map is a different matter: it follows from Equation (7.18) by taking $v=0$ and $F=0$ if $\sum_i\beta_i b_i\simeq0$.

The force fields $b_i$ are fixed; continuity of $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ therefore gives strong continuity of the finite linear combination in $\mathcal H$. For the residual it will suffice to know continuity after testing modulo gradients, as shown in Equation (7.58).

ns7-data-s031|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The residual is a representative of the left side of Equation (7.10) modulo gradients. In Lean `defect` chooses it by adding `pressureGrad` to the displayed momentum terms and the approximate forcing coefficients. This sum, not each of its terms, must be in $\mathcal H$. With the sign convention of (7.10), the force in the approximate momentum equation is $-\sum_i\beta_i^{\mathrm a}b_i$; the correction has to remove that force as well as the residual.

ns7-data-s032|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: For a fixed $\alpha$, a representative $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ may include a gradient. Its full norm is the bound in Equation (7.23) and in Lean's squared-integral hypothesis. Projection can decrease the norm, but a computation need not find the orthogonal representative in order to supply a sufficient upper bound.

ns7-data-s033|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: A gradient in $\mathcal H$ can be added to $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ without changing the solution of the constrained equation. But the residual-and-constraint budget (7.24) is a bound for a chosen representative: the gradient may change both its norm and the additional row measurements. In contrast, the adjoint pairing in Equation (7.34) is independent of this choice, since the adjoint estimate (7.33) with $v=0$ implies that $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is solenoidal.

ns7-data-s033|Breakdown.Cert.extendedDat.annotation: For the linear solve it is enough that $\alpha\mapsto\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ be weakly continuous. Indeed, in a solenoidal test pairing one can replace the residual by Equation (7.10) and move one derivative off the Laplacian; the remaining profile coefficients converge uniformly on the compact support of the test. By Equation (7.23) the projected residuals are uniformly bounded in $\mathcal H$, so density of the periodized solenoidal tests upgrades the continuity of these pairings to weak continuity. There is no corresponding assertion of norm continuity, or even weak continuity, for an arbitrary choice of unprojected representatives.

ns7-data-s035|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The paper prescribes $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$, while Lean prescribes the value $t(\alpha)$ on the corrected profile. Since $\ell$ is linear, these formulations agree with $\bar\ell(\alpha)=t(\alpha)-\ell(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})$, the quantity `targetGap`. In particular a target of substantial size need not cost much in Equation (7.24) if it is already nearly attained by the approximate profile. When the parameter is fixed, this gap cancels upon subtracting two linear solves.

ns7-data-s036|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: At a fixed parameter the free inverse identifies $f=\mathcal T_Sv$ with $v$. The predicate `IsHeldSolution` states that the resulting velocity solves the nonlinear constrained equation and obeys the pair and slice-gradient bounds. It still allows a nonzero total force; cancellation is the additional conclusion of Proposition 7.10. Its finite-dimensional coefficient variable is normalized to $\omega\beta$, with the forcing fields divided by $\omega$.

ns7-data-s036|Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvec.annotation:
Expanding the convection of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ gives the approximate convection, the mixed terms $(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $(v\cdot
abla)v$. The first two mixed terms form the linear operator $\mathcal C_\alpha$ in Equation (7.13), so the only unknown nonlinear right-hand side in a trial solve is $-(v\cdot
abla)v$.

ns7-data-s037|Breakdown.Cert.extendedHel.annotation: At each parameter the residual cancels on adding Equations (7.10) and (7.12), but the force in the equation for $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ is still $-\sum_i(\beta_i^{\mathrm a}+\beta_i)b_i$. Thus neither solving the correction equation nor finding a small $\beta$ gives an unforced profile. The last step must cancel the total coefficients, including those already present in the approximate equation.

ns7-data-s040|Breakdown.weightedEnergy|1.annotation: The norm is chosen for two different estimates. Control of $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ in the period integral gives $\|v(\theta)\|_\infty\le c_w|v(\theta)|_w$ almost everywhere in time. To integrate the product $|v||\nabla v|$ in $L^2$ one also needs a bound for the maximum of the gradient norm; controlling just the two period integrals would not give this product estimate. The latter bound comes from Equation (7.22), not from Equation (7.18) alone.

ns7-data-s041|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The coefficient weight trades velocity allowance against force allowance in the same estimate. At a fixed pair radius, $\omega|\beta|\le2\varepsilon$ gives the crude force bound used outside $\mathcal J$. Increasing $\omega$ changes the inverse bound (7.18) that must be verified; it cannot be done merely to make the complementary-ball enclosure (7.37) easier.

ns7-data-s042|Breakdown.weightedEnergy|1.annotation: The two terms of the weighted norm are used differently. The Laplacian is paired with the right-hand side in the slice energy identity (7.42), so $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}\le\|v\|_w$. The gradient term gives $\int_0^1\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2\,d\theta\le\|v\|_w^2/w_*$, the bound for the minimum slice energy.

ns7-data-s042|Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ|3.annotation: Set $\widehat\beta=\omega\beta$ and $\widehat b_i=b_i/\omega$. The force is unchanged, and the norm now has coefficient weight one. To preserve the parameter update (7.30) one must also replace $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ by $\omega\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $V_j$ by $V_j/\omega$. The bound $b_*$ scales by $1/\omega$, as does $\langle b,\psi_j\rangle-V_j$. Thus the normalization leaves both the physical forcing and the parameter enclosure unchanged.

ns7-data-s042|Breakdown.supBoundFactor|4.annotation: Xie's inequality bounds $\|u\|_\infty^2$ by $(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$. Apply $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ with $a=\|\Delta u\|_2$, $b=\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_2$: the resulting coefficient is $1/(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})=c_w^2$. This explains the square root in the definition of $c_w$, the constant in the weighted supremum bound (7.48).

ns7-data-s044|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation:
Lemma B.9 separates the difference into $Z_0=W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and $Z_1=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$. The transport term is bounded by $(\|Z_0\|_\infty+\|Z_1\|_\infty)\|
abla u\|_2$ at each phase; for the other term use $\|u\|_\infty\|
abla Z_0\|_2$ and $\|u\|_6\|
abla Z_1\|_3$, with operator norms on the coefficient gradients. All three are bounded by constants times $|u|_w$. Squaring and integrating the resulting slice bound gives Equation (7.19).

ns7-data-s045|Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvec.annotation: The map $W\mapsto\mathcal C_Wv$ is linear in $W$ at fixed $v$. Therefore replacing $W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$ by $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ adds $(D\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)D$, where $D=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$. Both terms must be controlled in Equation (7.19).

ns7-data-s046|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: For fixed constraint values the right-hand side has two different costs. If $F$ is orthogonal to all the $e_k$, its cost in Equation (7.18) is $c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$; in the worst case it is $(c_1+c_0)\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. Thus a large inverse response in a few directions need not impose that same large constant on every right-hand side. In Appendix B the additional measurements arise from a finite-dimensional estimate of the lower quadratic form; the error components not measured by the rows still have to be controlled.

ns7-data-s047|Breakdown.rowNorm|1.annotation: In Lean the row fields are orthonormal and carry weights $\tau_k\ge0$. The paper's fields $e_k$ correspond to $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ times these unit fields; hence $\tau_k\le c_0^2$ gives exactly the length bound in Equation (7.17). A zero weight removes that row from the seminorm.

ns7-data-s048|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Lean assumes $c_2\ge0$ explicitly, while Equation (7.18) allows real $c_2$. In fact, once Proposition 7.8 is proved and $n>0$, one may solve the transferred linear equation with $F=0$ and any nonzero constraint value. Inequality (7.52) then forces $c_2>0$. When $n=0$ the constraint term vanishes and its sign is immaterial.

ns7-data-s050|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Projection decreases the norm of $F$ but not necessarily its row measurements. For example let $p$ be a unit solenoidal field, $q$ an orthogonal unit gradient, $F=p-q$ and $e_1=(p+q)/\sqrt2$. Then $[F]=0$ but $[\mathbb PF]=1/\sqrt2$. Thus the two terms of Equation (7.18) should be evaluated for the same chosen representative; one cannot replace each independently by its projected value.

The inverse estimate may use the full representative $F$. The adjoint estimate has an additional consequence: putting $v=0$ in Equation (7.33) makes every gradient $F\in\mathcal H$ invisible to $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Consequently its pairing depends only on the projected residual, even when the finite row measurements in Equation (7.17) do not.

ns7-data-s051|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The constant $c_L$ estimates a linear solve with zero constraint values, or the difference of two solves at the same parameter with equal constraint values. It need not estimate the entire response with prescribed nonzero constraints. This is why it controls the nonlinear iteration, whereas Equation (7.24) uses $c_1$, $\delta_0$ and $c_2$ separately.

ns7-data-s053|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: After transfer, the inverse bound has the same form as Equation (7.18), with $c_1,c_2$ and the row seminorm divided by $1-\vartheta$. In the formal data this means dividing the row weights by $(1-\vartheta)^2$, since the seminorm takes a square root, and dividing both the row bound and the residual row allowance by $1-\vartheta$. The reference field is then set equal to the approximate field; the frozen-form bound is transferred separately.

ns7-data-s054|Breakdown.weightedEnergy|1.annotation: An integral bound alone can be compatible with very large values on a short interval. Let $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$. The bound $\min E\le\|v\|_w^2/w_*$ supplies a starting value, and Equation (7.22) bounds the increase of $E$ from this value. Integrating the differential inequality, rather than estimating a time derivative separately, is what supplies the maximum needed in Equation (7.49).

ns7-data-s054|Breakdown.Cert.ProductBoun.annotation:
For different fields $v,z$, the pointwise inequality $|(v\cdot
abla)z|\le |v||
abla z|$ and Equation (7.48) give $\|(v\cdot
abla)z\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_w\|v\|_w\sup_	heta\|
abla z(	heta)\|_2$. In particular the weighted norm always estimates the undifferentiated factor and the time supremum estimates the differentiated one. The same bound will be used on each of the two products in a difference of quadratic terms.

ns7-data-s055|Breakdown.Cert.Internal.Ex.annotation:
The positive gradient term in Equation (7.22) comes from the similarity drift, not from an additional dissipation assumption. For a compactly supported smooth $u$, $
abla((y\cdot
abla)u)=
abla u+(y\cdot
