abla)
abla u$, so pairing $(y\cdot
abla)u$ with $-\Delta u$ gives $(1-3/2)\|
abla u\|_2^2$. Half this value, together with the zeroth-order term, gives $ rac14\|
abla u\|_2^2$. Lemma 7.4 proves the interval identity on $\mathcal D_S$ without requiring the drift separately to be square integrable. The remaining contribution to the form is diffusion and the convection at the chosen phase.

ns7-data-s056|Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedSup.annotation: Write $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$ and $Q_\alpha(\theta,v)$ for the left side of Equation (7.22). With right-hand side $F$ in the linear problem, the slice energy identity (7.42) gives $E'/(2S)=-Q_\alpha(\theta,v)+\langle F-\sum_i\beta_i b_i,-\Delta v\rangle_{L^2}$. The upper bound on $E'$ is integrable even without control of the separate time derivative of $v$. Start at a minimum of $E$, bounded by $\|v\|_w^2/w_*$. Sum the increments over $m$ translates by $1/m$, which have the same energy increment but disjoint integration intervals. The bound over one period divided by $m$ gives the slice-gradient bound (7.55), even for a residual representative without the shorter period.

ns7-data-s060|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: In the paper the inequality says that the linear response to a trial quadratic term of norm $2c_w\varepsilon M$ fits in the radius $\varepsilon$ left by the residual. Strictness is not needed for that inclusion alone. It matters for the formal fixed-parameter contraction: the difference of two quadratic terms has two products, and Equation (7.26) controls the scaled gradient supremum of the output difference. The resulting contraction constant is $2c_Lc_wM$, not a constant involving the derivative of the parameter update.

Subtract two solves at the same parameter and let $h$ be the difference of their right-hand sides. The constraints and the approximate residual disappear, and the pair norm of the difference is at most $r=c_L\|h\|_{\mathcal H}$. Substitution in Equation (7.55), with $|\beta_{\rm diff}|\le r/\omega$, gives $\sup E_{\rm diff}\le Ar^2$, where $A=1/w_*+(2S_{\max}/m)(c_3+b_*/\omega+1/c_L)$ is the bracket in Equation (7.26). Hence $(2\varepsilon/M)\sup\|\nabla v_{\rm diff}\|_2\le r$. Lean needs this estimate to contract in both norms; the joint Schauder proof does not.

This inequality is for one solve rather than the difference of two. With $F=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$ and the pair bound $2\varepsilon$, the right side of Equation (7.55) is bounded by $4\varepsilon^2(1/w_*+2S_{\max}c_3/m)+(4S_{\max}\varepsilon/m)(\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2\varepsilon b_*/\omega)$. Thus Equation (7.27) supplies the slice-gradient bound $M$ for the output, including the effect of the approximate residual. This is distinct from the role of Equation (7.26) for differences.

ns7-data-s061|Breakdown.Cert.extendedHel.annotation:
Measure a difference of pairs by $D=\max\{\|(x-y, eta_x- eta_y)\|_{w,\omega},(2\varepsilon/M)\sup_	heta\|
abla(x-y)(	heta)\|_2\}$. In the convection difference, $((x-y)\cdot
abla)x$ costs at most $c_wMD$ and $(y\cdot
abla)(x-y)$ costs at most the same, since $\|y\|_w\le2\varepsilon$. The inverse and Equation (7.26) bound both output components of $D$ by $c_L$ times the forcing difference. Hence the contraction factor is $2c_Lc_wM<1$.

ns7-data-s065|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The columns $V_j$ are the directions in which the total coefficient vector is tested. They need not coincide with the forcing fields or be orthogonal. In particular $V_j$ can be chosen close to the vector of adjoint pairings in Equation (7.31). Their linear independence is needed at the end: if every tested component vanishes, then $V^{\mathsf T}(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)=0$ implies $\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta=0$.

ns7-data-s068|Breakdown.Held.testSetZero.annotation: The condition required of a nonlinear solution at $\alpha$ is $\alpha'\in K$, not merely that its force be small. In one dimension, a projected update from $\alpha=1$ to $\alpha'=2$ on $K=[-1,1]$ has a fixed point at $1$, even though the change is nonzero. The enclosure inequalities (see Equation (7.61)) exclude this possibility: at a fixed point the projection acts on a point already in $K$, hence $\alpha'=\alpha$.

ns7-data-s070|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The exact model for $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is a row of the inverse of the constrained linear problem, not an adjoint eigenfunction. At fixed $\alpha$, the linear inverse sends $(\mathbb PF,\ell)$ to $(v,\beta)$; by Equation (7.52) its coefficient functional $V_j\cdot\beta$ is bounded. Its Hilbert-space representation is $V_j\cdot\beta=\langle F,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y\ell)_j$ with solenoidal $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Testing first on $v=0$, then on $\beta=0$, gives the ideal forms of Equations (7.31) and (7.33). The certificate uses approximate representatives of these rows and additionally requires control of their nonlinear pairings.

ns7-data-s071|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The measurement vector $\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ can vary with $\alpha$, while $V_j$ in the parameter update is fixed. Define $E_j$ to be their difference. Replacing the measured scalar by $V_j\cdot\beta$ introduces $\beta\cdot E_j$, bounded by $|E_j|\,\omega|\beta|/\omega$ as in Equation (7.35).

ns7-data-s072|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Here one needs only a scalar pairing, not the full $\mathcal H$ norm of the quadratic term. For example a uniform slice bound $\|\psi_{\alpha,j}(\theta)\|_2\le n_j$ gives $|\langle(v\cdot\nabla)v,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}|\le n_jc_w\|v\|_w^2/\sqrt{w_*}$, by applying Equation (7.48) and the gradient bound at each phase and then integrating. Lemma B.10 also gives an alternative using the slice $L^3$ norm. Neither estimate pays for the gradient supremum $M$, which is needed for the full norm of convection.

sec7-nonlinear-058|Breakdown.FarField.De.annotation: The extra pressure-gradient bound in `DecayBounds` needs more than the velocity derivative estimates of Remark 1.2. The formal argument takes the divergence of Equation (1.2), giving $-\Delta q=\sum_{i,j}\partial_i\partial_j(W_iW_j)$. In the Newton potential for $\nabla q$, away from the kernel singularity, two integrations by parts move the two derivatives onto the cut-off kernel. The second derivatives of this cut-off gradient kernel are bounded uniformly by $O(r^{-4})$, where $r=\max(1,|y|)$, and $\int_{|z|<2r}|W(z)|^2dz=O(r)$, giving $O(r^{-3})$ for this part. The complementary tail and the local source give the same bound; the square-integrability of $\nabla q$ is used to identify it with the Newton field.

ac-017|Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBou.annotation: The mean of $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ vanishes: as a periodic distribution it is $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$, whose integral is its pairing with the constant test. Thus Equation (3.19) applies to both advections in Equation (3.17). Hölder with Equation (3.18) bounds their $L^{3/2}$ norms by a constant times $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\|v\|_{\dot H^1}$, independent of $L$. The linked bound is in the unit-torus inhomogeneous norm for lags at most one.

ns7-data-s004|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Appendix B proves the inverse estimate by combining two inequalities. In Equations (B.20) and (B.21) the integrals of the mode density and the stretching term, as well as the pairing of the unknown force with $\mathsf Mv$, disappear when the inequalities are combined. Lemma B.2 then has the scalar form $P^2\le c_M\|F\|_{\mathcal H}P+Q^2$, with $P^2$ containing $\frac3{50}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}^2$ and $Q^2=\frac3{50}[F]^2+1000|\ell(v)|^2$. Bounding the positive root by $c_M\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+Q$ and using $\sqrt{3/50}\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le P$ gives Equation (7.18). The cell computations thus bound an inverse on the full domain, not the smallest singular value of the discretization alone.

Lemma B.9 estimates the change $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$ in the convection operator by $c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$. Applying the reference estimate to $F-G$ costs at most $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ in addition to the cost of $F$. Hence Equation (7.21) makes the extra cost absorbable into the left side of Equation (7.52).

The transfer of the frozen form is a second use of the same convection difference. If $G(u)=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})u$ at a phase, the change in the form is $-\langle G(u),\Delta u\rangle_{L^2}$. Lemma B.9 controls this pairing from below; its contribution adds to the reference lower-bound constant rather than being absorbed as in Equation (7.52). This gives the constant $c_3$ for the energy-growth estimate.

b12-rotation-coordinate|Breakdown.axialR.annotation: At $r>0$, the frame at $R_{\phi_0}y$ is the image under $R_{\phi_0}$ of the frame at $y$. Thus $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta,R_{\phi_0}y)$ has the cylindrical components of $v$ at the shifted angle, expressed in the frame at $y$. This is the operation averaged in Equation (B.12); averaging the Cartesian components without that rotation would give different mode labels.

b12-two-generators|Breakdown.CertCell.In.annotation: To prove invariance of a represented field, it suffices to prove the identities for the two pairs in Equation (B.1). The identity for a product follows by applying the two identities successively; period one accounts for the remaining integer time translation. This is the use of the generation condition, as opposed to membership of the two pairs, which is sufficient for restricting the modes of an already invariant perturbation.

pdf-item-equation-B-2|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The integer lattice may be read in terms of the two traveling phases of Appendix C.1: with $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$ and $m$ the angular integer, the phase change under the combined shift is $\pi(j+m/k)=2\pi\iota_2$, where $k$ is the angular order. In particular a purely time-dependent mode has even $j$, but a mode with odd $m/k$ must have odd $j$.

b12-harmonic-parity|Breakdown.CertCell.l.annotation: Under the simultaneous half-period and half-angle shifts, the scalar phase acquires the factor $e^{i\pi(j+j'/k_{\mathrm{rot}})}$. It is one precisely for the lattice (B.2). Thus Equation (B.12) can project onto that lattice without a Fourier truncation of the unknown perturbation.

b12-first-symmetry|Breakdown.CertCell.Gi.annotation: The scalar components are unchanged under the combined shift, whereas the cylindrical frame rotates by the angle of the generator. Reassembling the components gives precisely the vector transformation in Equation (7.5). The linked theorem proves it for the admissible fields Equation (B.6), including points on the axis.

b12-label-reflection|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The time integer $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ is unchanged by $\iota^\flat$, whereas the angular integer is negated. In particular the two travelling families $\iota_2=0$ and $\iota_2=\iota_1$ of Appendix C.1 are exchanged. Applying the map twice gives the original label. Conjugation instead negates both integers (and, in Equation (B.5), the radial index).

pdf-item-equation-B-3|Breakdown.CellCert.annotation: The value assigned to $\eta$ at the origin is only a convention for the total coordinate function. Limits taken along different rays still give different height ratios; the amplitude factors in Equations (B.7) and (B.8) must remove this dependence when the full velocity is assembled.

b12-weighted-unit-vectors|Breakdown.Cell.annotation: Near a nonzero point of the axis, the factor $r/R$ in the length of $\mathbf p$ removes the singular unit polar vector. In Equation (B.8) this allows the axisymmetric radial amplitude $u_0$ to be nonzero on the axis while the tangential amplitude contributes zero there. The nonaxisymmetric construction instead makes all three amplitudes vanish to fourth order in $r$.

Since $|e_z\times y|=r$, the length of $\mathbf a$ is $r/|y|=(1-\eta^2)^{1/2}$ away from zero. The amplitude multiplying it in Equation (B.8) can therefore describe an axisymmetric swirl without a singular unit vector on the axis.

b12-phase-condition|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: For $R=|y|$, the first two radial derivatives of $f(R^2)$ are $2Rf'(R^2)$ and $2f'(R^2)+4R^2f''(R^2)$, of orders $R^{-1}$ and $R^{-2}$ at infinity; the third is of order $R^{-3}$. The third derivative is needed because Equations (B.7) and (B.8) already differentiate the phase once in the velocity amplitudes, before the equation differentiates the velocity twice. A bound on the phase itself is unnecessary.

pdf-item-equation-B-5|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: For a fixed $\iota$, all the indices $l$ have the same factor $E_\iota(\theta,\phi)$. Their amplitudes, multiplied by $e^{ilf(R^2)}$, add before any norm of $\hat v_\iota$ is taken. The orthogonality used in Appendix B.2 is in $\iota$, not in the radial phase index $l$.

pdf-item-equation-B-6|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The divergence calculation is performed on the complex summand, before taking its real part. In Equation (B.7) the azimuthal derivative cancels the divergence of the meridian components; in Equation (B.8) the meridian components already have zero divergence. Thus changing the coefficients within the admissible amplitude spaces preserves solenoidality without a further linear constraint in the numerical solve.

The finite list of keys and the two scalar splines for each key determine a field by Equations (B.6)–(B.8). The data predicate imposes the further conditions on the exponents, joins, origin values and paired keys. It is these conditions, not the finite-sum formula alone, that give a periodic solenoidal $C^1$ field with the stated decay.

b12-finite-mode-data|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: For each nonzero angular integer the two free splines prescribe the radial and polar amplitudes, and the angular amplitude is obtained by dividing the meridian divergence by the angular derivative in Equation (B.7). At angular integer zero this division is unavailable: one instead prescribes a stream function and a swirl, with the extra origin coefficient in the stream function. These are the independent coefficients of the velocity representation.

b12-zero-stream|Breakdown.CertCell.Given.annotation: For $\iota_1=0$ an azimuthal velocity has zero divergence regardless of its radial and height dependence, so it cannot be used to cancel the divergence of the other two components. Instead Equation (B.8) imposes the cancellation between those components by a stream function, and leaves the swirl free.

b12-origin-function|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: At an interior join $\sigma_g$ the polynomial must have zero first and second derivatives, since it is followed by a constant. This ensures two derivatives of $g$ agree there: $u_1$ in Equation (B.8) already contains one radial derivative of $g$.

b12-field-data-description|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: Changing $f$ leaves the spline data unchanged, but it changes two places in the field: the scalar factor $E_{\iota,l}$ and the radial derivative $\mathcal V_l$ used to construct the dependent amplitudes. The latter change is essential for retaining the divergence identity when the phase is varied in Equation (B.9).

adapted.N5-20.1|Breakdown.CertCell.Given.annotation: The traces to be matched along a spline edge are polynomials in the tangential variable. Equality of these polynomials implies equality of their tangential derivatives, so matching the indicated normal derivatives also matches the mixed derivatives required after applying $\mathcal V_l$ or $\partial_\eta$. This is why the free splines in Equations (B.7) and (B.8) need different join orders.

b12-conjugation|Breakdown.CertCell.Given.annotation: Conjugation negates the radial index as well as the harmonic label, so that $\overline{\mathcal V_l u}=\mathcal V_{-l}\overline u$. In Equation (B.7) the simultaneous negation of the azimuthal integer conjugates the purely imaginary prefactor of $u_2$ as well. The two constructed vector terms are thus conjugate, and a pair of distinct keys contributes twice the real part of one term.

b12-reflection-data|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: Write $D_l=\mathcal V_l+2$ and $L_\eta u=\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)u)$. Under the half-turn $u_0$ is reflected without a sign and $u_1$ with a minus sign, so $D_lu_0-L_\eta u_1$ is reflected without a sign. The angular integer changes sign, giving the required minus sign of $u_2$ in Equation (B.7). In Equation (B.8) the stream function and swirl are odd in $\eta$, which yields the same vector transformation.

b12-axis-factors|Breakdown.CertCell.Give.annotation: The factor in $u_1$ is $(1-\eta^2)^2$, so the height derivative in Equation (B.7) differentiates a factor $(1-\eta^2)^3$ and leaves at least $(1-\eta^2)^2$. Thus the dependent amplitude has the same fourth-order vanishing in $r$ as the free amplitudes at a nonzero point of the axis. At the origin the common factor $\sigma^{h_0}$ persists as well, since $\mathcal V_l$ uses the scaled derivative $R\partial_R$.

b12-axis-zero-mode|Breakdown.CellCert.Gi.annotation: Write $R=|y|$. Since $\sigma=R/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$, Equation (B.8) gives $u_0=\gamma R(3\eta^2-1)/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$ and $u_1=-3\gamma R\eta/\mathsf L+O(R^2)$. Substitution of $\mathbf p=\eta y/R-e_z$ cancels the two terms proportional to $3\eta^2y$. The remaining vector is $-(\gamma/\mathsf L)(y_1,y_2,-2y_3)$, to be multiplied by the phase at zero. In particular the linear term is independent of the direction used to approach zero.

b12-decay-one|Breakdown.CellReduction.In.annotation: The order-one tail is compatible with the homogeneous energy space: $R^{-1}\in L^6(R>1)$, $R^{-2}\in L^2(R>1)$ and $R^{-3}\in L^2(R>1)$. It need not be in $L^2$ itself. For the residual, the combination $S^{-1}\partial_\theta W+W/2+(y\cdot\nabla)W/2$ must also be in $\mathcal H$; order-one decay alone does not establish this. The phase choice in Subsections C.1 and C.4 cancels the leading transport of the oscillatory tail.

b12-profile-dependence|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: The field has two parameter dependences: the explicitly affine sum of coefficients and the common change of phase. For a key with radial index $l$ the latter gives a factor $e^{il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)f_*}$ and changes the dependent amplitude through $\mathcal V_l$. Both changes vanish on the cutoff ball, allowing the exact polynomial residual expansion in Equation (B.57). Outside, even the field indexed by $0$ depends on the parameter.

b12-phase-cutoff|Breakdown.CellReduction.annotation: The cutoff is identically zero near the lower endpoint of the integral, where $d\rho/\rho$ would be singular. Near infinity the integrand is exactly $d\rho/\rho$. The $C^2$ join of $\chi$ gives a $C^3$ radial phase, including at the transition radii, as required for differentiating Equations (B.7) and (B.8) twice in space.

pdf-item-equation-B-9|Breakdown.CellRedu.annotation: The function $f_*$ allows the logarithmic slope of the radial phase at infinity to change while leaving the field on the interior ball unaffected by the phase change. Thus the same parameter can enter the interior residual polynomially and alter the leading similarity transport of an oscillating tail. The split between these two calculations is used in Appendix B.4.

For $R\le r_\chi$, the whole interval $0\le\rho\le R$ in Equation (B.9) has $\rho/(\rho+\mathsf L)\le\sigma_\chi$. Not only is the integral zero, but its radial derivatives vanish at the transition as well, to the orders implied by $\chi\in C^2$. This matters because $\mathcal V_l$ in the velocity formulas differentiates the phase.

Beyond the last transition of $\chi$, the difference $f_*(R^2)-\log R$ has zero derivative in $R$. The resulting addition to the phase changes its logarithmic slope by $\mathsf k\cdot\alpha$, while leaving the power $(1-\sigma)^h$ unchanged (see Appendix C.4 for the phase–period compatibility condition when the leading tail oscillates). In the squared-radius variable the tail is $\tfrac12\log\rho+C$.

b12-period-affine|Breakdown.CellReductio.annotation: The operator $\mathcal T_S$ contains $S^{-1}\partial_\theta$, so affine dependence of $S^{-1}$ makes this part of the interior residual a quadratic polynomial in $\alpha$. Affine dependence of $S$ itself would introduce a denominator. In the exterior the matching change of the logarithmic radial phase cancels the leading time and similarity transport terms as in Appendix C.4.

adapted.N5-22.1|Breakdown.CellReduction..annotation: `PressureShapeEntry.pressure` represents the scalar pressure by a center plus parameter-weighted tangent pressures, all evaluated using the phase data at the chosen parameter. The shift by half the squared speed in this passage is the paper's convention for the residual in the curl formulation of Equation (C.1); the definition evaluates the represented pressure and does not itself establish the pressure-shift identity.

b12-forcing-data|Breakdown.CertCell.Give.annotation: Multiplying an arbitrary solenoidal field by a scalar cutoff would produce the extra divergence $\nabla\chi\cdot b$. Here support is imposed instead on the free amplitude splines before Equations (B.7) and (B.8) construct the dependent components. With the zero origin coefficient the field is compactly supported and the divergence cancellation is unchanged.

b12-forcing-smooth|Breakdown.CertCell.Gi.annotation: The support is imposed on the free splines, not by multiplying the resulting field by a discontinuous characteristic function. At the last support sphere their joined traces also vanish to the orders required in Equations (B.7) and (B.8). This is consistent with the global $C^1$ assertion for $b_i$ even at that sphere.

b12-forcing-divergence|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: No projection is needed to make the represented force divergence-free: each harmonic is constructed by Equations (B.7) or (B.8), and the divergence of each term vanishes under the shape hypotheses. The cutoff is built into the amplitudes, rather than applied afterwards to a solenoidal vector field.

b12-forcing-support|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: The last possible nonzero radial coordinate is $\sigma_i$, whose inverse image is the sphere of radius $\mathsf L_i\sigma_i/(1-\sigma_i)$. All terms, including the origin term, are zero beyond it: the free polynomials vanish there, and $\gamma=0$. The meridian square in Appendix B.3 encloses this ball, so no forcing term is omitted in treating the complement.

b12-adjoint-data|Breakdown.CellReduction.annotation: The choice $h\ge3$ makes $\psi_j$ itself square integrable over the period, since its square is $O(R^{-6})$, and $y\cdot\nabla\psi_j$ has the same decay. In Equation (7.33) the period and linearized operator can vary with $\alpha$ even though the field used to test the equation is fixed. The error in the adjoint equation is accordingly estimated uniformly.

b12-adjoint-rows|Breakdown.CellReduction.annotation: The adjoint conditions of Equations (7.32)–(7.34) use only $j\in\mathcal J$. For those rows the stored entries are the same for every parameter; the approximate adjoint fields are fixed as well. These identities specify the chosen rows, not the invertibility of the matrix appearing in the parameter argument.

b12-mesh-cover|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenS.annotation: The square contains the meridian image of each actuator support ball: $|y|<r_*$ implies $r<r_*$ and $|z|<r_*$. Thus no actuator remains in the exterior region used in Appendix B.3. The support condition and the disjoint-interior mesh coverage are separate hypotheses.

pdf-item-equation-B-10|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Write $G=\nabla v$ as the linear map $G e_a=(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$. Then $\langle e_b\otimes e_a,G\rangle=e_b\cdot G e_a$. In the Lean `frameMap`, $x_{ab}$ multiplies $e_a\otimes e_b$; hence the polynomial in Equation (B.10) with indices $(a,b)$ corresponds to the stored entry $(b,a)$. With this convention the assembled tensor gives exactly the pairing in Equation (7.11).

b12-tensor-support|Breakdown.CertCell.Ce.annotation: The cell boundaries can be assigned values without affecting the integral in Equation (B.10), since they have zero volume. The test tensor is bounded with bounded support, so it belongs to $\mathcal H$; the linear constraint only uses the weak first derivative of $v$.

b12-phi-error|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Ad.annotation: For a vector $x$ of coefficients, the error in the combined constraint is $\langle\nabla v,\sum_i x_i(\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. It is bounded by $c_\Xi |x|\|v\|_w/\sqrt{w_*}$. In Lemma B.12 one uses $x=(Y_{ji})_i$; hence the whole rounding error costs $\mathsf n_Y c_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$ in Equation (B.53), without a factor counting the constraints. The separate replacement of $\Phi_i$ by a solenoidal field is estimated there in a different norm.

b12-row-polynomial-data|Breakdown.CertCe.annotation: For a fixed cell and label, if the polynomial triples are $\varphi_j$ and their Hermitian Gram matrix is $H$, then $c^*Hc=\int_Q|\sum_j c_j\varphi_j|^2r\,dr\,dz$. Positivity means that no nonzero linear combination vanishes in this integral. This is the independence needed for Equation (B.11), not an assumption that the triples are already orthogonal.

b12-row-divergence|Breakdown.CertCell.In.annotation: The polynomial identity is the cylindrical divergence equation after multiplication by $r$: the derivative in the azimuthal direction contributes $ik_{\mathrm{rot}}\iota_1\varphi_\phi$. This is a local condition; zero extension across a cell face need not preserve distributional divergence. The row tests in Equation (7.17) belong to $\mathcal H$, not necessarily $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{div}}$.

pdf-item-equation-B-11|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The two factors in Equation (B.11) serve different purposes: $G^{-1/2}$ changes coordinates to an orthonormal basis of the row space, while $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ determines how strongly the corresponding component of $F$ is measured. The implementation stores the unit row and the weight separately.

With $c=3/50$, `testWeight` stores $c\tau_k$ and `rowWeightOf` divides it by $c$, giving the weight $\tau_k$ in Equation (7.17). For one block of common weight $\tau$, if $m$ denotes the pairings with the real generators and $G$ their Gram matrix, its contribution to $[F]^2$ is $\tau m^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}m=\tau\|P_E F\|_{\mathcal H}^2$, where $E$ is their span. This also explains why the local row matrices in Appendix B.3 can use the original polynomial generators.

The local Hermitian Gram matrices establish independence of the real generators after reflection. The linked orthonormality theorem takes positive definiteness of the full real Gram matrix as a hypothesis and applies the inverse-square-root identity to that matrix. It gives unit rows; multiplication by $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ in Equation (B.11) is a separate operation.

b12-row-cap|Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.annotation: The bound $400(1+2^{-18})$ applies to `testWeight`, namely $c\tau_k$ for $c=3/50$, because the form in Equation (B.21) contains $c[F]^2$. Dividing by $c$ gives the bound on `rowWeightOf`, the squared length of the corresponding paper row $e_k$. Confusing these two weights would lose the factor $50/3$ in Equation (B.22).

b12-row-orthogonality|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: It is precisely orthogonality, not just the bound on each row, that yields $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$ in Equation (7.17). In the unit-row convention this follows by pulling the largest $\tau_k$ out of the sum of squared pairings and applying Bessel's inequality.

adapted.N5-15.1|Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.e.annotation: The coefficient energy enters from Equation (B.21), not from the construction of the multiplier. This distinction is important for the bordered problem of Section 7: a bound for $v$ alone would leave the force coefficients uncontrolled. The assembled estimate controls the pair $(v,\beta)$ in the norm (7.14).

pdf-item-equation-B-12|Breakdown.modeVel.annotation: At a fixed $(r,z)$, write the velocity in the cylindrical frame. The components of $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta+\theta_0,R_{\phi_0}y)$ in the frame at $y$ are precisely those of $v$ at the shifted time and angle. Thus Equation (B.12) is ordinary Fourier projection of those three component functions; the radial and height arguments are untouched. The conjugate exponential in the average selects the stated label.

b12-harmonic-support|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: Applying the half-period generator twice gives invariance under rotation through twice the angle of the generator. This restricts the ordinary angular frequencies to multiples of the rotation order. One application then imposes the parity condition in Equation (B.2). These identities hold also for the weak derivative tensors, with the rotation acting on their derivative indices. This removes forbidden Fourier labels, not the large allowed ones.

pdf-item-equation-B-13|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: For a fixed $r,z$, Equation (B.13) gives $\hat v_\iota(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))=E_\iota(\theta,\phi)R_\phi\hat v_\iota(0,(r,0,z))$. The gradient and Hessian transform by rotating their values and inversely rotating their arguments. Thus all five squared norms in Equation (B.16) are independent of time and angle, and their space-time integrals reduce to $2\pi\int |\cdot|^2 r\,dr\,dz$. The products in $J$ do not separately have this property; their time and angle mean is formed in Appendix B.3.

pdf-item-equation-B-15|Breakdown.PieceWe.annotation: If the rotating coordinate advances by $\nu s$, substitution into the scalar phase $2\pi j s/S+j'\phi$ gives $\Omega=2\pi j/S+\nu j'$. The change of vector frame also contributes a rotation term to the equation, treated separately among the losses. In Lean `frameFreq` takes the ordinary integer pair $(j,j')$, obtained from Equation (B.2), rather than the indices $\iota$ themselves.

pdf-item-equation-B-18|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation:
Put $\omega_v=\operatorname{curl}v$ and $\omega_r=\operatorname{curl}W^{\mathrm r}$. In the curl of the linearized convection, $W^{\mathrm r}\cdot
abla\omega_v$ integrates to zero against $\omega_v$; the other three terms give $J$. In particular, for $A=\omega_r\cdot
abla$, integration by parts (using $\operatorname{div}\omega_r=0$ and self-adjointness of curl) gives $-\langle Av,\operatorname{curl}vangle=-	frac12\langle v,[\operatorname{curl},A]vangle$. The commutator is $\sum_k
abla(\omega_r)_k	imes\partial_k v$, yielding the last term of Equation (B.18). This explains its factor $1/2$ and the presence of the derivative of the reference vorticity. Products with the reference harmonics couple distinct perturbation modes, so the mean of $J$ is handled separately in Appendix B.3.

adapted.N5-32.1|Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.d.annotation: The positive and negative parts are taken before adding the mode contributions, so finiteness of the difference is not automatic. The negative integral is finite by Proposition B.4 under the cell and regional hypotheses. Proposition B.8 then establishes Equation (B.21) (with extended value allowed at first), and Proposition B.1 ensures that the positive integral is finite. Only then can both integrals be cancelled in Lemma B.2.

pdf-item-equation-B-19|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Put $A=\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p|\mu_p$. Even when some signs are opposite, the combined multiplier coefficient has modulus at most $A$, so its squared norm is bounded by $A^2$, not by the sum of the squared weights. If every selected frequency has modulus at least $\Omega_0>0$ and $A\le M$, then $A^2\le M A\le(M/\Omega_0)\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p||\Omega_p|\mu_p$. This is one sufficient way of obtaining the last bound of Equation (B.19).

pdf-item-equation-B-19|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: At a fixed label put $A=\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p|\mu_p$ and $B=\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p||\Omega_p|\mu_p$. The modulus of the combined zero-order multiplier coefficient is at most $A$. By Equation (B.19), $|A\hat v_\iota|^2\le n_\mu B|\hat v_\iota|^2$; summing and integrating gives the squared norm bound $n_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$.

b12-prop-b1-hypotheses|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: The multiplier is solenoidal, so $\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\mathbb PF,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. But $[F]$ in Equation (7.18) uses the original representative: a row that is solenoidal in its cell can have a nonzero normal trace on its boundary, so its pairing with a gradient need not vanish. This is why the pressure representative of Appendix B.1 can be used in the linear estimate without computing the projection or assuming that it decreases the row seminorm.

b12-prop-b1-existence|Breakdown.Coercive.annotation: Before projection, the two skew terms have the $L^2$ representatives $\sum_{p,\iota} i\operatorname{sgn}_p(\iota)\operatorname{curl}(\lambda_p\operatorname{curl}\hat v_\iota)$ and $\sum_{p,\iota} i\operatorname{sgn}_p(\iota)\mu_p\hat v_\iota$. Their bounds follow from Equation (B.19) and Parseval, using finiteness of the $\mu$ seminorm. Taking the solenoidal projection gives the unique field representing Equation (B.14) on the dense solenoidal tests. In particular no derivative of a test field remains in the norm estimate.

b12-prop-b1-norm|Breakdown.CoerciveWeak..annotation: Put $A=1+n_\lambda+n_{\nabla\lambda}/\sqrt{w_*}$. In the estimate $A\|v\|_w+\sqrt{n_\mu}\|v\|_\mu$, apply Cauchy–Schwarz to the vectors $(A/\sqrt{3/50},\sqrt{n_\mu/c_\mu})$ and $(\sqrt{3/50}\|v\|_w,\sqrt{c_\mu}\|v\|_\mu)$. This gives exactly the stated $c_{\mathsf M}$ and the two energies reserved in Equation (B.20).

b12-prop-b1-finiteness|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: The formal inequality can be written $\mathcal I^++X^-\le\mathcal I^-+X^+$, where $X$ is the real left side of Equation (B.20) and $X^\pm=\max(\pm X,0)$. If the negative integral is finite, the positive integral is therefore finite as well. Only then does subtraction give the real inequality printed here.

pdf-item-equation-B-20|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: If $F\simeq\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r}v+\sum_i\beta_i b_i$, the multiplier pairs only with the solenoidal part of this equation. Subtracting the reserved energies $\frac3{50}\|v\|_w^2+c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$ gives the lower bound by the signed density. The unknown force is kept as an explicit linear pairing, to be cancelled by Equation (B.21), rather than estimated at this step.

adapted.N5-36.1|Breakdown.Coercive.curlW.annotation: Applied with $u=\partial_j\hat v_\iota$ and summed in $j$, the identity with weight $\mathsf D_\iota$ trades a weighted gradient-of-curl square for a weighted Hessian square. Applied with $u=\hat v_\iota$ and weight $\mathsf Z_\iota$, it trades the curl square for the gradient square. For complex modes the calculation is done on the real and imaginary parts. The negative operator-norm terms in Equation (B.16) bound the two resulting Hessian pairings.

pdf-item-equation-B-21|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: The right side of Equation (B.21) supplies precisely the quantities absent from Equation (B.20): the positive coefficient energy $c\omega^2|\beta|^2$ and the opposite of the linear actuator term, with $c=3/50$. Once the inequalities are combined, the only other costs are the measured components of $F$ and the constraint values. This is an estimate for the bordered problem, not for the velocity operator alone.

pdf-item-equation-B-21|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Proposition B.8 supplies this inequality for arbitrary admissible $v,\beta,F$, not just their retained coefficients. ns-b3-reflect-stretch|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The rotation $R_*$ is the half-turn about the first coordinate axis and has determinant one. ns-b3-degrees|Breakdown.CertCell.CellCal.annotation: The degree $\mathsf d_0$ bounds the tests of the equation. ns-b3-leaf-coefficients|Breakdown.CertCe.annotation: The lower bounds $\mathsf I_2>0$ and $\mathsf I'_2\ge0$ apply to different second-derivative squares. pdf-item-equation-B-26|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The direction of Equation (B.26) is dictated by Equation (B.33): we seek a lower bound for the density integral, so the form of $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$ must be no greater than the sum of the forms obtained from that integral and the permitted pairings. ns-b3-b27|Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.he.annotation: The minimum of the two eigenvalues is used because high degree in either variable suffices to put a gradient coefficient outside the retained space. ns-b3-polynomial-eigenvalues|Breakdown.C.annotation: The scalar eigenvalues in Equation (B.27) come from the polynomial derivative forms, not from the operator of the linearized Navier–Stokes equation. ns-b3-unresolved-charges|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: The quantities $\mathsf a'_1,\mathsf a_1,\mathsf a_0$ account for the curl, gradient and velocity squares left out of the finite cell form. ns-b3-b28|Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.of.annotation: The left side of Equation (B.33) consists of the finite matrix form, the error term and the sum of these residual integrals for the modes with no resolved polynomial. ns-b3-modified-stretch-constant|Breakdow.annotation: In Equation (B.25) the factor $\sqrt{7/2}$ multiplies the mean-gradient product $\mathsf s_2|G||u|$ and the two Young terms with $\mathsf s_3$. ns-b3-rectangle-region|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The rectangle does not introduce a second copy of the trace. ns-b3-region-coefficient-data|Breakdown..annotation: The labels in a regional set must share the enclosures for the multiplier pieces. ns-b3-charged-coefficients|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: Subtract Equation (B.25) with $\mathsf c^*$ and the three charges in Equation (B.28) from the five lower coefficients of Equation (B.16). ns-b3-effective-coefficients|Breakdown.C.annotation: Put $q=(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$. For $\mathsf t\ge0$, $\mathsf t|\nabla u|^2\ge q\mathsf t|u|^2$. ns-b3-exterior-shapes|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The square exterior is a ray exterior with inner radius $a/\max(r/\rho,z/\rho)$ in the direction $(r,z)/\rho$. Its separate condition exploits the component symmetries of the zero angular mode. The constant $2$ in place of $1/4$ in Equation (B.31) reduces the velocity cost in Equation (B.30) by a factor of eight and the mixed cost by $\sqrt8$.

Fixing a direction fixes a single inner radius. The proof of Equation (B.37) uses the interval from this radius to infinity, and differentiates only along the ray; no regularity of an angular boundary derivative is used. The formal condition requires a measurable radius with uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds, constant along each ray.

ns-b3-exterior-integrated-test|Breakdown.annotation: At a label with zero angular wave number, Equation (B.29) cannot repair a negative $\mathsf f_0$, because $(k_0-1)_+=0$. ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-bounds|Breakd.annotation: The factors $\rho^2$ and $\rho$ remove precisely the powers of radius controlled by Equation (B.31). For an actuator-gradient error $e_i$, a mixed term of the form $\beta_i\langle e_i,\nabla v\rangle$ can be estimated by a positive multiple of the gradient square plus a coefficient of $|\beta_i|^2$ proportional to the weighted square of $e_i$. This is why the rectangle forms are added in Equation (B.38), although they are paid for by energy deducted from unresolved harmonics.

pdf-item-theorem-B-5|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: These derivative inequalities use the spatial transformation law (B.13), at fixed $\theta$. abla u|^2\ge324|u|^2/r^2$ and $|
abla^2u|^2\ge289|
abla u|^2/r^2$. The zero angular modes have neither gain, irrespective of their time frequency. The lemma also applies to the smaller orders allowed by Equation (B.1).

pdf-item-equation-B-36|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Equation (B.36) retains all the Hessian gain in $\mathsf f_1^*$ while discarding any positive remainder in the curl square. ns-b3-curl-differences|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: For each pair of indices $j<l$, the estimate $|\partial_ju_l-\partial_lu_j|^2\le2(|\partial_ju_l|^2+|\partial_lu_j|^2)$ holds also for complex components. pdf-item-theorem-B-6|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The first assertion of Lemma B.6 is an inverse-square inequality for the ray geometry and the angular mode, with no multiplier coefficients in it. ns-b3-b6-integrated-claim|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: After Equation (B.31) is available, the shape of $Z$ no longer enters the coefficient calculation. ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-signs|Breakdo.annotation: Set $s=\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$, $G=\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/(2s)$ and $A=\mathsf f_0^\infty+s\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/2$. ns-b3-exterior-lower-bound|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: The lower bound from `quad_lower` contains only $|\nabla u|^2$, $|u|^2/\rho^2$ and their geometric mean. ns-b3-attached-matrices|Breakdown.CertCe.annotation: Partitioning a cell matrix into blocks does not partition its coordinates into independent problems. ns-b3-b40|Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.annotation: Write $C=|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime$ for the entrywise error bound in Equation (B.40) and put $a_j=1/\mathsf w_j$. The column-count condition and the pivot condition are used for different conclusions. If there are $f$ free coordinates, the common kernel of the real negative-column pairings has codimension at most $f$. The positive pivot coefficients make the root lower form strictly positive there, and the signed-tree bound transfers this to the total form. Proposition B.8 supplies the additional fact that the kernel meets the free-coordinate subspace only at zero.

ns-b3-b41|Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.annotation: With $D$ the diagonal of the accumulated positive pivots and $Y$ the matrix of negative columns, Equation (B.41) reads $x^{\mathsf T}\mathsf N x\ge x^{\mathsf T}D x-|Y^{\mathsf T}x|^2$. ns-b3-column-kernel-positive|Breakdown.C.annotation: For a vector in the common kernel the only surviving terms in Equation (B.41) are the positive pivot squares. Each coordinate has at least one strictly positive coefficient, so the sum can vanish only at zero. The formal positivity assertion is for the root lower form, which bounds the total form from below by the preceding lemma.

ns-b3-weighted-row-proof|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: The row-sum argument controls the residual $B$ and the two enclosure errors together. ns-b3-strict-positivity-proof|Breakdown..annotation: On the column kernel the lower bound is a sum of positive multiples of coordinate squares, and every coordinate has a pivot at some node. ns-b3-b43|Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Tr.annotation: The normalization of the global leaf is the same as that of the cell inequalities. The coefficient $-\mathsf n_b$ on $|\beta|^2$ cancels the allowance of Equation (B.34), while the remaining two penalties become $-3\omega^2|\beta|^2/50$ and $-|\zeta|^2/1000$ on multiplication by $4\pi$. The inequality for $\mathsf A_0$ must hold on every extension of the prescribed vector.

ns-b3-b43|Breakdown.CertCell.globalForm|.annotation: `globalForm` is the scalar penalty $-(c\omega^2/(4\pi)+e)|\beta|^2-|\zeta|^2/(4\pi t)$, giving Equation (B.43) for $c=3/50$, $e=n_b$, $t=1000$. Its definition fixes the signs and normalization. The inequality that the actual global leaf is no greater than this penalty is a separate condition.

pdf-item-theorem-B-8|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: Proposition B.8 is the passage from finitely represented data and their inequalities to a bound on every admissible perturbation. It supplies Equation (B.21), not yet Equation (7.18); the latter follows by Lemma B.2 together with Equation (B.20). The Lean implication has the cell, region, tree and field-data conditions as hypotheses. Neither the statement nor its proof is an enclosure of the numerical matrices of a particular certificate.

ns-b3-b8|Breakdown.CertCell.rowRestClaus.annotation: Fix any $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. The same supplied conditions give the lower density bound for every solution of the reference linearized equation at that parameter. Lemma B.2 combines this with the multiplier estimate to obtain Equation (7.18); only afterwards are the bounds (7.19)–(7.21) used to transfer the estimate to the approximate profile.

ns-b3-b8-finiteness-proof|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: The negative integral is finite by Proposition B.4. If the positive integral is infinite, the left side of Equation (B.21) is $+\infty$ while its right side is finite for the given $v,\beta,F$. It is therefore enough to prove the remaining inequalities in the case where both contributions are finite.

ns-b3-finite-signed-integrals|Breakdown..annotation: Finiteness of both sign integrals implies summability of the absolute modal integrals and integrability of the stretching term. In particular the quarter-plane expression in Equation (B.23) can now be restricted to the cells and their complement and added back as an ordinary integral. This is the reason for disposing of the infinite-positive case first.

ns-b3-free-state-choice|Breakdown.CertCe.annotation: At this point the same prescribed vector $x_{\rm p}$ is held fixed throughout the calculation. Keeping $x_{\rm f}$ arbitrary proves Equation (B.44) on the entire affine space of extensions. Only after this uniform bound is available will the tree select an extension; choosing the pinning variable or other free coordinates beforehand would restrict the space available to that argument.

ns-b3-cell-off-modes|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The finite cover makes the negative-part integral of the unresolved density zero for each unresolved label. The formal cover can use larger regional curl, gradient and velocity charges, with the same stretching constant, than those subtracted in the cell: this only decreases the tested form. The sum of unresolved negative-part integrals is therefore zero (`OffModesVanish`), which leaves the absolutely convergent nonnegative remainder in Equation (B.33).

ns-b3-exterior-loss-comparison|Breakdown.annotation: The original stretching loss uses $\sqrt{7/2}$; Equation (B.28) enlarges it to $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and subtracts further nonnegative charges on the complement. Consequently $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L_\iota\ge\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$. On bounded regions the latter is nonnegative pointwise by Equation (B.29), whereas on unbounded regions only its integral need be nonnegative. Either estimate suffices to show that the exterior makes no negative contribution after summing the modal integrals.

ns-b3-exterior-sum-positive|Breakdown.Ce.annotation: For a fixed label, sum the regional inequalities over the partition of the complement. Since $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and the three exterior charges are nonnegative, Equation (B.28) is no greater than $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L(\nabla\hat v_\iota,\hat v_\iota)$. It follows that the integral of $\mathcal I_\iota$ pays for the integral of the stretching majorant for this label.

We are now in the case $\mathcal I^+<\infty$ and $\mathcal I^-<\infty$. By Lemma B.3, the sum of the integrals of $|\mathcal I_\iota|$ is finite. The nonnegative $\mathcal L_\iota$ on the complement has integral at most that of $\mathcal I_\iota$ for each $\iota$, so its sum is integrable as well. This permits Equation (B.32) to be integrated and gives the nonnegative exterior contribution to Equation (B.21).

ns-b3-sum-before-b44|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: After dropping the nonnegative unresolved residuals, add the cell bounds and move the four error terms to the right. Add the rectangle forms; Equation (B.34) bounds the resulting error by the forcing rows, actuator and pin pairings, and $\mathsf n_b|\beta|^2$. The last term cancels with Equation (B.43). Multiplication by $4\pi$ now puts both the density and the pairings back in their original normalization. The exterior can be included because its integral is nonnegative.

pdf-item-equation-B-44|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Put $D$ equal to the left side of Equation (B.21) minus its right side. By completing the square, Equation (B.44) reads $4\pi\langle\mathsf N x_{\rm g},x_{\rm g}\rangle\le D-|\zeta-1000\ell(v)|^2/1000\le D$. It is enough to find one extension of the prescribed vector on which the form is nonnegative. The bound is available on all extensions, which is crucial for the following dimension argument.

By Equation (B.38) the cell forms, twice the rectangle forms and the global form constitute the same real quadratic form that is bounded by Lemma B.7. The auxiliary matrices used in the tree have zero total contribution. Thus no further matrix approximation is needed between the analytic inequality (B.44) and the signed tree bound.

ns-b3-final-nonnegativity|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: All negative column pairings vanish on the chosen extension, so its form is nonnegative. Inequality (B.44) bounds it above by the desired gap divided by $4\pi$. The choice was made only in the auxiliary coordinates; there has been no change to the perturbation or its equation. This proves Equation (B.21) even if $\mathsf N$ is indefinite.

pdf-item-equation-B-45|Breakdown.sixthPo.annotation: The linked inequality is the squared vector estimate, with coefficient $4/3$. Its hypotheses are $u\in L^6$ and a weak gradient in $L^2$; neither zero divergence nor the symmetries in Equation (7.5) are required. In Lemma B.10 it is applied at a fixed time, before integration over the period.

pdf-item-equation-B-46|Breakdown.CertRed.annotation: The constant in the last bound uses the same product inequality as the third: Equation (7.48) gives $\|u\|_{L^\infty}^2\le(2\pi)^{-1}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. Bounding the product, instead of bounding each factor separately, gives $c_w^2=(4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1}$. This saves a factor of two in the squared estimate.

pdf-item-theorem-B-9|Breakdown.CellLayer.annotation: There are two fields associated with the centre of the parameter set: $W_0^{\mathrm a}$ is the member used in Equation (B.9), while $W^{\mathrm r}$ is the field used to prove the inverse estimate in Subsections B.2–B.3. The latter can be chosen for ease of certification and need not be a member of the approximate family. Its difference from the centre is estimated once, and the additional variation from the centre is estimated uniformly on $\mathcal K$.

pdf-item-theorem-B-9|Breakdown.CertReduc.annotation: In Equation (7.52) the use of the reference estimate costs $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ because the change of forcing is measured in both the norm and the seminorm Equation (7.17). Thus $c_{\mathrm r}<1/(c_1+c_0)$ is needed when $c_1+c_0>0$. The inverse constant for zero constraints is then bounded by $(c_1+c_0)/(1-(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r})$. The first bound of Equation (B.48) must be sufficiently small for the chosen $c_L$ in Equation (7.21).

A bound for the period norm in Equation (7.19) by itself gives no bound on the supremum of the gradient energy over time. For the latter, Proposition 7.9 uses the energy identity and integrates from a phase of minimum energy. The spatial form (7.22) controls the increase between phases, so its estimate is required for each $\theta$, before time integration.

ns-b4-006|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Shif.annotation: The supremum in $\theta$ of the spatial norm is taken separately for each parameter, and the same bound must hold for all parameters in $\mathcal K$. It cannot be replaced by an $L^3$ norm in space-time: the product involving $u$ is to be estimated also for a single time slice in Equation (7.22). For the fixed centre error the parameter quantifier is redundant.

pdf-item-equation-B-48|Breakdown.CellLay.annotation: Group the first budget as $A+B$, where $A=c_w\mathsf n_0^{(2)}$ and $B=(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty+2\mathsf n_1^{(3)}/\sqrt3)/\sqrt{w_*}$. The third budget is $A+B/2$. Its terms multiplying $\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$ gain the factor $1/2$ from Equation (B.46); the term $\|u\|_\infty\|\Delta u\|_2$ has already used the mixed product in the derivation of $c_w$ and is bounded by $c_w|u|_w^2$.

pdf-item-equation-B-48|Breakdown.CertRed.annotation: The middle budget concerns only $W^{\mathrm r}$. The strain loss is at most $\mathsf s_-\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2\le(\mathsf s_-/w_*)|u|_w^2$. The remaining convection term has one gradient and one Laplacian norm, so Equation (B.45) and the product estimate in Equation (B.46) give the coefficient $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-008|Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTra.annotation: At fixed $\alpha$, the reference equation and the approximate-field equation use the same $S(\alpha)$, constraints and forcing fields. Hence the change in the equation is exactly the two convection terms with $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$. There is no estimate of a time derivative of this difference in Equation (7.19).

ns-b4-008|Breakdown.CertReduction.frozen.annotation: The middle inequality of Equation (B.48) is a bound at $W^{\mathrm r}$ alone. The first and last inequalities involve the difference of the profiles, whereas this middle one requires a bound on the strain and on the full $L^3$ gradient of the reference. It is not necessary for $W^{\mathrm r}$ itself to be small.

ns-b4-009|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Shif.annotation: Here both profiles are evaluated at the same $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$ in period-one coordinates. The centre error $Z_0$ is fixed as a function of these coordinates. By Equation (B.9), $Z_1$ is affine in $\alpha$ inside $B_{r_\chi}$ (and vanishes at $\alpha=0$); outside the ball the radial phase varies as well. The gradient norm in Equation (B.47) must enclose the derivative of that phase, not just the affine coefficient variation.

pdf-item-equation-B-49|Breakdown.CertRed.annotation: In the second inequality of Equation (B.49), the prescribed $L^2$ gradient is multiplied by a perturbation bounded in $L^\infty$; in the third, the prescribed $L^3$ gradient is multiplied by a perturbation in $L^6$. These are the two cases of `gapGradCoeff`. The former uses both spatial derivative norms in $|u|_w$, while the latter uses only its gradient term.

To obtain the squared norm bound, apply Hölder to $|\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}^2|u|^2$ with exponents $3/2$ and $3$. The resulting factors are $\||\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}\|_{L^3}^2$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}^2$, respectively. The latter gives the constant $4/3$ by Equation (B.45), which becomes $2/\sqrt3$ in Equation (B.49).

ns-b4-016|Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftG.annotation: Hölder bounds the second pairing in magnitude by $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. Use Equation (B.45), then $2\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le|u|_w^2$. Its cost is thus at most $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}|u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-017|Breakdown.CertReduction.frozen.annotation: In Equation (7.22) we may discard $\|\Delta u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2/4$ when obtaining a lower bound. The remaining two terms are the strain contribution and the term estimated by Sobolev. The resulting bound may be negative; Proposition 7.9 controls the increase of the energy over an interval, without requiring the form to be coercive at every phase.

ns-b4-018|Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftS.annotation: The supremum terms of Equation (B.49), paired with $\Delta u$, give $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. The third inequality of Equation (B.46) gives the coefficient $(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty)/(2\sqrt{w_*})$ in the form-shift estimate.

ns-b4-018|Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftG.annotation: The $L^2$ gradient error is bounded using $\|u\|_{L^\infty}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le c_w|u|_w^2$. For the $L^3$ error, apply Equation (B.45) and the third inequality of Equation (B.46) to get $\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le |u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$. These give the remaining two terms in the third budget of Equation (B.48).

ns-b4-018|Breakdown.CertReduction.formSh.annotation: Pairing the operator-norm bound (7.19) with $-\Delta u$ at the slice level would give the first budget of Equation (B.48) as a sufficient coefficient. The proof instead keeps the separate terms in Equation (B.49) until multiplying by $\|\Delta u\|_2$. It thereby gains a factor of two in the costs of transport and of the $L^3$ gradient error, but not the $L^2$ gradient error.

ns-b4-019|Breakdown.CertReduction.formSh.annotation: For each $u$ and $\theta$ the form at the reference is at least $-c'_3|u|_w^2$, and the change to $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ is at least $-c''_3|u|_w^2$. Adding proves Equation (7.22). In Lean the two assertions are combined in `ExtendedFrozenBridge.profile_form`, using the inequality for the declared total form bound.

ns-b4-019|Breakdown.CertReduction.frozen.annotation: In Equation (7.55), the total $c_3\ge c'_3+c''_3$ contributes $(2S(\alpha)/m)c_3\|v\|_w^2$ to the bound for the squared gradient supremum. At $\|v\|_w\le2\varepsilon$, the cost is at most $8S_{\max}c_3\varepsilon^2/m$, which appears in Equation (7.27). The bound on $c_{\mathrm r}$ is used earlier, to obtain the joint norm estimate in Equation (7.52).

pdf-item-theorem-B-10|Breakdown.CertRedu.annotation: `cubicForm j` selects the norm for Equation (7.32), and `sizeNum j` bounds it for every phase and parameter. The choice is independent for different $j$. Even when the $L^3$ estimate is better, the formal analytic certificate still has a separate slice $L^2$ condition on $\psi_j$.

The bridge first bounds the integral of $|(v\cdot\nabla)v|\,|\psi_j|$ on the period. This is sufficient both to define the pairing and to bound its absolute value by $\tilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. In contrast to Lemma B.11 below, the estimate does not use cancellation between angular or temporal modes.

ns-b4-023|Breakdown.CertReduction.adjoin.annotation: There is no smallness hypothesis on $v$ in Lemma B.10. Its coefficient is computed before solving Equation (7.12); only when Equation (7.32) is used in Equation (7.35) does the radius $2\varepsilon$ give a quadratic error of size $4\tilde a_j\varepsilon^2$.

ns-b4-025|Breakdown.CertReduction.adjoin.annotation: Compare Lemma 7.6: the square of the full $L^2$ norm of the quadratic forcing involves the product $\|v(\theta)\|_\infty^2\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$, for which a supremum bound is needed. Here the pairing is integrated without squaring the spatial estimate. The energy over one period therefore suffices, and the coefficient in Equation (7.35) is $4\tilde a_j\varepsilon^2$.

ns-b4-029|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Azimut.annotation: Here $k$ is the wave number of a scalar Cartesian component, not the label $\iota_1$ in Equation (B.2). Indeed a cylindrical mode of angular number $m$ has $u_1\pm iu_2=e^{\pm i\phi}(u_r\pm iu_\phi)$, hence scalar wave numbers $m\pm1$, and its third component has number $m$. It is these scalar numbers that enter $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}$. For $|k|=1$ the resulting dual norm coefficient is $2/3$ instead of $2$.

ns-b4-031|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBo.annotation: An adjoint residual with dual bound $\mathsf n$ contributes at most $\mathsf n\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}\le (\mathsf n/\sqrt{w_*})\|v\|_w$. This is the estimate used not only for $\mathsf R_{j,\alpha}$ in Equation (B.56) but also for the transposed stretching and time-derivative terms. No $L^2$ bound for $v$ is needed.

pdf-item-equation-B-50|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The paper passes Equation (B.50) to a weak function of a prescribed angular number. Lean instead proves the summed estimate $\sum_k (|k|+1/2)^2\|P_k U/|y|\|_2^2\le\|\nabla U\|_2^2$, encoding a complex $U$ as two real components. This follows by passing each projected estimate to the limit and bounding the sum of the projected gradient energies. It will allow a test against several angular modes at once.

ns-b4-035|Breakdown.CertCell.Internal.sl.annotation: At $k=0$ the coefficient in Equation (B.50) is $1/4$, giving $\|U/|y|\|_2\le2\|\nabla U\|_2$. The argument for $k\ne0$ uses the vanishing of a smooth mode on the axis; that vanishing is not available for $k=0$ and is not needed.

ns-b4-044|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPote.annotation: The auxiliary fields are a way of representing a functional of the perturbation in norms already present in Equation (7.14). A term $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ can be paired with $\Delta v$ by moving two derivatives, whereas $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ can be paired through the gradients by moving one. Thus a potential of size $O(|y|^{-1})$ is allowed for $\mathsf U_j$, even though it need not have finite $L^2$ norm. The remaining defect is measured by Lemma B.11.

pdf-item-equation-B-51|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The bounds $O((1+|y|)^{-2})$ on $\mathsf G_j,\nabla\mathsf U_j,\mathsf F_j,q_j$ give square integrability in space. The common bound on their indicated derivatives is in $L^{6/5}$, both near zero and at infinity, as required in Equation (B.55). The linked condition also bounds $\mathsf U_j=O((1+|y|)^{-1})$ and gives the stronger separate decay estimates for $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ and $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ of orders $-4$ and $-3$. These are regularity requirements, not the smallness requirements in Equation (B.53).

pdf-item-equation-B-52|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The sign of the constraint source follows from $\langle v,-\Delta\tilde\Phi_l\rangle=\langle\nabla v,\nabla\tilde\Phi_l\rangle$. Thus the desired adjoint equation has right side $-\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\tilde\Phi_l$, and moving it to the left gives the plus sign in Equation (B.52). The three auxiliary terms may reduce the dual norm of the remainder, but their own costs must be included in Equation (B.53).

`adjointTransport` is the zero- and first-order part of the adjoint, with the time derivative taken on the test field. The diffusion is kept in divergence form: $-\Delta\psi_j$ is $-\operatorname{div}(\nabla\psi_j)^{\mathsf T}$, combined in `pinFlux` with the constraint generators. This permits testing using the weak gradient of $v$ through Equation (B.55).

Write $A_l=

abla	ilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T}$ in the paper's matrix convention. Its transposed divergence is $\Delta	ilde\Phi_l-
abla\operatorname{div}	ilde\Phi_l=\Delta	ilde\Phi_l$. The formal flux is $

ns-b4-049|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Potent.annotation: The decay of $\mathsf G_j$ gives an $L^2$ bound for the field itself, but for $\mathsf U_j$ Equation (B.51) supplies only the corresponding bound on its gradient. After integration by parts their costs are therefore $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}$ and $w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$. The matrix term is also paired with $\nabla v$. This explains the grouping in the first square root of Equation (B.53).

ns-b4-049|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Adjoin.annotation: Although the test and the potentials are fixed, the residual of Equation (B.52) varies with $\alpha$ through $W_\alpha^0$. Its dual bound must be verified throughout $\mathcal K$. In the general formal data one can fit auxiliary potentials also to individual tangent defects; the represented cell instance has no such directions, by `fitted_empty`.

pdf-item-theorem-B-12|Breakdown.AdjointD.annotation: Lemma B.12 gives a bound for the difference between two linear functionals of $v$, before the constraints are imposed. In Equation (B.56) the first line is the adjoint equation defect with its auxiliary terms, the second changes the operator to the one at the actual parameter, and the third changes the represented constraint back to Equation (7.11). Each is bounded by a multiple of the same energy norm.

The two operator-related costs in Equation (B.53) make up `defectSum`: the first covers the residual of the adjoint about $W_\alpha^0$ with period $S(0)$, and the second covers the remaining changes in the operator. The formal definition also has a sum for individually fitted tangent defects; it is empty for the represented family. The pin error is a separate charge.

Smallness of the remainder alone would be meaningless if the added auxiliary terms were large. The first term of Equation (B.53) accounts for both; the next two terms then restore the parameter-dependent operator and the original constraints. The resulting estimate controls the adjoint of the full linearized operator, not only the residual of Equation (B.52).

pdf-item-theorem-B-12|Breakdown.CellRedu.annotation: To use the general adjoint bound, its data must describe the same operator and constraint as Equation (7.33). The links set the adjoint field to the represented $\psi_j$, the coupling coefficients to the row $Y_{jl}$, and the base and tangent fields to $W_\alpha^0,W_\alpha^i$. They also identify the rates in $1/S(\alpha)$ and set the fitted set empty.

pdf-item-equation-B-53|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The number $a_j$ is an upper bound for an operator norm on the perturbation space, uniform over $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. For example, the first square root alone is not sufficient if the inverse period or the tangent fields change appreciably. The other terms in Equation (B.53) restore the full operator and the actual constraint, respectively.

pdf-item-equation-B-53|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: The expression in Equation (B.53) is recovered from the general formal budget by substituting the links of this represented instance. In particular, no tangent direction is fitted by a separate potential, so the sum over fitted directions is zero and the free-direction sum runs over all coordinates. The row of coupling coefficients is the one used in the constraints.

ns-b4-053|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjo.annotation: Although $F$ is only specified modulo gradients, its pairing with the divergence-free $\psi$ is independent of the representative: $\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle PF,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. This is why the pressure of the unknown correction is absent from Equations (B.54)–(B.56). The statement still assumes $F\in\mathcal H$.

ns-b4-057|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.testFi.annotation: Cutting off $\psi$ itself can destroy solenoidality, so for the weak solenoidal equation the formal proof uses a curl potential $A$ and takes $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A)=\chi\psi+\nabla\chi\times A$. The latter term is supported on the cutoff annulus. The decay assumptions allow convergence of the test and its gradient as well as of its time derivative and radial derivative in the norms needed for Equation (B.54); smoothing gives admissible compact tests.

pdf-item-equation-B-55|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: Both sides of Equation (B.55) extend from compact tests in the gradient norm. The matrix pairing uses $A\in L^2$ and the velocity pairing uses $\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}\in L^{6/5}$ with Sobolev. The linked weak pairing instead uses $|y|\operatorname{div}A^{\mathsf T}\in L^2$ with Hardy, together with local integrability and the weak divergence identity. Neither argument requires $v\in L^2$.

ns-b4-059|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Intern.annotation: For $A=q_j I$, the right side of Equation (B.55) is $-\int q_j\operatorname{div}v=0$. This removes the auxiliary pressure from the defect bound, not from the definition of the strong residual. In Lemma B.13 the pairing will instead be restricted to a ball, where the same cancellation cannot be made without a boundary condition.

ns-b4-060|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Intern.annotation: The decomposition does not expand the radial phase in powers of $\alpha$. It is exact at the current phase: $W_\alpha^{\rm a}-W_\alpha^0=\sum_i\alpha_iW_\alpha^i$. Hence the difference from the operator in Equation (B.52) consists only of this convection change and the inverse-period change $\varsigma\cdot\alpha$. No term involving $W_\alpha^0-W_0^0$ has to be added to Equation (B.56).

ns-b4-060|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: The base and tangent fields in the adjoint equation and in the offset calculation must come from the same represented family. `centre_eq` and `free_eq` use the phase at $\alpha$; `centrePeriod_eq` and `periodRate_eq` identify the reciprocal period and its affine coefficients with those in Lemma B.13. The matching-ball restriction in Lemma B.13, not these links, is what permits evaluating the fields at $\alpha=0$.

ns-b4-061|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Intern.annotation: Solve Equation (B.52) for the first line. The three auxiliary terms to be paired with $v$ are then $-\Delta\mathsf G_j$, $-w_*\Delta\mathsf U_j$ and $+\operatorname{div}\mathsf F_j^{\mathsf T}$. Moving two, one and one spatial derivatives respectively gives the signs $-,+,-$ in the first line of Equation (B.56); the pressure pairing vanishes. The linked slice identity formalizes this part of the calculation.

The inverse-period change contributes $-(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)\iint v\cdot\partial_\theta\psi$ because it is the adjoint of the time derivative. The convection change contributes $\sum_i\alpha_i[(W_\alpha^i\cdot\nabla)v\cdot\psi+v\cdot\sum_k\psi_k\nabla W_{\alpha,k}^i]$ under the integral. These are exact differences of linear operators; there are no products of two direction fields as in Equation (B.57).

ns-b4-061|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.pinCha.annotation:

ns-b4-063|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.potent.annotation: Put $B=w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}+\mathsf n_{\mathsf F}+\mathsf n_{\mathsf R}$. The bound $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}+B\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ is the dot product of $(\mathsf n_{\mathsf G},B/\sqrt{w_*})$ with $(\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H},\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H})$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the square root in Equation (B.53), rather than the larger sum $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}+B/\sqrt{w_*}$.

ns-b4-064|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.freeSh.annotation: At fixed $\alpha$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\sum_i\alpha_i W_\alpha^i|\le(\sum_i\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i)^{1/2}(\sum_i\varpi_i|W_\alpha^i|^2)^{1/2}$. Pair the latter factor times $|\psi|$ with $|\nabla v|$. For the transposed stretching term use Lemma B.11 first, then the same weighted Cauchy–Schwarz on $\sum_i|\alpha_i|\mathsf n_i$. Thus the common radius factor multiplies $\mathsf n_{\rm v}+\mathsf n_{\rm d}$.

ns-b4-067|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjoin.annotation: The final inequality has the form $|\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j|\le a_j\|v\|_w$. It has been established for any $v\in\mathcal D_{S(\alpha)}$ with the indicated $F$, not just for a perturbation of size $2\varepsilon$. The size restriction enters only when the inequality is used for the parameter bound in Equation (7.35).

ns-b4-068|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: One could try to expand $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ on the whole space, but a change of period changes the logarithmic radial phase at infinity (Appendix C.4). The phase correction vanishes on $B_{r_\chi}$, where the velocity and inverse period are affine. Therefore the coefficient calculation on that ball is exact and the exterior needs just a norm enclosure, not bounds on the parameter derivatives of the phase.

pdf-item-equation-B-57|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: The coefficient conventions just described also determine the enclosure: `quadraticCoefficient` adds the two ordered terms off the diagonal and takes only one on the diagonal. Since Equation (B.59) sums over $i\le i'$, no factor of two is inserted when using a mixed-coefficient error bound.

The constant coefficient of the ball response is $V_j\cdot\beta^0-\langle F^{(0)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. It includes the centre's prescribed force as well as its residual, even though the desired diagonal response vanishes at $\alpha=0$. The corresponding whole-space constant differs by the exterior pairing, bounded later in Lemma B.13.

ns-b4-072|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: Solenoidality removes a gradient from a pairing on all of space under the indicated integrability hypotheses. On the ball, however, $\int_{B_{r_\chi}}\nabla p\cdot\psi_j=\int_{\partial B_{r_\chi}}p\,\psi_j\cdot\nu$ for smooth fields, and there is no zero-normal condition on $\psi_j$ there. Thus the pressure and kinetic-energy gradients in Equation (B.57) are retained in Equation (B.58). Lean integrates on the closed ball; the sphere has measure zero.

pdf-item-theorem-B-13|Breakdown.CellRedu.annotation: The intervals in Equation (B.58) enclose coefficients of the signed scalar response, not of the norm of the residual. In particular the centre and linear coefficients subtract the residual pairing from the corresponding force coefficient. For the quadratic part the force is affine, so its coefficient is just $-\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$.

The monomial estimates use an enclosing box of the parameter set. For distinct $i,i'\notin\mathcal J$ one could use $|d_i d_{i'}\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}|\le\varrho_*^2/2$ from the sum of their two squares; Equation (B.59) instead uses the simpler product of the individual radii. Thus the budget is sufficient, not necessarily the supremum of the response error on $\mathcal K$.

Write the ball response as $P_j(\alpha)=V_j\cdot\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. Then the quantity to bound in Equation (7.34) is $P_j(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi},\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, since $\bar\ell=0$. The polynomial enclosures are used only for the first difference.

pdf-item-equation-B-59|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: A bound on the absolute response itself would also charge the term $d_j\alpha_j$ needed for the Newton update. Instead the diagonal linear coefficient is centered at $d_j$ and the other coefficients at zero. The sum in Equation (B.59) encloses the remainder after these subtractions, which is the approximate-family part of $-d_j\alpha'_j$ in Equation (7.35).

ns-b4-076|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: On the selected coordinates, Equation (7.29) gives the individual radii $\varrho_i$. On the other coordinates it bounds the Euclidean norm of $(d_i\alpha_i)_{i\notin\mathcal J}$, hence also each $|d_i\alpha_i|$ by $\varrho_*$. Dividing by $|d_i|$ gives the second radius; it is essential that $d_i\ne0$. The formal definition writes $|\varrho_*|$, equal to $\varrho_*$ under the sign assumption.

ns-b4-077|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: Equation (7.34) is an enclosure of the approximate-family contribution to the new scaled coordinate, not the whole coordinate. In Equation (7.35) one still needs the quadratic pairing, the linear adjoint defect, and the difference of the force pairings from $V_j$. The coordinates outside $\mathcal J$ are estimated by Equations (7.36)–(7.37), without the ball polynomial for an adjoint row.

ns-b4-078|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: On the open ball the correction to the radial phase in Equation (B.9) is identically zero, so its derivatives vanish there as well. One may freeze the phase before taking derivatives in the residual. The boundary sphere has measure zero in the ball pairing, so no expansion across the transition of the radial phase is needed.

adapted.N6-31.1|Breakdown.CellLayerSyste.annotation: These conditions concern the parts of the analytic argument not supplied by the local coercivity inequality alone. For example the two residual budgets enter the first step of Equation (7.59); the frozen-form and smallness conditions enter its second step; Equation (7.28) prevents cancellation of the whole profile. Condition (7.26), unused in the paper's Schauder argument, is used for the fixed-parameter contraction in Lean. All must hold for the same family.

ns-b4-087|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isEx.annotation: The conclusion supplies the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1, not its solution. The theorem will solve the constrained correction problem with the certified inverse estimate, choose the parameter using the adjoint and stiff-coordinate enclosures, and use Equation (7.28) to exclude the zero profile. The formal assembly likewise establishes the certificate predicate; the profile construction is a subsequent theorem.

ns-b4-094|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Cell.annotation: The upper bounds on $M$ and $\varepsilon$ restrict the permitted correction radius before a numerical certificate is verified. Indeed Equation (7.25) bounds $M$, and Equation (7.27) gives $2\varepsilon\le\sqrt{w_*}M$ even without the other positive costs. The formal unresolved-mode and exterior conditions allow any stretching constant at least $\sqrt{7/2}$, subject to their remaining inequalities.

adapted.N6-42.1|Breakdown.CellReduction..annotation: The exponent $h=1$ prescribes the leading inverse-radius decay; differentiating in space yields the corresponding extra powers under the radial phase and degree conditions. The linked field-decay theorem verifies bounds of the form required in Equation (7.8) for the represented field under its structural hypotheses. A decay constant for the fitted coefficients must be controlled using the actual supplied data.

ac-049|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.log.annotation: For $f(\rho)=A\log(1+\rho/r_c^2)$ one has $\rho^j|f^{(j)}(\rho)|=|A|(j-1)!(\rho/(r_c^2+\rho))^j$ for $j=1,2,3$. These are bounded by $|A|(j-1)!$ since $r_c>0$. Thus the phase grows logarithmically but meets exactly the derivative conditions of Appendix B.1.

ac-038|Breakdown.SimilarityResidual|1.annotation: For a solenoidal smooth field, $-\Delta W=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W$. Also $(W\cdot\nabla)W=(\operatorname{curl}W)\times W+\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Substituting both identities into Equation (1.2) gives the curl formulation, with the kinetic-energy gradient absorbed into $H$. `SimilarityResidual` uses the original advection and diffusion form.

ac-038|Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestD.annotation: For any smooth vector field, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W=\nabla\operatorname{div}W-\Delta W$. In Equation (C.1) the second displayed equation sets the first term on the right to zero. The linked lemma is the solenoidal specialization of this identity; it explains why the diffusion term in the residual of Equation (C.1) is the positive double curl.

adapted.N6-46.1|Breakdown.IsExtendedCert.annotation: The row bound controls the vector of weighted residual pairings, not the individual coefficients of the auxiliary force. It is possible to have $[F]=0$ and $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}>0$ when the residual is orthogonal to every row. The separate inequality $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]\le\delta_0(\alpha)$ preserves that information in Equation (7.24); the quadratic trial, for which no comparable directional information is given, uses the general bound (7.17).

ac-043|Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.I.annotation: The differential expression in Equation (C.2) is the linearization at the current profile. The formal strong right-hand side also allows the actuator forcing and the gradient of pressure: its diffusion term is minus the Hessian trace, using solenoidality to replace $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v$ by $-\Delta v$. In Appendix C the expression is tested in a finite space to find an approximate field; in Appendix B its cellwise pairings are estimated for arbitrary perturbations of the reference field.

adapted.N6-52.1|Breakdown.CellReduction..annotation: At a fixed phase the represented field is the center plus $\sum_i\alpha_i$ times the corresponding tangent fields, evaluated at the same phase. In the region where $f_*=0$, the phase correction in Equation (B.9) disappears and gives this affine representation. `affineField` defines the latter expression; its agreement with the phase-dependent field on the ball needs a separate identity.

s1-headline|Breakdown.Periodic.breakdown.annotation: The periodic statement requires more than taking the quotient of the whole-space velocity, which generally has no spatial period. The construction in Section 6 yields a periodic flow; the linked implication excludes global smooth periodic velocity from its datum. The singular time and quantitative approximation in Equation (1.7) are not part of this implication's conclusion.
