pdf-item-equation-1-2|Breakdown.IsSimila.annotation: `IsSimilarityProfile` is the local equation-and-decay part of the profile hypothesis; neither recurrence nor nonvanishing is included. One constant $C$ controls the velocity and its first two spatial derivatives, with one more inverse power of $1+|y|$ at each differentiation, as well as $\nabla q$. The last bound is additional to Equation (1.3) and Remark 1.2.

pdf-item-equation-1-3|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation:
The additional formal bounds on $
abla^2W$ and $
abla q$ have the same exponent three as $(W\cdot
abla)W$. By Equation (1.2) they imply $|\partial_sW+	frac12W+	frac12(y\cdot
abla)W|\lesssim(1+|y|)^{-3}$. The separate terms in this combination may decay only as $|y|^{-1}$. Their cancellation gives a square-integrable bound for the physical time derivative in the proof of Proposition 4.1.

s1-similarity-time|Breakdown.physicalSca.annotation: The velocity scale and the reciprocal spatial length scale are both $a(t)=(1-t)^{-1/2}$. In `physicalScale` this is the factor applied to both $W$ and its spatial argument. The corresponding dilation parameter in Equation (3.4) is $a(t)^2$, not $a(t)$.

pdf-item-equation-1-5|Breakdown.physical.annotation: To see the inverse isometry in the argument, put $\delta=T-t$. At $t'=T-\lambda\delta$, Equation (1.4) evaluates $W(s+S,x/\sqrt{\lambda\delta})$. Replace this by $RW(s,\lambda^{-1/2}R^{-1}x/\sqrt\delta)$ using Equation (1.2), and take out the velocity factor $(\lambda\delta)^{-1/2}$. This gives the stated scaling law.

s1-theorem-premise|Breakdown.breakdownOn.annotation: The input is an exact nonzero recurrent profile on $\mathbb R^3$. No approximate profile or compact support is assumed here. `breakdownOnSpace_of_profile` uses the stronger formal decay premise to deduce nonexistence of a global smooth bounded-energy flow from suitable compactly supported data; the numerical construction of a profile is a separate implication (Theorem 7.1 gives an exact profile from a certificate).

s1-theorem-space|Breakdown.TransferHolds.annotation: The dense subspace in `TransferHolds` is chosen before the datum: take it to be the embedded smooth compactly supported solenoidal fields. The result finds a datum from this subspace within $\varepsilon$ of $W(0)$ in $X$ whose mild evolution satisfies the rescaled estimate. Density by itself gives the initial approximation but does not select a solution with that estimate; this is the role of the finite-dimensional correction in Proposition 2.1.

s1-theorem-periodic|Breakdown.Periodic.T.annotation: `TorusBlowup` gives smooth periodic data and a mild curve in $V$, the unit-period space with full $H^1$ norm (including the zero Fourier mode). A hypothetical global solution with periodic velocity can first be changed to one with periodic pressure and the same datum. Its curve in $V$ is continuous through $T$, hence bounded on $[0,T]$; mild uniqueness contradicts the unboundedness on $[0,T)$. The predicate does not itself retain the quantitative estimates of Equation (1.7).

s1-symmetry-class|Breakdown.certificate_.annotation: The perturbation is required to have the same space-time symmetries as the approximate field. Consequently the linearized and quadratic terms stay in that class, and the inverse estimate need only hold there. For instance, a rotation after half a period gives a half-period for the gradient energy, even when the velocity itself needs the full period; this improves Equation (7.55).

s1-stable-convergence|Breakdown.Transfer.annotation: Apply $D_{1-t}$ to the difference in Equation (1.6). Since $D_{1-t}u^*(t)=W(s)$ and $\|D_{1-t}f\|_X=(1-t)^{1/4}\|f\|_X$, this gives $\|D_{1-t}u(t)-W(s)\|_X\lesssim e^{-\kappa s}$. Convergence is to the same phase $s=-\log(1-t)$, not merely to the set of slices of the profile.

s1-unforced|Breakdown.IsSmoothSolution|1.annotation: The momentum equation in `IsSmoothSolution` has only viscosity and pressure on its right-hand side. There is no force that can be chosen to sustain the singularity. The total auxiliary force used in the certificate construction must therefore vanish at the selected parameter (Proposition 7.10), and the periodic cutoff defect must be removed.

s1-outline-base-solution|Breakdown.Trans.annotation: The free return map has norm at most $e^{-S/4}$, not one: the gain comes from undoing the spatial dilation. The interaction with the reference changes the return by a compact operator. Hence a spectral circle of radius $\Theta\in(e^{-S/4},1)$ off the spectrum leaves only a finite-dimensional exterior range, including multipliers of modulus below one which decay too slowly (the spectral splitting of Lemma 4.5).

s1-outline-contraction|Breakdown.Contrac.annotation: Expanding the mild equation at the exact reference cancels its self-interaction and leaves the mixed term $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)$ and the quadratic term $\mathcal B(v,v)$. The first need not be small; it belongs to the equation to be inverted. It is the quadratic term, evaluated on a small error, that has a small Lipschitz constant (the quadratic estimate in Lemma 4.7).

s1-outline-space|Breakdown.Freq.X|1.annotation: The decay in Equation (1.3) gives an integrable squared gradient, even if the velocity has infinite energy. In the Fourier realization the quantity stored is $g(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|\hat u(\xi)$, rather than $\hat u$ itself; $g\in L^2$, $g(-\xi)=\overline{g(\xi)}$ and $\xi\cdot g(\xi)=0$. Reconstruction of the physical velocity uses the Sobolev inequality of Subsection 3.1.

s1-outline-space|Breakdown.Freq.gradSixD.annotation: At infinity the radial integrals for $\|W(s)\|_6^6$ and $\|\nabla W(s)\|_2^2$ are bounded by constants times $\int_1^\infty r^{-4}\,dr$ and $\int_1^\infty r^{-2}\,dr$, respectively. The constants are independent of $s$ by Equation (1.3). The same argument for $\|W(s)\|_2^2$ gives only $\int_1^\infty 1\,dr$. The linked Sobolev estimate is proved for the smooth solenoidal decay class containing these slices.

s1-outline-torus-space|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The mean-zero condition removes the constants, on which the gradient norm vanishes. On a cell of side $L$, Poincaré gives $\|u\|_2\le (L/2\pi)\|\nabla u\|_2$, but the Sobolev bound $\|u\|_6\lesssim\|\nabla u\|_2$ has a constant independent of $L$ (the uniform Sobolev estimate (3.18)). The latter bound is needed for the contraction on large tori. In `V` the period is already one; the full $H^1$ norm is used and constants are allowed.

s1-outline-similarity-equation|Breakdown.annotation:
On substituting $U=W+V$ in Equation (1.2), the terms containing only $W$ vanish. The linearized convection is $(W\cdot
abla)V+(V\cdot
abla)W$, and the only remaining quadratic term is $(V\cdot
abla)V$. The equations for $V$ have the free drift and diffusion of (1.2), but no prescribed return law. One seeks decay of $V$, not a second periodic orbit.

s1-outline-monodromy|Breakdown.Monodromy.annotation: The endpoint $h_\chi(t_1)$ is a physical velocity perturbation at the smaller spatial scale of the next period. Applying $D_\lambda$, with $\lambda=e^{-S}$, restores the original scale, and $\rho_R^{-1}$ restores the original orientation. Thus the output of the period map is in the same coordinates as its input; its powers describe successive normalized returns (the map is defined in Equation (4.10)).

s1-outline-compactness|Breakdown.monodro.annotation: It suffices to compare the returns at the last time of a period. Lemma 3.2 makes the mixed kernel compact at positive lag. If we omit the last $\varepsilon$ units of the integral, the omitted operator has norm $O(\varepsilon^{1/4})$, by Equation (3.7) and the bounded local linear evolution. The compactness argument therefore needs no compact kernel at lag zero.

s1-outline-right-inverse|Breakdown.StepD.annotation: The right side of Equation (4.8) is a continuous additive curve, with the same weight as $v$. Its value at zero can be nonzero. Consequently a prescribed change of datum $\chi$ can be included as the curve $e^{t\Delta}\chi$, along with any Duhamel term, while the unknown compact correction is still a separate heat datum.

s1-outline-fixed-time|Breakdown.Transfer.annotation: For the recurrence $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$, impose $\chi_n=O(\Theta^n)$ with $\Theta$ strictly inside the exterior spectral radii. Multiplying the projected recurrence by the backward powers and summing gives $P_u\chi_0=-\sum_{m\ge0}M_u^{-(m+1)}P_uf_m$. The initial correction changes the projection of the given discrepancy to this value (the construction in Section 4.4). The source itself depends on the nonlinear error, so the correction is determined together with the trajectory; neither the singular time nor the phase is varied.

s1-outline-cutoff-error|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The cutoff has two useful properties: it leaves the field unchanged where the singularity forms, and it confines the interaction with a perturbation to the support ball (see Equation (6.9)). In `approxFieldProperties_holds` the two radii are $1/16$ and $1/8$ about $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$; the support is strictly inside the unit cell. Neither property by itself estimates the change in the gradient norm.

s1-outline-kernel-decay|Breakdown.FarFie.annotation: For $x\in Q_L$ and $x\prime\in B_{L/8}$, the distance to the translated source at $x\prime+Lj$ is at least $3L|j|_\infty/8$ for $j\ne0$. Consequently the sum of the noncentral heat responses is bounded by $CL^{-4}\|F\|_1$ and its gradient by $CL^{-5}\|F\|_1$, using Equation (3.9) for derivatives of orders one and two. Taking the $L^6$ and gradient $L^2$ norms over the cell gives $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$ in each case. The linked `lerayKernelBound_holds` supplies the first-derivative bound; the second is also needed for Equation (6.2).

s1-outline-flow-comparison|Breakdown.Per.annotation: For a compact solenoidal datum $f$, writing $f=\operatorname{div}(x\otimes f)$ allows the use of the same decaying kernel as for the nonlinear term. The factor $\|x\otimes f\|_1\le (L/8)\|f\|_1$ changes $L^{-7/2}$ into $L^{-5/2}$ in Equation (6.3). For $f=\bar u(0)$ the mass bound gives $\|f\|_1\lesssim L^2$, so the final error is $O(L^{-1/2})$. For the formal `FreeHeatComparison` the datum is a fixed test field; the comparison is local and includes lag zero, with no claimed power of $L$.

For the nonlinear term the tensor is $\bar u\otimes\bar u$, of $L^1$ norm $\|\bar u\|_2^2\lesssim L$. Hence Equation (6.2) gives $O(L^{-5/2})$ before time integration. In Lean the source is a compactly supported $L^2$ vector field and the comparison is in the local velocity-and-gradient norm, bounded by $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$ for normalized lags in $[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$. Uniformity over the supported sources is needed for an operator comparison; lags below $\varepsilon$ can be estimated by the separate integrable smoothing bound.

s1-outline-neumann|Breakdown.Periodic.ri.annotation: Let $D=I-\mathcal L\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}$. Solving for $g$ by $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}$ leaves $Dg$ to be solved, and solving for that remainder leaves $D^2g$. Thus $\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\sum_{j\ge0}D^j$ is a right inverse, with norm at most $2\|\mathcal R^{\mathrm a}\|$ when $\|D\|\le1/2$ (as used in Section 6.4). In `rightInversePerturb` one starts with $AR=I$ and takes $D=-(A\prime-A)R$. Only the composition on the source space must be invertible; the linearized map itself need not be injective.

s1-outline-torus-final|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The paper chooses $\kappa$ by the whole-space spectral argument. In the sequence construction let $\lambda=e^{-S/k}$ for $k$ subdivisions of a return, $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$ and $t_n=T-\mu_n$. The selected weight $\lambda^{1/4}<\theta<1$ can be written $\theta=\lambda^\kappa$ with $0<\kappa<1/4$. The normalized velocity is $U_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u(t_n+\mu_ns)$, on $0\le s\le1-\lambda$. Writing $U_n=\bar U_n+\theta^n z_n$ with bounded $z_n$, endpoint matching forces $z_{n+1}(0)=(\lambda^{1/4}/\theta)z_n(1-\lambda)$. This ratio is less than one. The physical error is bounded by $C\mu_n^{-1/4}\theta^n=CT^{-\kappa}\mu_n^{\kappa-1/4}$, which has the rate of Equation (4.5) since $\lambda\mu_n\le T-t\le\mu_n$.

s1-outline-unforced-correction|Breakdown.annotation: The two errors are removed in order. Once the right inverse of $\mathcal L$ has been made exact, the equation for $u=u^{\mathrm a}+z$ is $\mathcal L(\gamma,z)=-F^{\mathrm a}+\mathcal B_{\mathbb T}(z,z)$. The term $-F^{\mathrm a}$ cancels the original mild residual; the mixed terms are already in $\mathcal L$. In `SeqPerturbation` the corresponding source on interval $n$ is $-\theta^{-n}\mathrm{res}_n+\theta^n\mathcal B_n(z_n,z_n)$, with an additional initial discrepancy $\xi$ on the first interval. The contraction makes the corrected mild equation exact (the correction lemma, Lemma 4.8). There is no external force in it, even though the cutoff field used in the construction has a differential residual.

`breakdownOnTorus_of_profile` is the implication from a recurrent nonzero similarity profile to periodic breakdown. Its profile hypotheses include bounds on $\nabla^2 W$ and $\nabla q$ in addition to Equation (1.3). The proof first constructs an unbounded mild trajectory, then uses uniqueness to exclude a global smooth solution with the same periodic datum. The moving-frame reduction allows one to start with a hypothetical global solution whose velocity is periodic without assuming periodic pressure; the breakdown conclusion holds for every positive viscosity. Neither construction here supplies the profile itself; that is the separate certificate problem of Section 7.

s1-outline-certificate-time|Breakdown.ce.annotation: For $\mathcal W(\theta,y)=W(S\theta,y)$ one has $\partial_s W(S\theta)=S^{-1}\partial_\theta\mathcal W(\theta)$. Thus $S$ appears in the coefficient of the time derivative, and the trial fields all have period one (the normalized equation (7.1)). In particular their residuals and constraints can be compared in a single period space when the parameter changes.

s1-outline-certificate-force|Breakdown.c.annotation: For a nonstationary time-periodic solution, translating its phase produces another solution: $\partial_s W$ is then a homogeneous solution of the linearized equation. A phase constraint and a corresponding force direction address this obstruction. Appendix C.4 explains why more such pairs can be useful: one chooses right-hand sides for which the discretized linearized equation has a large response, and constrains the correction in the corresponding response directions. The finite-dimensional computation chooses the fields; Equations (7.18)–(7.21) and Proposition 7.8 establish invertibility on the full domain.

s1-outline-certificate-fixed-point|Break.annotation: At a trial $(\alpha,g)$ solve the linear equation with $-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$ as right-hand side; replace $g$ by the resulting $(v\cdot\nabla)v$, and replace $\alpha$ by the projection onto $K$ of Equation (7.30). The projection is needed at this stage because the adjoint estimates apply to the actual quadratic term, not to an independent trial $g$. The ball of trial fields is weakly compact in $\mathcal H$. At the joint fixed point $g=(v\cdot\nabla)v$, so the adjoint estimates make the projection redundant and force cancellation follows. Lean instead solves the constrained nonlinear equation before updating the parameter.

s1-formal-space-result|Breakdown.breakdo.annotation: The formal theorem excludes every global smooth solution in the bounded-energy class for the constructed datum. It does not give the finite-time solution together with its rate and profile error as in Equation (1.6). This is still sufficient for Fefferman's whole-space nonexistence alternative, provided the profile hypothesis is supplied.

s1-formal-weak-result|Breakdown.certific.annotation: The weak result gives an exact recurrence and the momentum equation tested against compactly supported solenoidal fields. Passing to the smooth profile of Equations (1.2)–(1.3) requires a separate regularity and decay argument. The link uses the earlier rectangular certificate, and neither its premise nor that of the extended theorem is an instantiated numerical certificate.

s2-heat-at-zero|Breakdown.Freq.heat_hold.annotation: At zero lag the heat multiplier is one. For a fixed state $g\in X$, dominated convergence gives $\|G(t)g-g\|_2\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$, even though there is no $L^1$ heat kernel at time zero. This is strong continuity on $X$, as needed for the initial value in Equation (2.4).

s2-bilinear-target|Breakdown.Freq.bilin_.annotation: The important point is not only that $K(\tau)(u,v)\in X$ for positive lag, but that the bound in Equation (3.7) is integrable in $\tau$ near zero. In the formal construction a bounded scalar functional of the third, solenoidal argument is represented by an element of the Hilbert space $X$. The linked theorem gives the resulting bilinear bound, not the full linear assertion of Lemma 3.1.

s2-diagonal|Breakdown.Freq.bilinForm|1.annotation: Putting $v=u$ gives two copies of the same advection term, which cancel the factor $1/2$ in Equation (2.3); the minus sign remains. In the formal dual expression this gives $-\int (u\cdot\nabla)u\cdot(-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}w)$, the pairing against a state with velocity $w$. The definition of the form does not itself establish its boundedness.

s2-duhamel-convergence|Breakdown.VarCons.annotation: Fix $t<b$ and let $M=\max_{[a,t]}\|u(t')\|_X$. By Equation (3.7) the norm of the integrand is bounded by $C_K M^2(t-t')^{-3/4}$, with integral $4C_KM^2(t-a)^{1/4}$. The value assigned to $K(0)$ at the single endpoint does not affect the integral. The abstract statement in Lean also gives continuity of the integral, and states the quantitative bound for intervals of length at most one.

s2-mild-convention|Breakdown.MildFramewo.annotation: A mild solution here is a continuous curve in $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfying Equation (2.4), not a velocity already known to solve the differential equations pointwise. In particular no $L^2$ bound on the curve follows from its definition. The use of smooth compactly supported data in Lemma 2.3 is what permits a return to classical solutions.

s2-every-nearby-datum|Breakdown.Contract.annotation: The heat curve of the prescribed displacement has norm $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa=\|\chi\|_X$: Equation (4.20) gives one inequality, and $t=0$ gives the other. Smallness of the datum is therefore precisely smallness of this particular source in the space on which the inverse acts.

s2-periodic-proposition|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The input of Proposition 2.2 is the whole-space profile; the conclusion is a different solution with periodic data. `TorusBlowup` specifies the existence of an unbounded mild trajectory on the unit torus from smooth periodic solenoidal data. Unlike Equation (2.6), it does not prescribe a two-sided rate or a local comparison with $u_T^*$.

s2-smooth-representative-definition|Brea.annotation: A value of the mild curve is an almost-everywhere class. Smoothness means that one jointly smooth velocity $U(t,x)$ and pressure $P(t,x)$ solve Equation (1.1), with $U(0)$ the specified datum and $U(t)$ representing the mild value for each time. The formal property imposes these conditions on a closed interval and also asks for bounded energy and bounded velocity and spatial gradient there.

s2-energy-nonincrease|Breakdown.EnergyBo.annotation: For the smooth local solution, pairing Equation (1.1) with $u$ and integrating eliminates the transport and pressure terms by zero divergence and yields $\tfrac{d}{dt}\|u(t)\|_2^2=-2\|\nabla u(t)\|_2^2$. This yields the same bound for every $t<T$, even if the gradient diverges as $t\uparrow T$. `EnergyBoundedOn` only asks for some finite bound on a specified closed interval; it is not the dissipation identity.

s2-proof-correction|Breakdown.Contractio.annotation: The cutoff gives a small displacement in $X$, but imposes no conditions on its exterior spectral projection. Inserting its heat evolution into the right inverse of Proposition 4.3 selects the correction needed for the linear problem. The same inverse is then evaluated on the heat curve plus the quadratic Duhamel term, so the corrected datum accounts for the nonlinear interaction as well.

s2-proof-correction|Breakdown.TransferHo.annotation: Take $w_0=\bar u(0)$ with cutoff radius sufficiently large for Equation (5.2). Both $w_0$ and each element of $E$ belong to $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$, so $w_0+\gamma$ belongs to the same class. `TransferHolds` supplies the abstract mild tracking conclusion for data from the dense class; the subsequent regularity argument uses the concrete field.

s2-norm-identification|Breakdown.Freq.X|.annotation: The norms in Equation (2.5) are already the physical gradient norms once the representative is recovered. Hence the lower bound gives gradient divergence and the error divided by the reference gradient norm is $O((1-t)^\kappa)$. The definition of the Fourier space explains the norm being tracked; actual gradient norm identification uses `embedNormLinear_holds` and the realization of the smooth curve, not `X` alone.

s2-finite-codimension|Breakdown.Contract.annotation: For $x\in\ker P_{\mathrm u}$, take $w_0=W(0)+x$. The linear right inverse applied to $e^{t\Delta}x$ gives zero datum correction, since the homogeneous solution already has the required decay. Thus $\gamma=(\mathcal R\mathcal B(v,v))_1$ and $\|\gamma\|_X\lesssim\|x\|_X^2$ by Equations (4.8), (4.19), (4.24). Over the interior space the selected data have the form $W(0)+x+O(\|x\|_X^2)$, giving the tangent space of the selected family at $W(0)$.

pdf-item-equation-3-1|Breakdown.Freq.gra.annotation: The bound (3.1) allows a velocity to be estimated using just its gradient, which is what closes the transport estimate in Lemma 3.1. The linked theorem proves this bound for smooth divergence-free fields with velocity and first-derivative decay as in Equation (1.3), with a constant independent of the decay constant. The paper uses the ambient Sobolev inequality without these pointwise hypotheses.

ns-s3-test-density|Breakdown.Freq.testDe.annotation: Density is used twice: to approximate the fixed argument of $K(\tau)(u,\cdot)$ by a compactly supported field in Lemma 3.2, and to choose test fields projecting onto the finite-dimensional exterior spectral subspace. The latter works since the image of a dense linear subspace under the spectral projection is dense, hence equal to the finite-dimensional range (the basis-lifting argument in Section 4.4). The formal construction cuts off a Schwartz vector potential and takes its curl; it also gives graph-norm density for the negative Laplacian.

pdf-item-equation-3-2|Breakdown.Freq.emb.annotation: Applying Plancherel to the three derivatives gives $\sum_j\int |2\pi\xi_j\hat u|^2=\int 4\pi^2|\xi|^2|\hat u|^2$. Thus the weighted Fourier norm is exactly the gradient norm. The linked equality is proved for embeddings of smooth solenoidal fields with decay as in Equation (1.3), even when the unweighted velocity is not square integrable.

pdf-item-equation-3-4|Breakdown.pushForw.annotation: The argument is pulled back by $R^{-1}$ and the velocity value is pushed forward by $R$. In particular $\nabla(\rho_Ru)(x)=R(\nabla u)(R^{-1}x)R^{-1}$, so its trace and Frobenius norm are preserved. The action includes reflections, as required by the possible isometry in Equation (1.2).

ns-s3-dilation-joint-continuity|Breakdow.annotation: The formal continuity statement fixes the input. For simultaneous changes of parameter and field use $\|D_\mu u-D_{\mu_0}u_0\|_X\le\mu^{1/4}\|u-u_0\|_X+\|(D_\mu-D_{\mu_0})u_0\|_X$. The first term tends to zero by Equation (3.5) near $\mu_0>0$ and the second by the fixed-input theorem. Thus joint continuity follows from the two separate facts.

ns-s3-projected-heat-forcing|Breakdown.F.annotation: For $L^2$ forcing the weighted heat multiplier $2\pi|\xi|e^{-4\pi^2\tau|\xi|^2}$ is bounded by a constant times $\tau^{-1/2}$. The paper needs $L^{3/2}$ forcing instead, because a velocity in $X$ need not be bounded. Heat smoothing from $L^{3/2}$ to $L^2$ costs the additional $\tau^{-1/4}$. The linked operator has only the $L^2$ input domain; it does not prove Equation (3.6).

The formal construction proves the consequence of Equation (3.6) needed in the mild equation directly, by estimating the scalar transport pairing and using the Hilbert-space representation theorem. Its conclusion is Equation (3.7) for the symmetrized transport of two states in $X$. It does not estimate the projected heat evolution of an arbitrary $L^{3/2}$ force as in (3.6).

ns-s3-projection-homogeneity|Breakdown.F.annotation: The longitudinal component at nonzero $\xi$ is $Q_\xi z=\xi(\xi\cdot z)/|\xi|^2$. On replacing $\xi$ by $c\xi$, $c\ne0$, numerator and denominator acquire the same factor $c^2$. Subtracting the unchanged $Q_\xi$ from the identity gives the homogeneity of $\mathbb P_\xi$ needed for the dilation in Equation (3.8).

ns-s3-integrable-divergence-kernel|Break.annotation: The undifferentiated tensor has the borderline bound $|x|^{-3}$ at infinity in dimension three. On a tensor divergence the derivative may instead be moved onto the Oseen tensor, giving the faster decay $|x|^{-4}$. The linked theorem establishes integrability of each derivative component and its $O(\tau^{-1/2})$ norm; the convolution identity itself is Equation (3.10).

ns-s3-derivative-convolution-definition|.annotation: For $u,v\in X$, the tensor $F=u\otimes v$ belongs to $L^3$ by Equation (3.1). At a fixed $\tau>0$, Equation (3.9) gives $\nabla O_\tau\in L^{3/2}$, so the integral defining `kernelConv` is absolutely convergent at each $x$, with bound $C\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{3/2}\|F\|_3$. In particular the second formula of Equation (3.10) does not require $F\in W^{1,1}$ as in the first.

ns-s3-tensor-product|Breakdown.FarField..annotation: The divergence is taken in the second index: $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)_j=\sum_m\partial_m(v_j u_m)=(u\cdot\nabla)v_j+v_j\operatorname{div}u$. Thus the order of the factors is reversed relative to the advection notation. Symmetrization in Equation (3.10) includes both orders.

ns-s3-convolution-mixed-inputs|Breakdown.annotation: For the density argument in the paper, $1+1/6=5/6+1/3$, so Young's inequality gives convergence of the convolutions in $L^6$. The formal proof uses $\nabla O_\tau\in L^{3/2}$ to obtain uniform convergence in $x$ instead. On the other side the reconstructed velocities converge in $L^6$ by Equations (3.7) and (3.1); take a subsequence converging almost everywhere to identify the limits. The formal extension assumes the identity and the decay of its convolution for test fields.

ns-s3-convolution-test-to-energy|Breakdo.annotation: For a compact solenoidal test $\varphi$, the tensor $\varphi\otimes\varphi$ is compact and smooth, so the first identity of Equation (3.10) applies directly. `BilinTestKernel` states the resulting diagonal identity in $X$, with the minus sign from Equation (2.3). The separate decay hypothesis ensures that the convolution can be embedded and recovered as a physical velocity.

ns-s3-compact-monodromy|Breakdown.Monodr.annotation: In the period map the initial datum is varied, while the reference $u^*(t')$ in the mixed integral is fixed at each $t'$. Lemma 3.2 gives norm-null integrands for weakly null linearized trajectories, and Equation (3.7) gives an integrable majorant. For the formal short-step proof, fix a test factor $f$ and truncate the last $\epsilon$ units, at cost $O(\epsilon^{1/4})$. At the remaining lags use $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)=G(\tau-\epsilon)K(\epsilon)(f,\cdot)$: the heat images of the compact closure at lag $\epsilon$ have compact closure over the bounded time interval. Approximation of the continuous coefficient curve by finite sums of such factors gives compactness of the mixed endpoint integral. The full return is obtained by composing short steps.

ns-s3-compactness-operator-continuity|Br.annotation: For $\|v\|_X\le1$, Equation (3.7) gives $\|K(\tau)(u,v)-K(\tau)(\varphi,v)\|_X\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u-\varphi\|_X$. The bound is independent of $v$, which is why this is convergence in operator norm, the topology in which compact operators are closed. `bilinX` selects the continuous bilinear map whose bound is proved in `bilin_holds`.

ns-3late-abstract-space|Breakdown.HeatBi.annotation: The time-integral arguments no longer use the Fourier transform or the spatial realization of $\mathcal X$. They use completeness for the Bochner integral, strong continuity, and the heat and bilinear laws (3.11)–(3.12). Consequently the same uniqueness and restart proof applies on $X$ and on the mean-zero torus spaces of Section 3.6.

ns-3late-abstract-mild|Breakdown.HeatBil.annotation: On $[a,b)$, each integral in Equation (2.4) only involves the compact interval $[a,t]$, $t<b$, on which the two inputs are bounded in $\mathcal X$. Thus the integral is well defined even when $\|u(t)\|_{\mathcal X}$ is unbounded as $t\uparrow b$. There is no initial assumption of a classical velocity or pressure.

pdf-item-theorem-3-5|Breakdown.restrict|.annotation: Evolve the equation at $m$ by $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$. The free term becomes $e^{(t-a)\Delta}u(a)$ and the integral becomes $\int_a^m K(t-t')(f(t'),h(t'))dt'$ by Equation (3.12). Subtract these terms from the equation at $t$. The only surviving integral is over $[m,t]$.

pdf-item-equation-3-13|Breakdown.restric.annotation: To move the heat operator through the integral, one uses boundedness of $e^{(t-m)\Delta}$ on $\mathcal X$ and Bochner integrability from Lemma 3.3. The upper endpoint $t'=m$ of the earlier integral is a null set, so Equation (3.12) is only needed at positive lag. `restrict` implements the identity when both inputs are the solution.

ns-3late-restart-consequence|Breakdown.r.annotation: The datum after a restart is the value of the same solution, so both uniqueness and estimates can be applied on an interval chosen for the time of interest. In Section 7.10 one takes $m=2t-1$ for an ancient solution, making the heat interval have length $1-t$ and keeping the similarity scale comparable throughout it.

ns-3late-weak-assumptions|Breakdown.Freq.annotation: In the weak equation the pressure drops out against compact solenoidal tests. The paper assumes continuity in $X$ and Equation (3.14). In `IsWeakSolution` one also requires smooth decaying slices and $u(t)-u(t')\in L^2$ for every pair of times, with $\|u(t)-u(t_0)\|_2\to0$ as $t\to t_0$ within the interval. The difference condition permits infinite energy of the slices themselves.

The weak equation gives the derivative of scalar test pairings, while Equation (2.4) gives an equality of velocities in $X$. It is the latter that permits uniqueness against the mild trajectories of Lemma 3.5. `MildOfWeak` has the same type of conclusion on $[a,b]$, under the stronger hypotheses of `IsWeakSolution`.

ns-3late-weak-equation|Breakdown.Freq.Is.annotation:
The linear term in Equation (3.14) is $\int u\cdot\Delta\psi=-\int
abla u:
abla\psi$. For the nonlinear term integrate $\sum_{i,j}u_i u_j\partial_i\psi_j$ by parts; since $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the result is $-\int (u\cdot
abla)u\cdot\psi$. These are the two negative terms in `IsWeakSolution`, where the scalar derivative is required in the interior and the pairings are continuous up to both endpoints.

ns-3late-weak-to-mild|Breakdown.Freq.Mil.annotation: Once the scalar test identity gives Equation (2.4), the same datum $u(a)$ and the same curve in $X$ can be used in the restart and uniqueness lemmas. No separate existence problem for a mild solution is being solved. The formal `MildOfWeak` makes this identification for the smooth-decay class with continuous $L^2$ differences.

ns-3late-periodic-functions|Breakdown.Pe.annotation: The $L^p$ norm in Section 6 uses the unnormalized measure of a cell. If $v(z)=f(Lz)$, the $L^p$ norms differ by the factor $L^{3/p}$, even though their Fourier coefficients at corresponding frequencies are the same. This accounts for the factor $L^3$ in Equation (3.15) and the volume factors in Equation (6.2). `IsPeriodic` fixes the period at one.

pdf-item-equation-3-17|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Because $K_{\mathbb T}$ is symmetric, the cross terms in $K_{\mathbb T}(u^{\mathrm a}+z,u^{\mathrm a}+z)$ combine to $2K_{\mathbb T}(u^{\mathrm a},z)$. The linearized operator in Equation (6.6) contains this term with a minus sign; the term with both inputs $z$ is the quadratic remainder. `kernel_symm` follows directly from the symmetrized convolution.

ns-3late-periodic-heat-laws|Breakdown.Pe.annotation: At $t=a$ in Equation (2.4) the integration interval has length zero. The free evolution must return the datum, which is precisely `heat_zero`: each Fourier multiplier is one, including at frequency zero.

s3-periodic-sobolev-proof-dependency|Bre.annotation: The two factors of the advection have norms in $L^6$ and $L^2$, giving $1/6+1/2=2/3$. To bound their product in $L^{3/2}$ by two gradient norms uniformly in the period one needs precisely Equation (3.18). A bound in terms of two inhomogeneous norms followed by Poincaré would not give such a uniform constant. The linked formal kernel estimate uses the full $H^1$ norm at unit period.

pdf-item-theorem-3-7|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: In `sourceOp_threeHalves` the source $A$ is inserted as $A((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$, with no amplitude change. Its $L^{3/2}$ norm is multiplied by $\mu$, and the heat lag $\mu\tau$ costs $(\mu\tau)^{-3/4}$; the resulting factor is $\mu^{1/4}$. The interaction operator used below includes the inverse factor $\mu^{-1/4}$, so its bound is uniform in the scale. The formal estimate takes supported $L^2$ sources and $0<\mu\tau\le1$, unlike the unrestricted positive lags of Equation (3.19).

The nonlinear source has mean zero because it is the divergence of $v\otimes u+u\otimes v$. Its $L^{3/2}$ norm is bounded by $\|u\|_6\|\nabla v\|_2+\|v\|_6\|\nabla u\|_2$. Inserting this into Equation (3.19) and using Equation (3.18) gives Equation (3.20), including the factor $1/2$ in Equation (3.17). The formal proof uses a Fourier trilinear bound and polarization to give the analogous operator estimate on `V`, for $0<\tau\le1$.

ns-3late-periodic-force-bound|Breakdown..annotation: For the dual estimate put $z=e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb P f$ and $\Psi=-\Delta e^{\tau\Delta}z$. The pairing $\int f\cdot\Psi$ equals $\|z\|_{\dot H^1}^2$. The multipliers of $\Psi$ and its gradient give $\|\Psi\|_2\lesssim\tau^{-1/2}\|z\|_{\dot H^1}$ and $\|\nabla\Psi\|_2\lesssim\tau^{-1}\|z\|_{\dot H^1}$. By Equation (3.18), interpolation gives $\|\Psi\|_3\lesssim\tau^{-3/4}\|z\|_{\dot H^1}$; pair with $f$ and divide by the norm of $z$ when nonzero. The inhomogeneous formal estimate uses the corresponding test with multiplier $1+4\pi^2|k|^2$.

ns-3late-periodic-kernel-bound|Breakdown.annotation: For bounded inputs on an interval of length $h\le1$, integrating Equation (3.20) costs $\int_0^h\tau^{-3/4}d\tau=4h^{1/4}$. The mixed linear term therefore has operator norm at most $8C_{\mathbb T}h^{1/4}$ times the bound of the reference velocity on that interval. The same small-interval factor is available from `KernelSharpBound` after the time normalization in `stepFrame`.

ns-s4-003|Breakdown.physicalField|1.annotation: In $D_\mu$ the velocity factor is $\sqrt\mu$. For Equation (4.1) the choice $\mu=(T-t)^{-1}$ therefore gives the spatial scale $\mu^{-1/2}=\sqrt{T-t}$ and the correct velocity prefactor $(T-t)^{-1/2}$. The argument of $W$ still uses its own logarithmic time.

pdf-item-equation-4-1|Breakdown.physical.annotation: Scaling the two bounds in Equation (1.3) gives $(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)^{-1}$ for the velocity and $(\sqrt{1-t}+|x|)^{-2}$ for its gradient. The inequalities on the right of (4.1) discard $\sqrt{1-t}$ to give bounds uniform in time away from zero. In the next paragraph the full denominators must be kept near zero, where $|x|^{-2}$ is not square integrable.

ns-s4-014|Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSi.annotation: The rescaling in `selfSimilar` reads the field in $X$. With $s_0=0$ the time advance adds $S$ to its phase, and recurrence replaces the slice by $\rho_R$ of the old one. The dilation gains $D_{1/\lambda}$; commuting the two actions gives Equation (4.2).

ns-s4-018|Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatemen.annotation: For the short-piece version of Equation (4.3), take $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $j=nk+r$ with $0\le r<k$. The $j$th piece samples the phase $jS/k-\log(1-\sigma)$ and its normalized profile equals $\rho_R^n$ of the $r$th piece. The additional $D_{\mu^{-j}}$ restores physical units. `ProfilePieceStatement` also verifies mildness and matching at the endpoints.

ns-s4-018|Breakdown.MildFramework.selfSi.annotation: Since $1-(t_n+\lambda^n\sigma)=\lambda^n(1-\sigma)$, the sampled phase is $nS-\log(1-\sigma)$. The physical dilation splits as $D_{\lambda^{-n}}D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}$. Substitution into `selfSimilar` and $n$ applications of recurrence prove Equation (4.3).

ns-s4-019|Breakdown.Freq.DilationAlgebra.annotation: In Equation (4.3) the isometry has norm one, and $D_{\lambda^{-n}}$ multiplies the gradient norm by $\lambda^{-n/4}$. Therefore $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u^*(t)\|_X=(1-\sigma)^{1/4}\|u^*(\sigma)\|_X$. The factor on the right lies in $[\lambda^{1/4},1]$ for $0\le\sigma<t_1$, giving the two constants in the proof.

ns-s4-019|Breakdown.monodromy|4.annotation: The dilation in Equation (4.3) is undone when defining the return of a linearized perturbation. If $h_\chi$ solves Equation (4.9), then $M\chi=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda h_\chi(t_1)$. Without the interaction with $u^*$ this becomes $M_0\chi=\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}\chi$, of norm at most $\lambda^{1/4}$. Lemma 4.4 makes $M-M_0$ compact. The growth rate of the reference itself in Equation (4.4) is not the norm of $M$.

ns-s4-020|Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatemen.annotation: In the induction the normalized variable $\sigma$ is unchanged by the advance: $1-\lambda(1-t)=t_{n+1}+\lambda^{n+1}\sigma$. Every application contributes one $\rho_R$ and one $D_{1/\lambda}$. Their commutation gives the powers in Equation (4.3); the short-piece theorem uses the same endpoint matching with step factor $\mu$.

ns-s4-022|Breakdown.orbitBound|2.annotation: The maximum on $[0,t_1]$ is finite by continuity into $X$, including at $t_1<1$. All subsequent periods have the same normalized values by Equation (4.3). Equivalently, `orbitBound` bounds the continuous similarity-time norm by its maximum on one period, before the physical dilation.

ns-s4-025|Breakdown.Piece|1.annotation: On $[0,b]$ the weight in Equation (4.5) lies between $(1-b)^{1/4-\kappa}$ and one; thus the ordinary and weighted supremum norms are equivalent there. The equivalence is not uniform as $b\uparrow1$. Subdividing in similarity time gives the same compact normalized interval on each step and puts all the dependence on the physical time into the scaling factors.

ns-s4-026|Breakdown.orbitSeq|4.annotation: An additive source curve acts throughout a period. Its endpoint alone is insufficient to determine the discrete forcing: in Equation (4.13) the relevant quantity is the endpoint of $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$, since the state is $v_n(0)-g_n(0)$. The bounded-sequence recurrence `orbitSeq` is obtained by dividing this state and forcing by $\Theta^n$.

ns-s4-027|Breakdown.PieceOperatorStateme.annotation: In Equation (4.8), $e^{t\Delta}\gamma$ means the entire heat curve. Its evaluation at time zero is $\gamma$, whereas its value at the end of a period is the freely evolved datum. `pieceFree` is the operator $\Gamma:X\to\mathrm{Piece}$ giving this curve on one short interval; it has norm at most one.

ns-s4-029|Breakdown.PiecePerturbationSta.annotation: The error equation retains the two mixed terms as $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)$ and the entire quadratic term as $\mathcal B(v,v)$. Since $u^*$ is an exact solution, its pure term cancels. Solving Equation (4.7) is therefore equivalent to solving the mild equation for $u^*+v$, with its shifted initial value; no approximation is made at this step.

pdf-item-equation-4-7|Breakdown.varConst.annotation: Equation (4.7) makes sense on every $[0,b]$ with $b<1$, since the inputs are bounded there and $(t-t')^{-3/4}$ is integrable. `varConstIntegral` gives this local assertion. Control of the quadratic term in the weighted norm on all of $[0,1)$ is a further estimate, proved in Equations (4.18)–(4.19).

ns-s4-032|Breakdown.exists_section|2.annotation: For a fixed $g$, any two admissible data in Equation (4.12) differ by an element of $\ker P_{\mathrm u}$: their difference evolves homogeneously, and the inverse power bound forces its exterior projection to vanish. Conversely an interior displacement has the required decay. Taking the datum in the complementary space $E$ selects exactly one point of this affine space.

pdf-item-equation-4-8|Breakdown.Contract.annotation: The use of (4.8) in the nonlinear problem is to insert $g=e^{t\Delta}\chi+\mathcal B(v,v)$. At a fixed point of its second component, the resulting pair solves Equation (4.7) with $v(0)=\chi+\gamma$. One does not first solve the nonlinear equation and then choose the correction.

ns-s4-037|Breakdown.MonodromyStatement|2.annotation: The recurrence of the background multiplies it by $\rho_R D_{1/\lambda}$ over one period. Both operations are invertible and commute, so undoing them on the final perturbation gives exactly $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda h_\chi(t_1)$. This is why there is no forward rotation in Equation (4.10).

ns-s4-039|Breakdown.MonodromyStatement|2.annotation: A free step is $B=D_\mu e^{(1-\mu)\Delta}$, with norm at most $\mu^{1/4}$. The Lean proof only needs $\|B^k\|\le\mu^{k/4}$. To identify it with the paper’s free map, use Equation (3.5): $B^2=D_{\mu^2}e^{(1-\mu^2)\Delta}$, since the heat times add as $(1-\mu)+\mu(1-\mu)$. Hence $B^k=D_\lambda e^{t_1\Delta}$ and $\rho_R^{-1}B^k$ is the desired return.

ns-s4-043|Breakdown.DichotomyHolds|1.annotation: The gap is needed for the forced equation, even if all homogeneous solutions under consideration decay. At a multiplier $\Theta$, the recurrence $x_{n+1}=\Theta x_n+\Theta^n$ has solution $\Theta^n x_0+n\Theta^{n-1}$. No choice of $x_0$ removes the factor $n$. The strict inequalities in Equation (4.11) make both sums converge at the desired rate.

ns-s4-053|Breakdown.PeriodicInverseState.annotation: Apply the semigroup restart to the part of Equation (4.12) which has a heat term and a Duhamel integral, namely $v-g$. The contribution of the earlier intervals is then the heat evolution of $(v-g)(t_n)$, and $g(t)$ is left unchanged. In particular the restarted datum is not $v(t_n)$ unless $g(t_n)=0$.

ns-s4-055|Breakdown.orbitSeq|1.annotation: The forcing in the recurrence is obtained from the entire response $\mathcal U g_n$ after subtracting $g_n$ itself. For example, if $g_n$ is a heat curve then $(\mathcal U-I)g_n$ is the part of its evolution produced by the mixed term. This explains why Equation (4.13) is not simply a rescaled value of $g$ at the next time.

ns-s4-057|Breakdown.orbitSeq|1.annotation: The key point of the second identity in Equation (4.14) is that $f_n$ is independent of $\chi_0$. Thus the datum can be chosen using the entire sequence of $f_n$, computed from the prescribed $g$. For the nonlinear equation we first fix a trial quadratic source, apply this linear selection, then use the resulting trajectory to update the source.

ns-s4-059|Breakdown.PeriodicInverseState.annotation: Splitting the integral at $t_n$ and using Equation (3.12), the part before $t_n$ is the heat evolution of $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)(t_n)$. Adding the original heat term yields the heat evolution of $v(t_n)-g(t_n)$. The remaining integral begins at $t_n$; this is the exact restart identity even when $g$ has no time derivative.

ns-s4-061|Breakdown.MildFramework.stepOp.annotation: Upon setting $t'=t_n+\lambda^n\sigma'$, the factor $dt'=\lambda^n d\sigma'$ cancels the inverse time-scaling factor of $K$. In formulas, for $\mu=\lambda^n$, $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(a,b)=K(\tau)(D_\mu a,D_\mu b)$. Isometry equivariance and Equation (4.3) then return the mixed kernel to $K(\sigma-\sigma')(u^*(\sigma'),v_n(\sigma'))$.

ns-s4-063|Breakdown.orbitSeq|1.annotation: At the common physical endpoint of periods $n$ and $n+1$ the two normalized values differ by $\rho_R^{-1}D_\lambda$. Applying this map to $v_n(t_1)-g_n(t_1)$ gives $\chi_{n+1}$. With $v_n=h_{\chi_n}+\mathcal U g_n$, its homogeneous term is $\mathcal M\chi_n$ and its source is precisely the difference in Equation (4.13).

ns-s4-075|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: The residual is the difference between the proposed curve and the mild formula with its own initial value. It is zero at the left endpoint whether or not the curve solves the equation. The sign in Equation (4.17) is negative because the error must cancel this defect; in the piece version this also makes the residual contribution zero at each restart.

ns-s4-076|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: The defect in Equation (4.16) is a mild-equation residual, so its norm is measured after the heat evolution and time integration, in the same space as the velocity error. This is the norm estimated in Lemma 6.2. In the formal sequence setting the analogous local defect is divided by $\theta^n$; its smallness is a bound uniform in $n$.

ns-s4-079|Breakdown.PiecePerturbationSta.annotation: At zero, Equation (4.17) gives $v(0)=\chi+J\gamma$ because both the residual and the integrals vanish there. With $u^{\mathrm a}=u^*$ the residual vanishes identically; the corresponding local perturbation implication gives the exact corrected mild solution on a compact interval.

ns-s4-083|Breakdown.varConstIntegral|1.annotation: The two products have different time dependence: the quadratic product has exponent $2\kappa-1/2$, and the interaction of a bounded field with a $C_0$ field has exponent $-1/4$. On $0<1-t'\le1$ both are bounded by $(1-t')^{\kappa-1/2}$. The common integral (4.18) therefore controls both the estimate in Equation (4.19) and the cutoff estimate (4.21).

ns-s4-083|Breakdown.PieceOperatorStateme.annotation: On a compact interval the kernel estimate gives the factor $4C_KL^{1/4}$ times two ordinary supremum norms. These norms need not be bounded as the interval approaches time one. Substitution in Equation (4.18) keeps the pointwise time-dependent input powers inside the integral and gives an output bound uniform in the weighted norm.

pdf-item-equation-4-19|Breakdown.PieceOp.annotation: The estimate loses some of the decay of a product of two errors: their product has the power $(1-t')^{2\kappa-1/2}$. In fact Equation (4.18) with $\eta$ in place of $\kappa$ bounds $\mathcal B(v,v')$ in $C_\eta$ whenever $\eta\le2\kappa$ and $0<\eta<1/4$. For the fixed point it is enough to take $\eta=\kappa$, without changing the spectral circle used for the inverse.

ns-s4-086|Breakdown.varConstIntegral|1.annotation: The bounded input in Equation (4.21) need not decay in physical time. In Section 6 it is the difference $\bar u-u^*$, whose ordinary supremum norm is $O(L^{-1/2})$ by Equation (6.4). The other factor is allowed the reference rate in $C_0$. This estimate makes their mixed Duhamel term small in the stronger $C_\kappa$ norm required by the inverse.

ns-s4-088|Breakdown.HeatBilinear|1.annotation: The lag $t-t'$ controls smoothing, while the time to the singularity $1-t'$ controls the size of the inputs. Their relation is $1-t'=(1-t)+(t-t')$. The substitution in Equation (4.18) separates out the current remaining time $1-t$ and leaves a dimensionless integral, whose finiteness is what makes the bound uniform in $t$.

pdf-item-equation-4-22|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: The inverse is applied to trial right-hand sides, and only its second component is iterated. The parameter space $E$ therefore needs no norm in Lemma 4.8. A bound for the parameter is available if the inverse has one, as in Equation (4.8) or the bounded sequence inverse, and is needed for the Lipschitz estimate of the selected datum in Section 5.2.

ns-s4-092|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: Let $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. The radius is $\delta=2C_{\mathcal R}a$, and on this ball the Lipschitz constant of the inverse applied to the quadratic term is at most $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta=4CC_{\mathcal R}^2a$. The square in Equation (4.23) thus comes once from the size of the solution and once from applying the inverse to a difference.

ns-s4-093|Breakdown.Periodic.SeqPerturba.annotation: With $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$, Equation (4.24) gives a trajectory of size at most $2C_{\mathcal R}a$. If the known input vanishes then the selected fixed point is zero. In the formal sequence estimate the bound is $2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$ on the divided pieces; the actual normalized error has the additional factor $\theta^n$.

ns-s4-095|Breakdown.ContractionInternal..annotation: For the generic fixed-point lemma take $b=C_{\mathcal R}a$ and $K=CC_{\mathcal R}$, with $a=\|e^{t\Delta}\chi-F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$. Its hypothesis $8Kb\le1$ is exactly Equation (4.23) for $\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$. It gives a fixed point in the closed ball of radius $2b$.

ns-s4-098|Breakdown.ContractionInternal..annotation: Bilinearity gives $\mathcal B(v',v')-\mathcal B(v'',v'')=\mathcal B(v'-v'',v')+\mathcal B(v'',v'-v'')$. Each term contains the difference once and an unchanged factor of norm at most $\delta$. With Equation (4.19) and the bound for the inverse this gives Lipschitz constant $2CC_{\mathcal R}\delta\le1/2$.

ns-s4-099|Breakdown.ContractionInternal..annotation: The fixed-point equation alone is an equality of trajectories. Recovering $\gamma$ from the first component of the same inverse evaluation gives the whole pair satisfying Equation (4.17). For a fixed inverse this choice is unique in the contraction ball; Lemma 4.8 does not assert uniqueness of corrections obtained from other inverses.

ns5.cutoff.parameter|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The radius is held fixed during each evolution. On $\mathbb R^3$ the cutoff changes only the datum; on the torus it changes the reference at every time. In the latter case $r=L/8$ makes the support a fixed ball, which is why the entire mixed advection in Equation (6.9) is determined by the perturbation restricted to that ball.

ns5.proof.uniformity|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The constants in the cutoff estimate do not deteriorate with time: outside $B_{r/2}$ the physical decay bounds of Equation (4.1) have no singular time factor, and inside the potential integral the powers of $\sigma$ compensate the bounds at $\sigma x$. The corresponding `cutoffGradientClose` estimate is uniform in $T,t$ with $T>0$ and $T-t$ positive and sufficiently small.

ns5.proof.differentiate|Breakdown.Period.annotation: Differentiating in a unit direction $v$ gives $\sigma^2 Dg(\sigma x)v\times x+\sigma g(\sigma x)\times v$. Thus a derivative of $g$ is accompanied by two powers of $\sigma$, and the undifferentiated $g$ by one. The two inverse-distance bounds of Equation (4.1) have precisely the powers that these factors cancel. `partialAt_potential` gives the coordinate version of the differentiation.

ns5.proof.exterior|Breakdown.Periodic.Ap.annotation: Outside the cutoff support, the error is exactly $-u^*$, and differentiation introduces no terms from $\eta$ or $A$. The gradient bound follows at once from Equation (4.1). `fderiv_diff_outer` gives the corresponding identity with the opposite sign for $D(W-f)$ beyond the scaled support radius; the boundary follows by continuity and the norm is insensitive to the sign.

ns5.correction.zerodefect|Breakdown.orbi.annotation: The reference has no defect: $F^{\rm a}=u^*-e^{t\Delta}u^*(0)-B(u^*,u^*)=0$ by Proposition 4.1. Accordingly Equation (4.17) has right-hand side $e^{t\Delta}\chi+B(v,v)$. The initial cutoff contributes only through $\chi$; there is no external force to cancel in the whole-space evolution.

ns5.correction.heat|Breakdown.Freq.HeatS.annotation: In Section 5.2 the reference in Lemma 4.8 is $u^*$ itself, so $F^{\rm a}=0$ and the known source is the heat evolution of $\chi=w_0-W(0)$. The heat contraction gives $\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le\|\chi\|_X$ since $(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\le1$; equality holds at $t=0$. By Equation (5.2), choosing $w_0=\bar u(0)$ with $r$ large makes this source small. No bound on the $L^2$ norm of $w_0$ is required in Equation (4.23).

ns5.correction.error|Breakdown.Contracti.annotation: By Equation (4.24), $\|v\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\|e^{t\Delta}\chi\|_\kappa\le2C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0$. Undoing the norm weight gives the first bound. The second uses the independently chosen inequality $4C_{\mathcal R}\varepsilon_0\le c_*$, not any improvement of the contraction estimate.

ns5.correction.error|Breakdown.TransferH.annotation: Using Equation (4.4), subtract the error estimate from the reference lower bound to obtain $\|u(t)\|_X\ge c_*(1-t)^{-1/4}[1-(1-t)^\kappa/2]$. The bracket is at least $1/2$ throughout the interval. This shows why the uniform comparison matters in addition to asymptotic convergence in similarity variables.

ns5.correction.blowupbounds|Breakdown.or.annotation: The second smallness condition $4C_R\varepsilon_0\le c_*$ is exactly what is needed here. Lemma 4.8 gives $\|v\|_\kappa\le 2C_R\varepsilon_0$. Since $(1-t)^\kappa\le1$, the reverse triangle inequality with Equation (4.4) gives $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_X\ge c_*-2C_R\varepsilon_0\ge c_*/2$ for every $t<1$. The upper bound follows by the ordinary triangle inequality.

ns6.intro-solution|Breakdown.Periodic.To.annotation: The approximate velocity is already smooth and solenoidal, with exactly the desired field on the inner ball. It does not generally solve the periodic equation. The correction must make the equation exact and retain the singular growth. `TorusBlowup` asks for smooth solenoidal data and an unbounded mild $H^1$ trajectory; it does not assert the rate or local approximation in Equation (2.6).

ns6.free-heat-comparison|Breakdown.Perio.annotation: In the divergence convention of Section 3.2, $\sum_m\partial_m(x_j f_m)=f_j+x_j\operatorname{div}f=f_j$. Thus Equation (6.2) can also be used for the free datum; the Leray projection acts trivially on the solenoidal field and on its periodic copy. `freeHeatComparison` proves a direct comparison for a fixed compact test velocity, including zero lag.

pdf-item-equation-6-3|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The factor $L$ lost from Equation (6.2) bounds the first moment $\|x\otimes f\|_1$. For the cutoff datum $\bar u(0)$ this estimate gives $L^{-5/2}O(L^2)=O(L^{-1/2})$, while for $\gamma\in E$ it gives $O(L^{-5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1})$ by the common support of $E$. The fixed-datum formal comparison is closer to the latter use.

ns6.cutoff-properties|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: Formula (5.1) also ensures that every mixed convection term involving $\bar u(t)$ is confined to the same ball, even when the perturbation is not compactly supported. The inner equality is used again at the end, for the comparison in Equation (2.6). `approxFieldProperties_holds` gives the corresponding support, inner equality and solenoidality on a centered unit cell.

pdf-item-equation-6-4|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The cutoff error is uniformly bounded in the unweighted gradient norm: on the annulus its squared gradient integral is $O(L^{-4}L^3)$ and beyond it the tail is $O(L^{-1})$. In the comparison of the linearized equations this lets us use Equation (4.21) with one bounded factor. `cutoffGradientClose` instead estimates the squared difference after pulling back to similarity coordinates, uniformly as the remaining time tends to zero.

ns6.periodic-continuity|Breakdown.Period.annotation: Apply Equation (6.1) to $\bar u(t)-\bar u(t_0)$ to get continuity of $u^{\mathrm a}$ without any comparison of heat flows. For `approxLinks_holds`, two consecutive pieces represent the same continuous physical curve at their common endpoint. The multiplier changes from $\mu_n^{1/4}$ to $\mu_{n+1}^{1/4}$, accounting for the factor $\lambda^{1/4}$.

pdf-item-theorem-6-2|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The equality of gradient norms in Equation (6.5) is exact, since $u^{\mathrm a}$ is one copy of the cutoff in each cell. The formal normalized $H^1$ identity contains a further nonnegative mass term. It can be dropped for the lower bound; the upper bound also needs the separate mass estimate.

pdf-item-equation-6-5|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: After multiplying Equation (6.4) by $(1-t)^{1/4}$, the cutoff contributes at most $CL^{-1/2}(1-t)^{1/4}$ to the error in the normalized profile norm. The estimate (6.5) replaces this by its maximum over time. In `ApproxSizes` the analogous bound is uniform over all normalized pieces.

ns6.residual-definition|Breakdown.Period.annotation: Put $d=\bar u-u^*$. Subtracting the mild equation for $u^*$ gives $\bar F=d-e^{t\Delta}d(0)-\mathcal B(d,\bar u)-\mathcal B(u^*,d)$. In each product one factor is the bounded curve $d$, so Equation (4.21) puts the residual in $C_\kappa$ for the same $\kappa$ as the inverse. Lean obtains a sequence residual by integrating a differential force instead.

ns6.residual-route|Breakdown.Periodic.Ap.annotation: One cannot periodize $\bar F$ using the compact-support construction of Section 6.1: the heat terms have spread outside the ball. The paper compares their compact inputs. In the formal differential route, `ApproxResidualBound` uses $\bar p=\eta(p^*-p^*(a_*))$ with a fixed annular point $a_*$. The subtraction makes the pressure term in the annulus controllable by the given pressure-gradient decay, regardless of the gauge of $p^*$.

ns6.residual-final|Breakdown.Periodic.Ap.annotation: The estimate (6.3) costs $L^{-5/2}\|\bar u(0)\|_1\lesssim L^{-1/2}$, and Equation (6.2) under the integral costs $L^{-7/2}\int_0^t\|\bar u(t\prime)\|_2^2dt\prime\lesssim L^{-5/2}$. Both errors are bounded before applying the time weight. Adding the $C_\kappa$ bound for $\bar F$ gives Lemma 6.2. The formal proof does not require either explicit comparison rate.

ns6.common-support|Breakdown.Periodic.Te.annotation: It suffices to enclose the supports of a finite basis of $E$ in $\bar B_{r_E}$. Every output of the inverse then has that support, regardless of its coefficients. In particular Hölder and Equation (3.1) give $\|\gamma\|_1\lesssim r_E^{5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1}$, with $r_E$ fixed while $L$ increases. `TestLiftExists` supplies this common support for a linear family of compact representatives.

ns6.datum-norm|Breakdown.Periodic.Transp.annotation: The condition $L\ge8r_E$ makes $J=\Pi_L|_E$ an isometry by Equation (6.1). It also ensures that the correction datum may be added to the cutoff before periodization. In `TransplantNorm` the corresponding normalized norm squared is $\|\nabla\gamma\|_2^2+T\|\gamma\|_2^2$ when $\sqrt T r_E\le1/8$; it is uniformly bounded on the unit ball of $E$.

ns6.candidate-inverse|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: A nonzero periodic right-hand side cannot be used as a whole-space $X$ field: its $L^6$ integral over all copies is infinite. But the mixed convection with $\bar u$ is determined by its restriction to the support ball. In Equation (6.12) it is the whole-space heat response to that local convection, not the periodic right-hand side, that is supplied to $\mathcal R$. `ShellInverseTransfer` uses the same separation in the sequence setting.

ns6.local-norm|Breakdown.Periodic.ShellD.annotation: For fixed $L$ this is an equivalent norm on $H^1(B)$, but equivalence constants need not be uniform in $L$: recovering the $L^2$ norm from $L^6$ costs $|B|^{1/3}$. The gradient and $L^6$ terms are the ones needed in Equation (6.8). `ShellData` uses the maximum of three $L^2$ derivative-entry norms and an $L^6$ value norm; arbitrary entries need not be the derivatives of the value field.

ns6.local-restriction|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: The notation $(g+v)|_B$ in Equation (6.12) means the sum of the two restrictions, since the full fields have different domains. In `restrictTorus`, a piece velocity $z$ is pulled back by $x=a+\sqrt\mu y$: its value entry is $\mu^{1/4}z(x)$ and its derivative entries are $\mu^{3/4}\partial_j z(x)$, each cut to the comparison ball.

pdf-item-equation-6-7|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: Restriction decreases the gradient integral, and $\|v\|_{L^6(B)}\le\|v\|_{L^6(\mathbb R^3)}\lesssim\|\nabla v\|_2$ by Equation (3.1). Both constants are independent of the size of $B$. `RestrictR3Bound` gives the analogous uniform bound for the local values and derivatives.

ns6.forcing-continuity|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: To prove continuity, subtract the two product expressions at times $t$ and $t_0$ and put the difference on one factor at a time. Hölder as in Equation (6.8), with both remaining factors bounded near $t_0<1$, gives convergence in $L^{3/2}$. The local curve need not be differentiable in time. `advectShell` supplies the spatial linear map for a fixed background.

ns6.integral-continuity|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The same endpoint estimate applies in the periodic norm because the heat bound is uniform in $L$. In particular the response is continuous in the full space on the torus, before restricting to $B$. This is needed when $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$ is used to reconstruct $z$ in Equation (6.12).

ns6.weighted-local-integral|Breakdown.Pe.annotation: From Equation (6.8) the source size is bounded by $(1-t\prime)^{\kappa-1/2}\|\zeta\|_\kappa$. Substitution $t-t\prime=(1-t)r$ produces $(1-t)^{\kappa-1/4}$ times an integral of $r^{-3/4}(1+r)^{\kappa-1/2}$. Its integrability at infinity requires $\kappa<1/4$. The upper bound on the normalized response in the formal interval construction is obtained using the integrable short-lag kernel and the uniform bound for the background pieces.

pdf-item-equation-6-11|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: For (6.11) the source estimate is on $F_\zeta$, not on its divergence. Hölder costs $L$ to bound the local $L^2$ norm of $\zeta$ by its $L^6$ norm, and Equation (6.4) costs $L^{1/2}$ for $\bar u$. The mass is therefore $O(L^{3/2}\|\zeta\|_B)$; Equation (6.2) leaves $L^{-2}$ with no singularity in the time lag. In Lean the comparison is qualitative and also includes free propagation from preceding pieces.

pdf-item-equation-6-12|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Write $z=g+h$ in Equation (6.6). The equation for $h$ has right-hand side $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}(g|_B)$, which has a whole-space counterpart $\mathcal A(g|_B)$. The inverse of Proposition 4.3 gives a compact datum correction $\gamma$ and a whole-space response $v$ to the latter. Use $g|_B+v|_B$ as the proposed local value of $z$ and reconstruct on the torus; $v$ itself is never periodized.

pdf-item-equation-6-13|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: In $\mathcal L(\gamma,z)-g$ the two heat curves of $\Pi_L\gamma$ cancel, leaving $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}\zeta-\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}(z|_B)$. In particular Equation (6.10) will give a global operator defect from a local estimate for $\zeta-z|_B$. In `chainOp` the interaction factors as $BR_r$ and the free shift and seed are separate linear maps.

ns6.local-agreement|Breakdown.Periodic.c.annotation: The two local values agree at zero for every input: $v(0)=\gamma$ since $\mathcal A(g|_B)(0)=0$, and $z(0)=g(0)+\Pi_L\gamma$. Hence the defect in Equation (6.13) has zero initial value. The remaining issue is the equality of the local values at positive time, not the matching of the prescribed datum.

pdf-item-equation-6-14|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Equation (4.8) uses $u^*$ in the mixed term, whereas Equation (6.9) uses $\bar u$. The identity $2\mathcal B(u^*,v)=\mathcal A(v|_B)-2\mathcal B(\bar u-u^*,v)$ gives (6.14) by linearity of $\mathcal A$. The last term is the sole error in the whole-space equation from changing the background; the periodic heat comparison has not yet entered.

ns6.lemma-6-3|Breakdown.Periodic.shellIn.annotation: In `chainOp`, denote the free shift by $S$, the datum response by $G$, the local interaction response by $B$ and restriction by $R_r$. Put $D=(I-S)^{-1}$. If $(e,v)=R_f(Bw)$ for a local source $w$, then $v=D(Ge+B(w+R_rv))$. Thus $\zeta=w+R_rv$ solves $\zeta-R_rDB\zeta-R_rDGe=w$. After changing these two response maps to their periodic counterparts, take $w=R_t(I-S_t)^{-1}g$ and reconstruct $(I-S_t)^{-1}(g+G_te+B_t\zeta)$. This is the reduced equation implicit in Equation (6.12), with the propagation included.

ns6.inverse-linearity|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: It is important that Proposition 4.3 gives a fixed linear right inverse. The existence of an admissible datum for each individual source would not by itself give a linear defect operator on which to use the series. All other maps in Equation (6.12) are linear, including restriction and the transport of the datum.

ns6.inverse-input-bound|Breakdown.Period.annotation: Restriction by Equation (6.7) followed by Equation (6.10) gives $\|\mathcal A(g|_B)\|_\kappa\lesssim\|g\|_\kappa$. Both constants must be independent of $L$, since the cutoff ball grows. This gives an admissible source for the fixed whole-space inverse. The formal `operatorNormBounds_holds` supplies the separate bounds for the analogous restriction and response operators.

ns6.inverse-local-bound|Breakdown.Period.annotation: The bound on $\zeta$ uses both domains: $\|g|_B\|_\kappa$ is controlled by the periodic Sobolev inequality, and $\|v|_B\|_\kappa$ by Equation (3.1). Their sum is $O(\|g\|_\kappa)$. Thus Equation (6.11) applies to the particular $L$-dependent source produced by the inverse, with the same constants as for an arbitrary local input.

ns6.defect-local-term|Breakdown.Periodic.annotation: In the paper Equation (6.11) applies to the output $\zeta$ of the candidate inverse, although it varies with $L$. In the sequence proof the comparison must be uniform also over the number of intervals. A contribution from piece $m$ to piece $m+j$ has a bound $Cq^j\|\zeta\|$, with $q=\lambda^{1/4}/\theta<1$. The terms with large $j$ have a uniformly small geometric sum. For bounded $j$ one compares the heat responses on bounded lag windows, with the short-lag part estimated separately. This gives the operator norm bound in `ComparisonSmall`.

ns6.defect-free-term|Breakdown.Periodic..annotation: The support of every $\gamma\in E$ is inside the fixed ball $\bar B_{r_E}$. Therefore the right-hand side in Equation (6.3) is $O(L^{-5/2}\|\gamma\|_{\dot H^1})$, unlike the cutoff datum in Lemma 6.2. In the formal seed comparison, the fixed-datum heat estimate is applied to a basis of the correction space; the finite basis and the geometric decay of the later propagated seeds give a uniform operator estimate.

ns6.defect-cutoff-term|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Use Equation (4.21) with $\bar u-u^*$ as the bounded factor and $v$ as the factor in $C_0$. Its absolute supremum bound is $O(L^{-1/2})$ by Equation (6.4), so the error in $C_\kappa$ is $O(L^{-1/2}\|v\|_0)$. The inequality $\|v\|_0\le\|v\|_\kappa$ then gives the desired bound. `cutoffGradientClose` is a normalized squared-gradient version of the cutoff estimate.

ns6.defect-final|Breakdown.Periodic.Comp.annotation: The three bounds give $\|\zeta-z|_B\|_\kappa\lesssim (L^{-2}+L^{-5/2}+L^{-1/2})\|g\|_\kappa$. Equation (6.13) then applies $\mathcal A_{\mathbb T}$, whose full output norm is bounded by Equation (6.10). Consequently the defect tends to zero in operator norm on the entire periodic source space. `ComparisonSmall` gives the propagated local response comparisons in Lean, not this global candidate-inverse estimate.

pdf-item-equation-6-16|Breakdown.Periodi.annotation: Put $a=\|F^{\mathrm a}\|_\kappa$ and $K=2C_2$. The quadratic map after applying the exact inverse has Lipschitz constant at most $4CK^2a$ on the ball of radius $2Ka$ by Equation (4.19). The bound $K^2a\le\varepsilon_1=(8C)^{-1}$ therefore gives a contraction; the square of the inverse bound comes from the radius and from applying the inverse to a difference. `SeqPerturbation` uses a corresponding sufficient condition including the prescribed datum discrepancy $\xi$.

ns6.global-inverse-hypothesis|Breakdown..annotation: The inverse is now exact on all of $C_\kappa$. Its bound is at most $2C_2$ for the pair, hence in particular for the trajectory as required by Equation (4.22). In the nonlinear equation the source depends on the unknown correction; exact inversion must hold for that source as well as for the original residual. `ShellInverseTransfer` exports such an exact right inverse on the periodic sequence space.

ns6.eq-6-18|Breakdown.Periodic.ApproxSiz.annotation: The reverse triangle inequality gives $(1-t)^{1/4}\|u(t)\|_{\dot H^1(\mathbb T_L^3)}\ge c_*-C_1L^{-1/2}-4C_1C_2L^{-1/2}(1-t)^\kappa$. The last condition of Equation (6.16) bounds the two losses by $c_*/2$ for all times. `ApproxSizes` controls the normalized leading field, before the correction is subtracted.

ns6.corrected-lower-bound|Breakdown.Peri.annotation: The bound in Equation (6.17) makes the correction small relative to the leading singular scale by the factor $L^{-1/2}(1-t)^\kappa$. Uniform smallness over all time gives Equation (6.18), whereas convergence of the ratio to zero suffices for blow-up along a subsequence. `glueUnbounded` uses the latter with $\theta^n Z\to0$.

ns6.scaled-mild-equation|Breakdown.Perio.annotation: The free term commutes with dilation as $D_{L^2}e^{L^2t\Delta}=e^{t\Delta}D_{L^2}$. For the quadratic integral the factor $L^2$ from $t\prime=L^2\tau$ is precisely the factor needed by the last identity of Equation (3.21). Thus the mild equation itself is unchanged, not merely its norm estimates. `GlueMild` constructs the unit-torus mild curve instead by joining normalized pieces.

ns6.inner-ball-rescaling|Breakdown.Perio.annotation: On $B_{1/16}$ the error equals $D_{L^2}z(L^2t)$. By the unit-cell norm equivalence (3.16) its local $H^1$ norm is bounded by a constant times the periodic gradient norm, which is at most $T^{-\kappa}(T-t)^{\kappa-1/4}\|z\|_\kappa$. The coefficient is $O(T^{1/4-\kappa})$ by Equation (6.17). The linked compact-transplant identity is not a statement of this local estimate for the corrected trajectory.

ns6.proposition-2-2-conclusion|Breakdown.annotation: Both estimates of Equation (2.6) have now been obtained. In particular the error on $B_{1/16}$ divided by the singular scale $(T-t)^{-1/4}$ is $O(T^{1/4-\kappa}(T-t)^\kappa)$. `TorusBlowup` retains existence of smooth solenoidal datum and an unbounded mild $H^1$ curve but not the quantitative rate or this local comparison.

ns7-data-s000|Breakdown.PeriodicSimilari.annotation: The input is a smooth nonzero solution in similarity variables, not initial data of compact support or finite energy. The formal proposition also includes decay of the second derivatives and pressure gradient. These are stronger displayed requirements than the velocity and first-derivative bounds in Equation (1.3).

ns7-data-s002|Breakdown.Cert.extendedHel.annotation: On adding Equations (7.10) and (7.12) and expanding the convection of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$, the two mixed terms form $\mathcal C_\alpha v$ and the two residual terms cancel. The remaining equation is $\mathcal T_S(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)+((W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)\cdot\nabla)(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v)\simeq-\sum_i(\beta_i^{\mathrm a}+\beta_i)b_i$. Thus solving for $v$ at a given $\alpha$ gives a forced solution; varying $\alpha$ is what removes the force.

ns7-data-s004|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Set $D=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$. The change of the linearized right-hand side is $(D\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)D$, and Equation (7.19) controls it by $c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$. The factor $c_1+c_0$ in Equation (7.20) occurs because this new right-hand side is charged both in norm and in the finite row measurements.

For each adjoint direction the quadratic term enters through a scalar pairing. Unlike its full $\mathcal H$ norm in Equation (7.49), the pairing in Equation (7.32) is bounded by the square of the period norm alone. On the correction ball this gives the allowance $4\widetilde a_j\varepsilon^2$ for the coefficient estimate.

The purpose of Equation (7.33) is to replace the pairing of the linearized equation with an adjoint field by $(Y\ell(v))_j$. Since the constraints prescribe $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$, this gives a known number plus an error bounded by $a_j\|v\|_w$. Subtracting the quadratic term then isolates a measurement of the auxiliary force.

The inverse estimate bounds the integral of the squared gradient norm over a period. The quadratic term requires its maximum in time as well. Pairing the equation with $-\Delta v$ makes the left side of Equation (7.22) appear with a minus sign in the derivative of the gradient energy; its lower bound therefore limits the increase from a phase of small energy.

ns7-data-s015|Breakdown.Cert.testDenseHo.annotation: Choose $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)$ with $\sum_k\chi(\theta+k)=1$. The periodization of $\chi(\theta)a(\theta)\psi(y)$ is precisely Equation (7.3). For spatial density, first smooth a solenoidal $L^2$ field by the heat flow to obtain a solenoidal $H^1$ field, then use density of compactly supported solenoidal smooth fields in $H^1$. Density of smooth functions on the time circle gives density of the finite sums of products. Thus testing against full-line compactly supported fields suffices for the equality of the period-space projections.

ns7-data-s017|Breakdown.IsPerturbation|1.annotation: For a field with a nonzero angular tail $r^{-1}A(y/r)$, the radial integrals for its sixth and second powers at infinity are proportional to $\int_1^\infty r^{-4}\,dr$ and $\int_1^\infty 1\,dr$, respectively. Thus a smooth cutoff of such a tail may have finite homogeneous $H^1$ norm without being in $L^2$. To belong to $\mathcal D_S$ it must in addition satisfy the transport condition in Equation (7.4), as the following example illustrates.

ns7-data-s019|Breakdown.Cert.Internal.Fr.annotation: The energy identity requires values at individual phases, whereas $v\in L^2((0,1);X)$ initially determines a field only almost everywhere in time. The paper obtains a continuous representative by passing to Eulerian variables as in Equation (7.40) and applying the Hilbert-space energy lemma there. In `exists_energyCurve` Lean instead approximates the free right-hand side $f$ by fields from a dense linear space: the estimate $\sup_\theta\|c_n(\theta)-c_m(\theta)\|_X\le\sqrt{4+6S}\,\|f_n-f_m\|_{\mathcal H}$ gives uniform convergence of the continuous periodic gradient states. The limit is an $X$-valued curve, not merely a continuous scalar energy.

ns7-data-s022|Breakdown.IsPerturbation.i.annotation: In Lean the relation is written with spatial argument $Ry$, so it becomes $v(\theta+\theta_0,Ry)=Rv(\theta,y)$. This is Equation (7.5) after changing variables. For the weak perturbation the equality is almost everywhere.

ns7-data-s023|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: When $(R,1/2)\in\Gamma$, the field at the next half-period may be different, but the gradient norm is unchanged under the orthogonal change of variables. It is the energy, not the velocity or the supplied residual representative, that can be followed for half a period in Proposition 7.9. Summing the energy increment over two translated intervals gives the improvement by $1/2$ in Equation (7.55). Lean also allows the conservative choice $m=1$ in this case.

ns7-data-s024|Breakdown.Cert.invariantHH.annotation: Writing the time shift with a minus sign in the operator $\rho_{R,\theta_0}$ makes Equation (7.5) precisely the fixed-point condition $\rho_{R,\theta_0}F=F$. Orthogonality of $R$ and translation invariance of the time-circle measure make this an isometry on $\mathcal H$.

ns7-data-s026|Breakdown.Cert.extendedInv.annotation: The residual need not itself be invariant. Nevertheless the other terms in Equation (7.10) are invariant distributions and therefore have invariant pairings with solenoidal tests. Since (7.10) fixes the Leray projection of the residual, $\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ belongs to $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma$. This is what allows the constrained solve to use the given residual.

ns7-data-s027|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The geometry of $K$ will be needed only to make the final parameter update admissible. At a fixed parameter the constrained inverse is constructed without using that geometry. The formal `params` already incorporates the scaled ball and intervals of Equation (7.29).

ns7-data-s028|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The family is chosen to make the eventual force cancellation possible, not merely to interpolate between numerical profiles. In Appendix C.4 the directions $W^i$, with changes in period and in forcing coefficients, are obtained by approximately solving linearized equations with prescribed constraint values. In Equation (B.9) the family is affine in $\alpha$ inside the ball where the radial phase is fixed; outside it, a change of the period also changes the phase. This explains why the construction is not globally affine.

For fixed $\alpha$, $1/S(\alpha)$ is a given coefficient of $\partial_\theta$. A single normalized time circle therefore suffices for the family. The choice (B.9) makes $1/S(\alpha)$, rather than $S(\alpha)$, affine in $\alpha$; the same variation in the far-field radial phase is needed to cancel the leading transport term in the oscillatory tail (Appendix C.4). No derivative of the unknown exact period is needed in the trial equation.

ns7-data-s029|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: In Equation (7.55) the factors $2S(\alpha)/m$ bound the growth of the slice energy over a period. Using the uniform $S_{\max}$ instead makes Equation (7.27) a single sufficient inequality for all trial parameters.

ns7-data-s030|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: In the limit of the equations (7.57), the two terms in $\mathcal C_\alpha v$ involve $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $\nabla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$. Joint continuity makes these coefficients converge uniformly on the support of each test; the weak gradient and local strong velocity convergence then suffice. In Equation (7.58) integration by parts similarly removes the need for continuity of the Hessian. Lean assumes a $C^1$ extension jointly in the ambient parameter, time and space, stronger than the stated continuity hypotheses.

ns7-data-s031|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Both convection and the free operator preserve the prescribed symmetry. Applied to Equation (7.10), this makes the projected residual invariant, even if the chosen residual representative is not. Later, the same symmetry of the correction and approximate field gives Equation (7.39) for their sum.

The map $\beta\mapsto\sum_i\beta_i b_i$ has operator norm from Euclidean space to $\mathcal H$ at most $(\sum_i\|b_i\|_{\mathcal H}^2)^{1/2}\le b_*$. This estimate does not require orthogonality. In the energy estimate (7.55) the force therefore contributes at most $b_*|\beta|\|v\|_w$. Injectivity of the projected forcing map is a different matter: it follows from Equation (7.18) by taking $v=0$ and $F=0$ if $\sum_i\beta_i b_i\simeq0$.

The force fields $b_i$ are fixed; continuity of $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ therefore gives strong continuity of the finite linear combination in $\mathcal H$. For the residual it will suffice to know continuity after testing modulo gradients, as shown in Equation (7.58).

ns7-data-s031|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The residual is a representative of the left side of Equation (7.10) modulo gradients.
