In Lean `defect` chooses it by adding `pressureGrad` to the displayed momentum terms and the approximate forcing coefficients. This sum, not each of its terms, must be in $\mathcal H$. With the sign convention of (7.10), the force in the approximate momentum equation is $-\sum_i\beta_i^{\mathrm a}b_i$; the correction has to remove that force as well as the residual.

ns7-data-s032|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: For a fixed $\alpha$, a representative $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ may include a gradient. Its full norm is the bound in Equation (7.23) and in Lean's squared-integral hypothesis. Projection can decrease the norm, but a computation need not find the orthogonal representative in order to supply a sufficient upper bound.

ns7-data-s033|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: A gradient in $\mathcal H$ can be added to $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ without changing the solution of the constrained equation. But Equation (7.24) is a bound for a chosen representative: the gradient may change both its norm and the additional row measurements. In contrast, the adjoint pairing in Equation (7.34) is independent of this choice, since Equation (7.33) with $v=0$ implies that $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is solenoidal.

ns7-data-s033|Breakdown.Cert.extendedDat.annotation: For the linear solve it is enough that $\alpha\mapsto\mathbb PF_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ be weakly continuous. Indeed, in a solenoidal test pairing one can replace the residual by Equation (7.10) and move one derivative off the Laplacian; the remaining profile coefficients converge uniformly on the compact support of the test. By Equation (7.23) the projected residuals are uniformly bounded in $\mathcal H$, so density of the periodized solenoidal tests upgrades the continuity of these pairings to weak continuity. There is no corresponding assertion of norm continuity, or even weak continuity, for an arbitrary choice of unprojected representatives.

ns7-data-s034|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: Use $f=\mathcal T_Sv$ as the unknown. On $\mathcal H_{\rm div}^\Gamma\times\mathbb R^n$ the bordered map then differs from the identity by $(\mathbb P\mathcal C_\alpha\mathcal T_S^{-1}f+\sum_i\beta_i\mathbb Pb_i,\,\ell(\mathcal T_S^{-1}f)-\beta)$. Its first velocity term is compact by Lemma 7.7 and the remaining terms are bounded and finite rank. Thus the map has index zero; Equation (7.52) rules out a kernel and the Fredholm alternative gives a unique solution for every admissible right-hand side and constraint vector.

ns7-data-s035|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The paper prescribes $\ell(v)=\bar\ell(\alpha)$, while Lean prescribes the value $t(\alpha)$ on the corrected profile. Since $\ell$ is linear, these formulations agree with $\bar\ell(\alpha)=t(\alpha)-\ell(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a})$, the quantity `targetGap`. In particular a target of substantial size need not cost much in Equation (7.24) if it is already nearly attained by the approximate profile. When the parameter is fixed, this gap cancels upon subtracting two linear solves.

ns7-data-s036|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: At a fixed parameter the free inverse identifies $f=\mathcal T_Sv$ with $v$ (the bijectivity in Proposition 7.5). The predicate `IsHeldSolution` states that the resulting velocity solves the nonlinear constrained equation and obeys the pair and slice-gradient bounds. It still allows a nonzero total force. Its finite-dimensional coefficient variable is normalized to $\omega\beta$, with the forcing fields divided by $\omega$.

ns7-data-s036|Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvec.annotation:
Expanding the convection of $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ gives the approximate convection, the mixed terms $(W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\cdot
abla)v+(v\cdot
abla)W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ and $(v\cdot
abla)v$. The first two mixed terms form the linear operator $\mathcal C_\alpha$ in Equation (7.13), so the only unknown nonlinear right-hand side in a trial solve is $-(v\cdot
abla)v$.

ns7-data-s037|Breakdown.Cert.extendedHel.annotation: At each parameter the residual cancels on adding Equations (7.10) and (7.12), but the force in the equation for $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}+v$ is still $-\sum_i(\beta_i^{\mathrm a}+\beta_i)b_i$. Thus neither solving the correction equation nor finding a small $\beta$ gives an unforced profile. The last step must cancel the total coefficients, including those already present in the approximate equation.

ns7-data-s038|Breakdown.extended_certifi.annotation: A solution of Equation (7.12) at a prescribed parameter need not be a solution without force: its coefficient vector is still $\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)+\beta$. The certificate first bounds the correction and then supplies conditions on that total vector. In the linked Lean proof a unique bounded constrained nonlinear solution is obtained at each parameter; continuity and the enclosure of its coefficient vector are used to find a zero. The paper obtains the parameter and the nonlinear solution together.

ns7-data-s040|Breakdown.weightedEnergy|1.annotation: The norm is chosen for two different estimates. Control of $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ in the period integral gives $\|v(\theta)\|_\infty\le c_w|v(\theta)|_w$ almost everywhere in time. To integrate the product $|v||\nabla v|$ in $L^2$ one also needs a bound for the maximum of the gradient norm; controlling just the two period integrals would not give this product estimate. The latter bound comes from Equation (7.22), not from Equation (7.18) alone.

ns7-data-s041|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The coefficient weight trades velocity allowance against force allowance in the same estimate. At a fixed pair radius, $\omega|\beta|\le2\varepsilon$ gives the crude force bound used outside $\mathcal J$. Increasing $\omega$ changes the inverse bound (7.18) that must be verified; it cannot be done merely to make Equation (7.37) easier.

ns7-data-s042|Breakdown.weightedEnergy|1.annotation: The two terms of the weighted norm are used differently. The Laplacian is paired with the right-hand side in the energy identity, so $\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}\le\|v\|_w$. The gradient term gives $\int_0^1\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2\,d\theta\le\|v\|_w^2/w_*$, an upper bound for the minimum slice energy, since the minimum is no larger than the period average (the starting point in the proof of Proposition 7.9).

ns7-data-s042|Breakdown.Cert.sizeZ|3.annotation: Set $\widehat\beta=\omega\beta$ and $\widehat b_i=b_i/\omega$. The force is unchanged, and the norm now has coefficient weight one. To preserve Equation (7.30) one must also replace $\beta^{\mathrm a}$ by $\omega\beta^{\mathrm a}$ and $V_j$ by $V_j/\omega$. The bound $b_*$ scales by $1/\omega$, as does $\langle b,\psi_j\rangle-V_j$. Thus the normalization leaves both the physical forcing and the parameter enclosure unchanged.

ns7-data-s044|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation:
Lemma B.9 separates the difference into $Z_0=W_0^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$ and $Z_1=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_0^{\mathrm a}$. The transport term is bounded by $(\|Z_0\|_\infty+\|Z_1\|_\infty)\|
abla u\|_2$ at each phase; for the other term use $\|u\|_\infty\|
abla Z_0\|_2$ and $\|u\|_6\|
abla Z_1\|_3$, with operator norms on the coefficient gradients. All three are bounded by constants times $|u|_w$. Squaring and integrating the resulting slice bound gives Equation (7.19).

ns7-data-s045|Breakdown.Cert.sliceConvec.annotation: The map $W\mapsto\mathcal C_Wv$ is linear in $W$ at fixed $v$. Therefore replacing $W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$ by $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ adds $(D\cdot\nabla)v+(v\cdot\nabla)D$, where $D=W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W_\alpha^{\mathrm r}$. Both terms must be controlled in Equation (7.19).

ns7-data-s046|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: For fixed constraint values the right-hand side has two different costs. If $F$ is orthogonal to all the $e_k$, its cost in Equation (7.18) is $c_1\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$; in the worst case it is $(c_1+c_0)\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. Thus a large inverse response in a few directions need not impose that same large constant on every right-hand side. In Appendix B the additional measurements arise from a finite-dimensional estimate of the lower quadratic form; the error components not measured by the rows still have to be controlled.

ns7-data-s047|Breakdown.rowNorm|1.annotation: In Lean the row fields are orthonormal and carry weights $\tau_k\ge0$. The paper's fields $e_k$ correspond to $\sqrt{\tau_k}$ times these unit fields; hence $\tau_k\le c_0^2$ gives exactly the length bound in Equation (7.17). A zero weight removes that row from the seminorm.

ns7-data-s048|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Lean assumes $c_2\ge0$ explicitly, while Equation (7.18) allows real $c_2$. In fact, once Proposition 7.8 is proved and $n>0$, one may solve the transferred linear equation with $F=0$ and any nonzero constraint value. Inequality (7.52) then forces $c_2>0$. When $n=0$ the constraint term vanishes and its sign is immaterial.

ns7-data-s050|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Projection decreases the norm of $F$ but not necessarily its row measurements. For example let $p$ be a unit solenoidal field, $q$ an orthogonal unit gradient, $F=p-q$ and $e_1=(p+q)/\sqrt2$. Then $[F]=0$ but $[\mathbb PF]=1/\sqrt2$. Thus the two terms of Equation (7.18) should be evaluated for the same chosen representative; one cannot replace each independently by its projected value.

The inverse estimate may use the full representative $F$. The adjoint estimate has an additional consequence: putting $v=0$ in Equation (7.33) makes every gradient $F\in\mathcal H$ invisible to $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Consequently its pairing depends only on the projected residual, even when the finite row measurements in Equation (7.17) do not.

ns7-data-s051|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The constant $c_L$ estimates a linear solve with zero constraint values, or the difference of two solves at the same parameter with equal constraint values. It need not estimate the entire response with prescribed nonzero constraints. This is why it controls the nonlinear iteration, whereas Equation (7.24) uses $c_1$, $\delta_0$ and $c_2$ separately.

ns7-data-s052|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Keep $(v,\beta)$ fixed and put $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$. If $F$ is a right-hand side at the approximate profile, then $F-G$ is one at the reference profile. The change therefore costs only the two right-hand-side terms of Equation (7.18), with no new constraint term. Since the equations are modulo gradients, it is not necessary to project $G$ before applying that estimate.

ns7-data-s052|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The triangle inequalities in the reference estimate give $c_1\|F-G\|+[F-G]\le c_1\|F\|+[F]+(c_1+c_0)\|G\|$. By Equation (7.19), the last term is at most $\vartheta\|v\|_w$. The row bound $c_0$ is needed even if $[F]=0$, since the change of convection can have components in the row directions.

ns7-data-s052|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The right-hand side of Equation (7.19) involves the unknown $v$, so the new term cannot be treated as an independently supplied small residual. It is at most $\vartheta\|v\|_w\le\vartheta\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}$. Absorbing it on the left is possible precisely with the strict margin $1-\vartheta>0$ in this argument. No smallness of the particular solution has been used.

With $\ell(v)=0$, Equation (7.52) gives $\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le(c_1+c_0)\|F\|_{\mathcal H}/(1-\vartheta)\le c_L\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$. This is the estimate for a difference of two solves at the same parameter. For the residual itself it is better to retain the separate seminorm and prescribed constraint terms.

ns7-data-s052|Breakdown.Cert.Internal.At.annotation: There are two useful consequences of the same transferred estimate (7.52). Retaining all three terms gives the bound for the particular approximate residual and prescribed constraint gap in Equation (7.24). For a difference of solves at fixed parameter the constraints cancel and the new right-hand side can be arbitrary; then use $[F]\le c_0\|F\|_{\mathcal H}$ to obtain the uniform constant $c_L$. Using the latter estimate for the residual as well could lose the benefit of small row measurements.

ns7-data-s053|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: After transfer, the inverse bound has the same form as Equation (7.18), with $c_1,c_2$ and the row seminorm divided by $1-\vartheta$. In the formal data this means dividing the row weights by $(1-\vartheta)^2$, since the seminorm takes a square root, and dividing both the row bound and the residual row allowance by $1-\vartheta$. The reference field is then set equal to the approximate field; the frozen-form bound is transferred separately.

ns7-data-s054|Breakdown.weightedEnergy|1.annotation: An integral bound alone can be compatible with very large values on a short interval. Let $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$. The bound $\min E\le\|v\|_w^2/w_*$ supplies a starting value, and Equation (7.22) bounds the increase of $E$ from this value. Integrating the differential inequality, rather than estimating a time derivative separately, is what supplies the maximum needed in Equation (7.49).

ns7-data-s054|Breakdown.Cert.ProductBoun.annotation:
For different fields $v,z$, the pointwise inequality $|(v\cdot
abla)z|\le |v||
abla z|$ and Equation (7.48) give $\|(v\cdot
abla)z\|_{\mathcal H}\le c_w\|v\|_w\sup_	heta\|
abla z(	heta)\|_2$. In particular the weighted norm always estimates the undifferentiated factor and the time supremum estimates the differentiated one. The same bound will be used on each of the two products in a difference of quadratic terms.

ns7-data-s055|Breakdown.Cert.Internal.Ex.annotation:
The positive gradient term in Equation (7.22) comes from the similarity drift, not from an additional dissipation assumption. For a compactly supported smooth $u$, $
abla((y\cdot
abla)u)=
abla u+(y\cdot
abla)
abla u$, so pairing $(y\cdot
abla)u$ with $-\Delta u$ gives $(1-3/2)\|
abla u\|_2^2$. Half this value, together with the zeroth-order term, gives $ rac14\|
abla u\|_2^2$. Lemma 7.4 proves the interval identity on $\mathcal D_S$ without requiring the drift separately to be square integrable. The remaining contribution to the form is diffusion and the convection at the chosen phase.

ns7-data-s056|Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedSup.annotation: Write $E(\theta)=\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$ and $Q_\alpha(\theta,v)$ for the left side of Equation (7.22). With right-hand side $F$ in the linear problem, Equation (7.42) gives $E'/(2S)=-Q_\alpha(\theta,v)+\langle F-\sum_i\beta_i b_i,-\Delta v\rangle_{L^2}$. The upper bound on $E'$ is integrable even without control of the separate time derivative of $v$. Start at a minimum of $E$, bounded by $\|v\|_w^2/w_*$. Sum the increments over $m$ translates by $1/m$, which have the same energy increment but disjoint integration intervals. The bound over one period divided by $m$ gives Equation (7.55), even for a residual representative without the shorter period.

ns7-data-s058|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The smallness of $F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$ is used in two different norms of the solution. To bound the period-integrated correction, use the inverse estimate with its special row measurements and constraint term, as in Equation (7.24). To bound a maximum in time, the energy identity pairs the forcing with $-\Delta v$, so only its full $\mathcal H$ norm is needed. The uniform bound $\delta_{\max}$ is used for this second purpose in Equation (7.27).

ns7-data-s059|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The quantity bounded by $\delta(\alpha)$ is $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}$ before projection. Lean states the squared integral inequality and separately imposes nonnegativity of the bound, so taking a square root gives Equation (7.23).

In the trial equation the right side is $-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$. Since $\|g\|_{\mathcal H}\le2c_w\varepsilon M$, the common bound $\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M$ is available in Equation (7.55) for every parameter and every trial $g$.

Let $L_\alpha^{-1}$ denote the constrained linear inverse of Proposition 7.8, with both forcing and constraint values as data. By linearity its response to $(-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g,\bar\ell(\alpha))$ is the sum of the response to $(-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\bar\ell(\alpha))$ and that to $(-g,0)$. The former has norm at most $\varepsilon$ by Equation (7.24); the latter has norm at most $c_L\|g\|_{\mathcal H}\le\varepsilon$ by Equation (7.25) for the trial forcing ball. The factor two in the correction radius leaves room for the nonlinear term.

ns7-data-s060|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: In the paper the inequality says that the linear response to a trial quadratic term of norm $2c_w\varepsilon M$ fits in the radius $\varepsilon$ left by the residual. Strictness is not needed for that inclusion alone. It matters for the formal fixed-parameter contraction: the difference of two quadratic terms has two products, and Equation (7.26) controls the scaled gradient supremum of the output difference. The resulting contraction constant is $2c_Lc_wM$, not a constant involving the derivative of the parameter update.

Subtract two solves at the same parameter and let $h$ be the difference of their right-hand sides. The constraints and the approximate residual disappear, and the pair norm of the difference is at most $r=c_L\|h\|_{\mathcal H}$. Substitution in Equation (7.55), with $|\beta_{\rm diff}|\le r/\omega$, gives $\sup E_{\rm diff}\le Ar^2$, where $A=1/w_*+(2S_{\max}/m)(c_3+b_*/\omega+1/c_L)$ is the bracket in Equation (7.26). Hence $(2\varepsilon/M)\sup\|\nabla v_{\rm diff}\|_2\le r$. Lean needs this estimate to contract in both norms; the joint Schauder proof does not.

This inequality is for one solve rather than the difference of two. With $F=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-g$ and the pair bound $2\varepsilon$, the right side of Equation (7.55) is bounded by $4\varepsilon^2(1/w_*+2S_{\max}c_3/m)+(4S_{\max}\varepsilon/m)(\delta_{\max}+2c_w\varepsilon M+2\varepsilon b_*/\omega)$. Thus Equation (7.27) supplies the slice-gradient bound $M$ for the output, including the effect of the approximate residual. This is distinct from the role of Equation (7.26) for differences.

ns7-data-s062|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation:
If the corrected field were zero, $
abla v=-
abla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}$, and $w_*\|
abla W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}^2=w_*\|
abla v\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le\|v\|_w^2\le4\varepsilon^2$. This contradicts Equation (7.28). The lower bound is required throughout $K$ because the parameter will only be determined at the end.

ns7-data-s068|Breakdown.Held.testSetZero.annotation: The condition required of a nonlinear solution at $\alpha$ is $\alpha'\in K$, not merely that its force be small. In one dimension, a projected update from $\alpha=1$ to $\alpha'=2$ on $K=[-1,1]$ has a fixed point at $1$, even though the change is nonzero. The enclosure inequalities exclude this possibility: at a fixed point the projection acts on a point already in $K$, hence $\alpha'=\alpha$ (the inclusion proved by the bounds (7.61)).

ns7-data-s070|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: The bound on $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ in Lean is a uniform slice $L^2$ bound, whereas the abstract paper asks only for membership in $\mathcal H$ and the pairing estimate (7.32). Lemma B.10 gives two sufficient ways of deriving the latter, one using a uniform slice $L^3$ bound and the other a uniform slice $L^2$ bound. The formal hypothesis selects the second type of slice control and also states Equation (7.32) separately.

ns7-data-s070|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The exact model for $\psi_{\alpha,j}$ is a row of the inverse of the constrained linear problem, not an adjoint eigenfunction. At fixed $\alpha$, the linear inverse sends $(\mathbb PF,\ell)$ to $(v,\beta)$; by Equation (7.52) its coefficient functional $V_j\cdot\beta$ is bounded. Its Hilbert-space representation is $V_j\cdot\beta=\langle F,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y\ell)_j$ with solenoidal $\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Testing first on $v=0$, then on $\beta=0$, gives the ideal forms of Equations (7.31) and (7.33). The certificate uses approximate representatives of these rows and additionally requires control of their nonlinear pairings.

ns7-data-s071|Breakdown.ExtendedCertific.annotation: The measurement vector $\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$ can vary with $\alpha$, while $V_j$ in the parameter update is fixed. Define $E_j$ to be their difference. Replacing the measured scalar by $V_j\cdot\beta$ introduces $\beta\cdot E_j$, bounded by $|E_j|\,\omega|\beta|/\omega$ as in Equation (7.35).

ns7-data-s072|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Here one needs only a scalar pairing, not the full $\mathcal H$ norm of the quadratic term. For example a uniform slice bound $\|\psi_{\alpha,j}(\theta)\|_2\le n_j$ gives $|\langle(v\cdot\nabla)v,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle_{\mathcal H}|\le n_jc_w\|v\|_w^2/\sqrt{w_*}$, by applying Equation (7.48) and the gradient bound at each phase and then integrating. Lemma B.10 also gives an alternative using the slice $L^3$ norm. Neither estimate pays for the gradient supremum $M$, which is needed for the full norm of convection.

In Equation (7.33) the representative $F$ corresponds to the linearized velocity equation alone, without forcing coefficients. Thus for a nonlinear correction one takes $F'=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-(v\cdot\nabla)v-\sum_i\beta_i b_i$. Substitution gives a scalar equation involving $V_j\cdot\beta$, the known residual and constraint pairings, and the quadratic pairing. Its linear-functional error is bounded by $a_j\|v\|_w$; the replacement of the actual actuator pairings by $V_j$ is estimated separately.

The expression before $-d_j\alpha_j$ is a computable approximation to the total force coefficient in direction $V_j$ after correcting the profile. One wants this predicted coefficient to be near $d_j\alpha_j$, not near zero for every $\alpha$. For the represented certificate, the prescribed constraint gap is zero when $\mathcal J$ is nonempty. In the interior ball of Appendix B the residual has an exact quadratic expansion in the parameters (Equation (B.57)); Lemma B.13 encloses the error in the intended slope and the other terms, including the exterior residual separately. The allowance $o_j$ is then independent of the unknown correction.

The tolerance in the scaled coordinate is $|d_j|\varrho_j$. The first term in Equation (7.35) bounds the quadratic adjoint pairing on $\|v\|_w\le2\varepsilon$; the square-root term bounds the two linear errors together, using the full pair radius. Adding the known offset $o_j$ leaves at most $|d_j|\varrho_j$ for $|V_j\cdot(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)-d_j\alpha_j|=|d_j\alpha'_j|$.

ns7-data-s072|Breakdown.Cert.extendedAdj.annotation: Apply Equation (7.33) with $v=0$ and $F=(I-\mathbb P)\psi_{\alpha,j}$. Then $F\simeq0$ and $\ell(v)=0$, so $\langle F,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle=0$. By orthogonality the same pairing is $\|F\|_{\mathcal H}^2$, giving $\psi_{\alpha,j}\in\mathcal H_{\rm div}$. In particular the adjoint measurement of Equation (7.12) is independent of the gradient representative of the residual.

ns7-data-s073|Breakdown.Cert.ExtendedAdj.annotation: Use $F'=-F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-(v\cdot\nabla)v-\sum_i\beta_i b_i$ in Equation (7.33), since $F'\simeq\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha v$. Moving the residual and constraint terms to the left then gives $|\beta\cdot\langle b,\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle+\langle F_\alpha^{\mathrm a},\psi_{\alpha,j}\rangle+(Y\bar\ell)_j|\le a_j\|v\|_w+\widetilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. The formal enclosure also accounts for replacing the measured direction by $V_j$.

ns7-data-s075|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Denote the computable prediction in Equation (7.34) by $p_j$. To enclose the next parameter, write $-d_j\alpha'_j=(p_j-d_j\alpha_j)+(V_j\cdot(\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta)-p_j)$. The first term is an error in the approximate family, bounded by (7.34) without solving for $v$. The second is the error in the adjoint prediction for the response of the constrained problem; its bound uses the radius of $(v,\beta)$. This separation is also the distinction between Lemmas B.13 and B.12.

ns7-data-s076|Breakdown.IsExtendedCertif.annotation: Let $A_*$ have rows $V_j^{\mathsf T}$ for $j\notin\mathcal J$. The first inequality of Equation (7.36) says $\|A_*\|_{2\to2}\le a_*$. This controls the entire complementary coefficient vector by $a_*|\beta|$; using the sum of squared row norms would be sufficient but can give a larger value of $a_*$.

The second inequality in Equation (7.36) compares two known vectors, $A_*\beta^{\mathrm a}(\alpha)$ and $(d_j\alpha_j)_{j\notin\mathcal J}$. It bounds the scaled parameter update that would result if the correction force were zero. The actual update differs by $A_*\beta$, which costs at most $2\varepsilon a_*/\omega$ in Euclidean norm.

For $j\notin\mathcal J$, $-d_j\alpha'_j=V_j\cdot\beta+(V_j\cdot\beta^{\mathrm a}-d_j\alpha_j)$. Taking the Euclidean norm of the vector of these identities gives at most $a_*|\beta|+o_*\le2\varepsilon a_*/\omega+o_*\le\varrho_*$. This is exactly the ball condition in Equation (7.29), including the coordinate scalings.

pdf-item-theorem-7-1|Breakdown.extended_.annotation: Theorem 7.1 must do more than find a small residual. It selects an $\alpha$ and gives an exact profile at that member's period, with the actual correction bounded by Equation (7.38). The linked upstream theorem concludes only weak-profile existence; the quantitative identification and the prescribed symmetries are additional conclusions of the printed theorem. Neither asserts that a particular numerical certificate satisfies the conditions.

pdf-item-theorem-7-1|Breakdown.Cert.exte.annotation: At the paper’s fixed point, Equation (7.61) puts the proposed parameter $\alpha'$ itself in $\mathcal K$. Projection therefore fixes it, so $\alpha'=\alpha$. Equation (7.30) and invertibility of $V$ then give $\beta^{\mathrm a}+\beta=0$. For normalized certificate data, Lean assumes held existence and uniqueness, continuity of the total multiplier, the two enclosures and a finite-dimensional zero theorem. It returns a held correction with zero total multiplier. The paper then constructs the smooth profile.

Add Equations (7.10) and (7.12). The two linear terms in $C_\alpha v$ together with $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ expand the convection of $\mathcal W=W_\alpha^{\rm a}+v$, and the residuals $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ cancel. Thus $T_{S(\alpha)}\mathcal W+(\mathcal W\cdot\nabla)\mathcal W\simeq-\sum_i(\beta_i^{\rm a}+\beta_i)b_i$. Its conclusion is existential: it does not display the selected parameter or the equality in $X$ at every phase in Equation (7.62). That equality in the paper is what transfers the quantitative estimates of Proposition 7.10, and is stronger than just obtaining a smooth recurrent profile.

sec7-nonlinear-043|Breakdown.FarField.Is.annotation: For each imposed symmetry the almost-everywhere equality of the correction extends to every phase by continuity in $X$. Equality of the smooth representatives in $X$ then gives spatial equality at every point. `IsSmoothOrbitField` records the equation, one prescribed recurrence and regularity and tail hypotheses; it is not a statement of all the relations in Equation (7.39) or the precise inverse-radius rates in Equation (1.3).

sec7-nonlinear-045|Breakdown.WeakProfile.annotation: Write $r=1-t$. For the velocity the scaling factor in $L^6$ is $r^{-1/2}r^{3/12}=r^{-1/4}$; for the gradient in $L^2$ it is $r^{-1}r^{3/4}=r^{-1/4}$. Thus Equation (7.63) is an equality of rescaled velocity norms. As $t$ runs over $(-\infty,1)$, $\theta$ runs over all of $\mathbb R$; continuity and period one bound the supremum by that on $[0,1]$.

sec7-nonlinear-048|Breakdown.WeakProfile.annotation: In `varConst` the nonlinear term is written with the abstract bilinear map $K$ and a plus sign. On the diagonal, (3.10) reads $K(\tau)(u,u)=-\nabla O_\tau*(u\otimes u)$, which accounts for the minus sign in Equation (7.64). Equality of the variation-of-constants expression with the velocity requires mildness; the spatial convolution identity is a separate ingredient.

In Equation (7.64) we can start at any $a<t$, since the physical curve is ancient. The choice $a=t-(1-t)$ puts every source time at a remaining time between $1-t$ and $2(1-t)$. Consequently the initial datum and the nonlinear sources are measured at comparable scales. The formal `mildFromGood_holds` gives the analogous freedom to restart within its own window.

sec7-nonlinear-049|Breakdown.FarField.le.annotation: A direct estimate of the integral in $L^\infty$ from Equation (7.63) would use $u\otimes u\in L^3$ and the conjugate kernel norm $\|\nabla O_\tau\|_{3/2}\lesssim\tau^{-1}$. Its time integral diverges at zero. Passing first to a finite $L^q$ with $q>6$ costs $\tau^{-1+3/(2q)}$ for the nonlinear term, and the next step to $L^\infty$ costs $\tau^{-1/2-3/q}$. Both powers are integrable. The choice $q=12$ gives the exponents $-7/8$ and $-3/4$ below.

sec7-nonlinear-050|Breakdown.FarField.le.annotation: The new $L^{12}$ estimate is available at every source time $t'$ in Equation (7.64), giving $\|u(t')\otimes u(t')\|_6\lesssim r^{-3/4}$ for $r=1-t$. Convolution into $L^\infty$ uses the conjugate exponent $6/5$, costing $\tau^{-3/4}$. Its integral over $(0,r)$ is $4r^{1/4}$, giving $O(r^{-1/2})$ in Equation (7.65). The free Gaussian now maps $L^{12}$ to $L^\infty$ with cost $r^{-1/8}$ and yields the same power.

sec7-nonlinear-056|Breakdown.FarField.De.annotation: With $t=1-e^{-s}$ and $x=e^{-s/2}y$, the denominator in Equation (7.66) is $e^{-s/2}(1+|y|)$. Multiplication by $e^{-s/2}$ removes the physical velocity factor, giving the first bound of (1.3) for all phases with the same constant. `DecayBounds` additionally records the derivative and pressure-gradient estimates.

sec7-nonlinear-058|Breakdown.FarField.fa.annotation: The formal far-field proof also uses the whole-past integral equation. Put $\delta=1-t$ and $\tau=(t-t')/\delta$ in Equation (7.64). The earlier similarity phase is $s-\log(1+\tau)$ and its spatial argument is $z/\sqrt{1+\tau}$ in the current spatial units. The squared velocity amplitude gives the factor $(1+\tau)^{-1}$ in `profileBilin`. Starting at $t-A(1-t)$, the rescaled heat term is bounded by $C(1+A)^{-1/2}$ because the heat kernel has mass one and the earlier velocity has smaller amplitude. It tends to zero as $A\to\infty$. Thus the profile is determined by the quadratic integral itself, to which the weighted decay estimates apply.

ac-005|Breakdown.varConstIntegral|1.annotation: In the original time variable the singularity moves with $t$. The substitution $\tau=t-t'$ fixes it at zero. Extend the inputs by their endpoint values and insert the indicator $0<\tau<t-a$ on the fixed interval $(0,b-a)$. At a limiting $t$ the indicator converges except at the single point $t-a$, and the majorant from Equation (3.12) is independent of $t$. Dominated convergence now applies in $\mathcal X$, also at $a$ where the integral vanishes.

ac-011|Breakdown.shift|1.annotation: Define $\widetilde u(s)=u(a+s)$. Then the fixed spatial test in Equation (3.14) is unchanged and differentiation in $s$ is differentiation in $t=a+s$; the datum is now $\widetilde u(0)=u(a)$. The linked `shift` proves the analogous invariance of (2.4) by the substitution $t'=a+s'$, which leaves the lag unchanged. It concerns the mild identity rather than the weak equation translated here.

ac-012|Breakdown.Freq.weak_holds|1.annotation: For a moving test $\varphi(t)$, split the increment of $\int u(t)\cdot\varphi(t)$ into one at fixed test and one at fixed velocity. Apply Equation (3.14) to the first and continuity in $L^6$ to the second. Integration gives the endpoint terms $\int u(m)\cdot\varphi(m)-\int u(0)\cdot\varphi(0)$, and the interior integral of $u\cdot(\partial_t+\Delta)\varphi+(u\otimes u):\nabla\varphi$. This is (NSW) in [46]. `weak_holds` uses a different integrated identity in $X$ against the fixed test $-\Delta\psi$.

ac-013|Breakdown.Freq.mild_holds|1.annotation: Dubois's integral is initially in $\mathcal S'$. Its integrand with the minus sign is $K(t-t')(u(t'),u(t'))$ since $\operatorname{div}(u\otimes u)=(u\cdot\nabla)u\in L^{3/2}$. By Equation (3.7) and continuity of $u$ in $X$, this integrand has an integrable $X$ norm. Pairing its Bochner integral with Schwartz fields (bounded functionals by Equation (3.1)) identifies it with the distributional integral. The datum is $u(0)$ by the continuous trace. Lean obtains the corresponding equality by heat testing instead.

ac-016|Breakdown.Periodic.heat_continuou.annotation: For a source in $L^{3/2}$ the value at lag zero need not be in the gradient space. To obtain continuity at a positive $\tau_0$, write $e^{\tau\Delta}Pf=e^{(\tau-\tau_0/2)\Delta}(e^{\tau_0\Delta/2}Pf)$ for $\tau$ near $\tau_0$. The inner field belongs to the space by Equation (3.19), so strong continuity of heat suffices. The linked heat-continuity theorem concerns the inhomogeneous unit-period space.

ac-017|Breakdown.Periodic.kernelSharpBou.annotation: The mean of $(u\cdot\nabla)v$ vanishes: as a periodic distribution it is $\operatorname{div}(v\otimes u)$, whose integral is its pairing with the constant test. Thus Equation (3.19) applies to both advections in Equation (3.17). Hölder with Equation (3.18) bounds their $L^{3/2}$ norms by a constant times $\|u\|_{\dot H^1}\|v\|_{\dot H^1}$, independent of $L$. The linked bound is in the unit-torus inhomogeneous norm for lags at most one.

ac-021|Breakdown.varConstIntegral|1.annotation: After applying the bounded embedding $H^1_{\rm div}\to X$, the free term and the integrand of the local $H^1$ equation are the same as in Equation (2.4). Lemma 3.3 gives continuity of the latter integral in $X$. Pairing with Schwartz tests identifies the integrals, and continuity of both sides in $X$ gives the equality at every time, as required by Lemma 3.5.

ac-028|Breakdown.mildRegular_realization.annotation: The smooth velocity representatives on two slabs agree at every common time: they represent the same element of $X$ and are continuous in space. Their pressure gradients agree by Equation (1.1), so their pressures differ by a function of time only; subtracting the value at $x=0$ gives a common gauge. Exhausting $[0,T)$ by slabs gives a single smooth pair there.

b12-intro-estimates|Breakdown.CellLayerS.annotation: The six estimates form the input to the analytic proof: (7.18) and (7.19) give the transferred inverse bound, (7.22) controls the maximum in phase, and Equations (7.32)–(7.34) give the selected-coordinate enclosure. Appendix B derives these estimates from conditions on the represented fields and on arbitrary perturbations. The linked `CellSystemCondition` specifies the common data and hypotheses; it does not produce a verified numerical instance.

b12-intro-condition|Breakdown.CellLayerS.annotation: The conditions refer to a single choice of the fields, mesh, weights and matrices. In particular the cell inequalities must cover every perturbation in Equation (7.18), not just the harmonics and polynomials used to represent the approximate profile. The linked structure includes the fifteen groups of conditions, including the further cell conditions named after Proposition B.14; it asserts no existence of data satisfying them.

b12-cell-kind|Breakdown.CertCell.CellMat.annotation: The indices of the printed coefficient $\Xi_{i,ab}^{Q,\iota}$ are the direction of differentiation $a$ and the component $b$. The Cartesian linear map in Lean has its indices in the opposite order: the term of `frameMap` with coefficient $x_{ab}$ sends $e_b$ to $x_{ab}e_a$. Thus the polynomial stored at `(b,a)` is the one multiplying $e_b\cdot(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$ in Equation (B.10).

b12-cell-kind|Breakdown.CertCell.RowValu.annotation: The polynomials give the real generators $\tilde e_{k'}$. If $m_{k'}=\langle F,\tilde e_{k'}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, the measurements against the unit rows are the components of $G^{-1/2}m$. The definition `rowFieldOf` forms these unit rows; Equation (B.11) then multiplies each by $\sqrt{\tau_k}$, represented by a separate weight in the formal seminorm.

b12-angular-coordinate|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Only $e^{im\phi}$ for integer $m$ enters the scalar harmonics, so the branch of the angle is immaterial. Assigning an angle on the axis does not by itself make a field continuous there. The factors in Equation (B.7) and the weighted polar and azimuthal vectors in Equation (B.8) address this separately.

b12-rotation-coordinate|Breakdown.axialR.annotation: At $r>0$, the frame at $R_{\phi_0}y$ is the image under $R_{\phi_0}$ of the frame at $y$. Thus $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta,R_{\phi_0}y)$ has the cylindrical components of $v$ at the shifted angle, expressed in the frame at $y$. This is the operation averaged in Equation (B.12); averaging the Cartesian components without that rotation would give different mode labels.

b12-two-generators|Breakdown.CertCell.In.annotation: To prove invariance of a represented field, it suffices to prove the identities for the two pairs in Equation (B.1). The identity for a product follows by applying the two identities successively; period one accounts for the remaining integer time translation. This is the use of the generation condition, as opposed to membership of the two pairs, which is sufficient for restricting the modes of an already invariant perturbation.

pdf-item-equation-B-2|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The integer lattice may be read in terms of the two traveling phases of Subsection C.1: with $j=2\iota_2-\iota_1$ and $m$ the angular integer, the phase change under the combined shift is $\pi(j+m/k)=2\pi\iota_2$, where $k$ is the angular order. In particular a purely time-dependent mode has even $j$, but a mode with odd $m/k$ must have odd $j$.

b12-harmonic-parity|Breakdown.CertCell.l.annotation: The first generator imposes $e^{i\pi(j+j'/\varkappa)}=1$. Hence $\iota_1=j'/\varkappa$ and $\iota_2=(j+\iota_1)/2$ are integers, and Equation (B.2) parametrizes all the allowed frequencies, including those with arbitrarily large integers.

b12-first-symmetry|Breakdown.CertCell.Gi.annotation: The scalar components are unchanged under the combined shift, whereas the cylindrical frame rotates by the angle of the generator. Reassembling the components gives precisely the vector transformation in Equation (7.5). The linked theorem proves it for the admissible fields (B.6), including points on the axis.

b12-label-reflection|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The time integer $2\iota_2-\iota_1$ is unchanged by $\iota^\flat$, whereas the angular integer is negated. In particular the two travelling families $\iota_2=0$ and $\iota_2=\iota_1$ of Subsection C.1 are exchanged. Applying the map twice gives the original label. Conjugation instead negates both integers (and, in Equation (B.5), the radial index).

b12-weighted-unit-vectors|Breakdown.Cell.annotation: Near a nonzero point of the axis, the factor $r/R$ in the length of $\mathbf p$ removes the singular unit polar vector. In Equation (B.8) this allows the axisymmetric radial amplitude $u_0$ to be nonzero on the axis while the tangential amplitude contributes zero there. The nonaxisymmetric construction instead makes all three amplitudes vanish to fourth order in $r$.

Since $|e_z\times y|=r$, the length of $\mathbf a$ is $r/|y|=(1-\eta^2)^{1/2}$ away from zero. The amplitude multiplying it in Equation (B.8) can therefore describe an axisymmetric swirl without a singular unit vector on the axis.

pdf-item-equation-B-5|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: For a fixed $\iota$, all the indices $l$ have the same factor $E_\iota(\theta,\phi)$. Their amplitudes, multiplied by $e^{ilf(R^2)}$, add before any norm of $\hat v_\iota$ is taken. The orthogonality used in Subsection B.2 is in $\iota$, not in the radial phase index $l$.

pdf-item-equation-B-6|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The divergence calculation is performed on the complex summand, before taking its real part. In Equation (B.7) the azimuthal derivative cancels the divergence of the meridian components; in Equation (B.8) the meridian components already have zero divergence. Thus changing the coefficients within the admissible amplitude spaces preserves solenoidality without a further linear constraint in the numerical solve.

The finite list of keys and the two scalar splines for each key determine a field by Equations (B.6)–(B.8). The data predicate imposes the further conditions on the exponents, joins, origin values and paired keys. It is these conditions, not the finite-sum formula alone, that give a periodic solenoidal $C^1$ field with the stated decay.

b12-finite-mode-data|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: For each nonzero angular integer the two free splines prescribe the radial and polar amplitudes, and the angular amplitude is obtained by dividing the meridian divergence by the angular derivative in Equation (B.7). At angular integer zero this division is unavailable: one instead prescribes a stream function and a swirl, with the extra origin coefficient in the stream function. These are the independent coefficients of the velocity representation.

pdf-item-equation-B-7|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: With $R=|y|$, the three contributions to $R E_{\iota,l}^{-1}\operatorname{div}(E_{\iota,l}(u_0y/R+u_1\mathbf p+u_2\mathbf a))$ are $(\mathcal V_l+2)u_0$, $-\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)u_1)$ and $i\varkappa\iota_1u_2$. The $2$ comes from differentiation of the spherical area factor $R^2$, and the minus sign from $\eta=\cos\vartheta$, where $\vartheta$ is the polar angle. Multiplication by $i\varkappa\iota_1$ in the last contribution cancels the first two by the factor $i/(\varkappa\iota_1)$ in Equation (B.7).

b12-origin-function|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: At an interior join $\sigma_g$ the polynomial must have zero first and second derivatives, since it is followed by a constant. This ensures two derivatives of $g$ agree there: $u_1$ in Equation (B.8) already contains one radial derivative of $g$.

b12-field-data-description|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: Changing $f$ leaves the spline data unchanged, but it changes two places in the field: the scalar factor $E_{\iota,l}$ and the radial derivative $\mathcal V_l$ used to construct the dependent amplitudes. The latter change is essential for retaining the divergence identity when the phase is varied in Equation (B.9).

b12-conjugation|Breakdown.CertCell.Given.annotation: Conjugation negates the radial index as well as the harmonic label, so that $\overline{\mathcal V_l u}=\mathcal V_{-l}\overline u$. In Equation (B.7) the simultaneous negation of the azimuthal integer conjugates the purely imaginary prefactor of $u_2$ as well. The two constructed vector terms are thus conjugate, and a pair of distinct keys contributes twice the real part of one term.

b12-reflection-data|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: Write $D_l=\mathcal V_l+2$ and $L_\eta u=\partial_\eta((1-\eta^2)u)$. Under the half-turn $u_0$ is reflected without a sign and $u_1$ with a minus sign, so $D_lu_0-L_\eta u_1$ is reflected without a sign. The angular integer changes sign, giving the required minus sign of $u_2$ in Equation (B.7). In Equation (B.8) the stream function and swirl are odd in $\eta$, which yields the same vector transformation.

b12-axis-factors|Breakdown.CertCell.Give.annotation: The factor in $u_1$ is $(1-\eta^2)^2$, so the height derivative in Equation (B.7) differentiates a factor $(1-\eta^2)^3$ and leaves at least $(1-\eta^2)^2$. Thus the dependent amplitude has the same fourth-order vanishing in $r$ as the free amplitudes at a nonzero point of the axis. At the origin the common factor $\sigma^{h_0}$ persists as well, since $\mathcal V_l$ uses the scaled derivative $R\partial_R$.

b12-decay-one|Breakdown.CellReduction.In.annotation: The order-one tail is compatible with the homogeneous energy space: $R^{-1}\in L^6(R>1)$, $R^{-2}\in L^2(R>1)$ and $R^{-3}\in L^2(R>1)$. It need not be in $L^2$ itself. For the residual, the combination $S^{-1}\partial_\theta W+W/2+(y\cdot\nabla)W/2$ must also be in $\mathcal H$; order-one decay alone does not establish this. The phase choice in Subsections C.1 and C.4 cancels the leading transport of the oscillatory tail.

pdf-item-equation-B-9|Breakdown.CellRedu.annotation: The function $f_*$ allows the logarithmic slope of the radial phase at infinity to change while leaving the field on the interior ball unaffected by the phase change. Thus the same parameter can enter the interior residual polynomially and alter the leading similarity transport of an oscillating tail. The split between these two calculations is used in Subsection B.4.

For $R\le r_\chi$, the whole interval $0\le\rho\le R$ in Equation (B.9) has $\rho/(\rho+\mathsf L)\le\sigma_\chi$. Not only is the integral zero, but its radial derivatives vanish at the transition as well, to the orders implied by $\chi\in C^2$. This matters because $\mathcal V_l$ in the velocity formulas differentiates the phase.

b12-phase-logtail|Breakdown.CellReductio.annotation: For $R$ beyond the transition of $\chi$, $\partial_R f_*(R^2)=1/R$. Hence the tail is $\log R+C$, or $\tfrac12\log\rho+C$ in the squared-radius argument $\rho=R^2$. The factor $1/2$ in the latter expression is needed when using $f_*'(\rho)$ in Equation (B.5).

b12-profile-affine|Breakdown.CellReducti.annotation: On the matching ball write $U=\sum_i\alpha_iW_0^i$. Then the terms of degree two in the residual are $(U\cdot\nabla)U+(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)\partial_\theta U-\nabla(|U|^2/2)$, or equivalently the rotational form of the convection plus the period term. The pressure and force coefficients are affine there. This is an exact degree-two expansion as in Equation (B.57), and the exterior is estimated separately; a gradient cannot simply be discarded in a pairing over the ball.

b12-phase-outside|Breakdown.CertCell.Giv.annotation: The change of phase alters the radial derivative even when the amplitude data are fixed. By $2R^2 f_*'(R^2)=\chi(\sigma)$, the new $\mathcal V_l$ differs by multiplication by $il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)\chi(\sigma)$. Retaining the old operator while changing the exponential would invalidate the divergence identity used in Equations (B.7) and (B.8).

b12-uniform-parameter-decay|Breakdown.Ce.annotation: For $\alpha$ in the bounded parameter box, $|\mathsf k\cdot\alpha|$ has one upper bound. Since $R\partial_R f_*(R^2)=\chi(\sigma)$, the scaled derivatives up to order three of $f_\alpha$ have common bounds, and the phase factors have modulus one. The finitely many amplitude splines then give uniform bounds in Equation (7.8); there is no need for a uniform bound on $f_\alpha$ itself.

b12-period-affine|Breakdown.CellReductio.annotation: The operator $\mathcal T_S$ contains $S^{-1}\partial_\theta$, so affine dependence of $S^{-1}$ makes this part of the interior residual a quadratic polynomial in $\alpha$. Affine dependence of $S$ itself would introduce a denominator. In the exterior the matching change of the logarithmic radial phase cancels the leading time and similarity transport terms as in Subsection C.4.

b12-pressure-gradient|Breakdown.CellRedu.annotation: Put $p_\alpha=q_\alpha-|W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}|^2/2$. Integration by parts against a compactly supported solenoidal test makes $\nabla p_\alpha$ disappear from the equation modulo gradients. It must nevertheless be included when computing $\|F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}\|_{\mathcal H}$ and $[F_\alpha^{\mathrm a}]$: the cell rows need not be globally solenoidal. The pressure is chosen to bound this particular representative (see the two residual bounds in Equation (7.23)), not just its action on solenoidal tests.

b12-forcing-data|Breakdown.CertCell.Give.annotation: Multiplying an arbitrary solenoidal field by a scalar cutoff would produce the extra divergence $\nabla\chi\cdot b$. Here support is imposed instead on the free amplitude splines before Equations (B.7) and (B.8) construct the dependent components. With the zero origin coefficient the field is compactly supported and the divergence cancellation is unchanged.

b12-forcing-smooth|Breakdown.CertCell.Gi.annotation: The support is imposed on the free splines, not by multiplying the resulting field by a discontinuous characteristic function. At the last support sphere their joined traces also vanish to the orders required in Equations (B.7) and (B.8). This is consistent with the global $C^1$ assertion for $b_i$ even at that sphere.

b12-forcing-divergence|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: No projection is needed to make the represented force divergence-free: each harmonic is constructed by Equation (B.7) or (B.8), and the divergence of each term vanishes under the shape hypotheses. The cutoff is built into the amplitudes, rather than applied afterwards to a solenoidal vector field.

b12-forcing-support|Breakdown.CertCell.G.annotation: The last possible nonzero radial coordinate is $\sigma_i$, whose inverse image is the sphere of radius $\mathsf L_i\sigma_i/(1-\sigma_i)$. All terms, including the origin term, are zero beyond it: the free polynomials vanish there, and $\gamma=0$. The meridian square in Subsection B.3 encloses this ball, so no forcing term is omitted in treating the complement.

b12-adjoint-data|Breakdown.CellReduction.annotation: The choice $h\ge3$ makes $\psi_j$ itself square integrable over the period, since its square is $O(R^{-6})$, and $y\cdot\nabla\psi_j$ has the same decay. In Equation (7.33) the period and linearized operator can vary with $\alpha$ even though the field used to test the equation is fixed. The error in the adjoint equation is accordingly estimated uniformly.

b12-mesh-cover|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenS.annotation: The square contains the meridian image of each actuator support ball: $|y|<r_*$ implies $r<r_*$ and $|z|<r_*$. Thus no actuator remains in the exterior region used in Subsection B.3. The support condition and the disjoint-interior mesh coverage are separate hypotheses.

pdf-item-equation-B-10|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Write $G=\nabla v$ as the linear map $G e_a=(e_a\cdot\nabla)v$. Then $\langle e_b\otimes e_a,G\rangle=e_b\cdot G e_a$. In the Lean `frameMap`, $x_{ab}$ multiplies $e_a\otimes e_b$; hence the polynomial in Equation (B.10) with indices $(a,b)$ corresponds to the stored entry $(b,a)$. With this convention the assembled tensor gives exactly the pairing in Equation (7.11).

b12-tensor-support|Breakdown.CertCell.Ce.annotation: The cell boundaries can be assigned values without affecting the integral in Equation (B.10), since they have zero volume. The test tensor is bounded with bounded support, so it belongs to $\mathcal H$; the linear constraint only uses the weak first derivative of $v$.

b12-phi-error|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Ad.annotation: For a vector $x$ of coefficients, the error in the combined constraint is $\langle\nabla v,\sum_i x_i(\Xi_i-\nabla\Phi_i)\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. It is bounded by $c_\Xi |x|\|v\|_w/\sqrt{w_*}$. In Lemma B.12 one uses $x=(Y_{ji})_i$; hence the whole rounding error costs $\mathsf n_Y c_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$ in Equation (B.53), without a factor counting the constraints. The separate replacement of $\Phi_i$ by a solenoidal field is estimated there in a different norm.

pdf-item-equation-B-11|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Let $u_k=\sum_{k'}(G^{-1/2})_{kk'}\tilde e_{k'}$. The formal row is $u_k$, of unit norm; the paper writes $e_k=\sqrt{\tau_k}u_k$. Both conventions give the same contribution $\tau_k|\langle F,u_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}|^2$ to $[F]^2$ (the squared row seminorm of Equation (7.17)).

With $c=3/50$, `testWeight` stores $c\tau_k$ and `rowWeightOf` divides it by $c$, giving the weight $\tau_k$ in Equation (7.17). For one block of common weight $\tau$, if $m$ denotes the pairings with the real generators and $G$ their Gram matrix, its contribution to $[F]^2$ is $\tau m^{\mathsf T}G^{-1}m=\tau\|P_E F\|_{\mathcal H}^2$, where $E$ is their span. This also explains why the local row matrices in Subsection B.3 can use the original polynomial generators.

b12-row-cap|Breakdown.CertCell.RowValues.annotation: The bound $400(1+2^{-18})$ applies to `testWeight`, namely $c\tau_k$ for $c=3/50$, because the form in Equation (B.21) contains $c[F]^2$. Dividing by $c$ gives the bound on `rowWeightOf`, the squared length of the corresponding paper row $e_k$. Confusing these two weights would lose the factor $50/3$ in Equation (B.22).

b12-multiplier-route|Breakdown.CoerciveW.annotation: The test $-\Delta v$ alone gives the free diffusion and similarity energies but also the stretching term $J$, with no sign. The skew terms add frequency gains at the expense of transport and reference-mode losses. After reserving the two norm terms in Equation (B.20), one must still control $\sum_\iota\mathcal I_\iota+J$ together with the actuator pairings; the cell and tree estimates of Subsection B.3 do precisely that.

pdf-item-equation-B-12|Breakdown.modeVel.annotation: At a fixed $(r,z)$, write the velocity in the cylindrical frame. The components of $R_{-\phi_0}v(\theta+\theta_0,R_{\phi_0}y)$ in the frame at $y$ are precisely those of $v$ at the shifted time and angle. Thus Equation (B.12) is ordinary Fourier projection of those three component functions; the radial and height arguments are untouched. The conjugate exponential in the average selects the stated label.

b12-harmonic-support|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: Applying the half-period generator twice gives invariance under rotation through twice the angle of the generator. This restricts the ordinary angular frequencies to multiples of the rotation order. One application then imposes the parity condition in Equation (B.2). These identities hold also for the weak derivative tensors, with the rotation acting on their derivative indices. This removes forbidden Fourier labels, not the large allowed ones.

pdf-item-equation-B-13|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: For a fixed $r,z$, (B.13) gives $\hat v_\iota(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))=E_\iota(\theta,\phi)R_\phi\hat v_\iota(0,(r,0,z))$. The gradient and Hessian transform by rotating their values and inversely rotating their arguments. Thus all five squared norms in Equation (B.16) are independent of time and angle, and their space-time integrals reduce to $2\pi\int |\cdot|^2 r\,dr\,dz$. The products in $J$ do not separately have this property; their time and angle mean is formed in Subsection B.3.

b12-excluded-force-modes|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: The excluded intersection is invariant under negation, since both defining inequalities use absolute values. Hence exclusion from $\mathcal N_p$ also excludes $-\mathcal N_p$. The forces and their curls have no selected modes, so their pairings with both skew terms are zero. Integration by parts reduces the remaining pairing to $\langle\nabla b_i,\nabla v\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, one of the signed cell pairings in Subsection B.3.

pdf-item-equation-B-15|Breakdown.PieceWe.annotation: If the rotating coordinate advances by $\nu s$, substitution into the scalar phase $2\pi j s/S+j'\phi$ gives $\Omega=2\pi j/S+\nu j'$. The change of vector frame also contributes a rotation term to the equation, treated separately among the losses. In Lean `frameFreq` takes the ordinary integer pair $(j,j')$, obtained from Equation (B.2), rather than the indices $\iota$ themselves.

b12-frequency-gains|Breakdown.PieceWeigh.annotation: The $\lambda_p$ gain all enters the density; the $\mu_p$ gain is split. This is because the norm of the zero-order skew term is paid for by $\|v\|_\mu$ via Equation (B.19). Spending the full gain in Equation (B.16) would leave no such positive term on the left of (B.20). The fixed fraction $c_\mu$ is retained for the multiplier norm, and only $1-c_\mu$ is available to offset the losses in the velocity-square coefficient.

b12-reflection-assumptions|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: The half-turn reverses the angular frequency and the frame rate, but not the time frequency. It also carries $j+\beta=i$ to $j^\flat+\beta^\flat=i^\flat$, because the label flip is linear on the integer lattice. Consequently the selected-mode gains and both ends of every reference-mode coupling are reflected together. The equality of coefficients in Equation (B.17) uses this reindexing, not just the equality of the weights at opposite heights.

pdf-item-equation-B-18|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation:
Put $\omega_v=\operatorname{curl}v$ and $\omega_r=\operatorname{curl}W^{\mathrm r}$. In the curl of the linearized convection, $W^{\mathrm r}\cdot
abla\omega_v$ integrates to zero against $\omega_v$; the other three terms give $J$. In particular, for $A=\omega_r\cdot
abla$, integration by parts (using $\operatorname{div}\omega_r=0$ and self-adjointness of curl) gives $-\langle Av,\operatorname{curl}vangle=-	frac12\langle v,[\operatorname{curl},A]vangle$. The commutator is $\sum_k
abla(\omega_r)_k	imes\partial_k v$, yielding the last term of (B.18). This explains its factor $1/2$ and the presence of the derivative of the reference vorticity. Products with the reference harmonics couple distinct perturbation modes, so the mean of $J$ is handled separately in Subsection B.3.

b12-positive-negative-densities|Breakdow.annotation: The positive part is taken of each complete $\mathcal I_\iota$, with its five signed coefficients, and of $J$, before summing the labels. This is less restrictive than taking positive parts of the five terms separately. Once both integrals are finite, $\sum_\iota\int|\mathcal I_\iota|+\int|J|=\mathcal I^++\mathcal I^-$; Fubini and subtraction are then legitimate in Equation (B.20) and the cell reduction.

pdf-item-equation-B-19|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: At a fixed label put $A=\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p|\mu_p$ and $B=\sum_p|\operatorname{sgn}_p||\Omega_p|\mu_p$. The modulus of the combined zero-order multiplier coefficient is at most $A$. By Equation (B.19), $|A\hat v_\iota|^2\le n_\mu B|\hat v_\iota|^2$; summing and integrating gives the squared norm bound $n_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$.

b12-uniform-admissibility|Breakdown.Coer.annotation: The theorem takes the same numerical enclosure constants for every parameter and the separate density lower bound for every admissible weak perturbation. The period and rotating rates can change with the trial, but the norm constant in Proposition B.1 must not. This is the uniformity needed to use Equation (7.18) in the parameter correction.

b12-prop-b1-hypotheses|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: The multiplier is solenoidal, so $\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\mathbb PF,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. But $[F]$ in Equation (7.18) uses the original representative: a row that is solenoidal in its cell can have a nonzero normal trace on its boundary, so its pairing with a gradient need not vanish. This is why the pressure representative of Subsection B.1 can be used in the linear estimate without computing the projection or assuming that it decreases the row seminorm.

b12-prop-b1-existence|Breakdown.Coercive.annotation: Before projection, the two skew terms have the $L^2$ representatives $\sum_{p,\iota} i\operatorname{sgn}_p(\iota)\operatorname{curl}(\lambda_p\operatorname{curl}\hat v_\iota)$ and $\sum_{p,\iota} i\operatorname{sgn}_p(\iota)\mu_p\hat v_\iota$. Their bounds follow from Equation (B.19) and Parseval, using finiteness of the $\mu$ seminorm. Taking the solenoidal projection gives the unique field representing (B.14) on the dense solenoidal tests. In particular no derivative of a test field remains in the norm estimate.

pdf-item-equation-B-20|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: If $F\simeq\mathcal T_Sv+\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r}v+\sum_i\beta_i b_i$, the multiplier pairs only with the solenoidal part of this equation. Subtracting the reserved energies $\frac3{50}\|v\|_w^2+c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$ gives the lower bound by the signed density. The unknown force is kept as an explicit linear pairing, to be cancelled by Equation (B.21), rather than estimated at this step.

b12-forcing-multiplier|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The coefficients of $b_i$ vanish on $\mathcal N_p\cup(-\mathcal N_p)$, and the same holds for its curl. Both skew pairings in Equation (B.14) therefore vanish with $b_i$ as the test. The remaining pairing is $\langle b_i,-\Delta v\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\nabla b_i,\nabla v\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, which uses the same first derivatives of $v$ as the cell unknowns and constraints.

pdf-item-equation-B-21|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: The right side of (B.21) supplies precisely the quantities absent from Equation (B.20): the positive coefficient energy $c\omega^2|\beta|^2$ and the opposite of the linear actuator term, with $c=3/50$. Once the inequalities are combined, the only other costs are the measured components of $F$ and the constraint values. This is an estimate for the bordered problem, not for the velocity operator alone.

pdf-item-equation-B-21|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Proposition B.8 supplies this inequality for arbitrary admissible $v,\beta,F$, not just their retained coefficients. The finite vector in Subsection B.3 records certain measurements of these fields; the omitted coefficients, omitted harmonics and the complement of the cells all have lower estimates. The linked theorem assumes the complete cell, region and tree conditions, and proves (B.21) together with finiteness of $\mathcal I^-$. It does not assert that those conditions have been verified for numerical data.

b12-density-from-cells|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: In Equation (B.44) the measured coordinates $x_{\rm p}$ are fixed by the perturbation and forcing, but the auxiliary coordinates $x_{\rm f}$ can still be chosen. The right side is at most the difference in Equation (B.21), for every choice, since $2\zeta\cdot\ell(v)-|\zeta|^2/1000\le1000|\ell(v)|^2$. Thus one only needs a single extension $(x_{\rm p},x_{\rm f})$ on which the tree form is nonnegative. The dimension argument after Lemma B.7 provides it; positivity on all auxiliary vectors is neither required nor expected.

pdf-item-equation-B-22|Breakdown.Coerciv.annotation: Set $c=3/50$ and $t=1000$. The scalar estimate gives $\sqrt c\|(v,\beta)\|_{w,\omega}\le c_{\mathsf M}\|F\|_{\mathcal H}+\sqrt c[F]+\sqrt t|\ell(v)|$. Dividing by $\sqrt c$ explains the first two comparisons in Equation (B.22), and the coefficient of the row seminorm is exactly one.

b12-lemma-b2|Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.exte.annotation: Lemma B.2 establishes the reference estimate (7.18). For the approximate profile put $G=(\mathcal C_\alpha-\mathcal C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$; the reference equation has right side $F-G$ with the same pins and force coefficients. The cost of $G$ in the two forcing terms is at most $(c_1+c_0)c_r\|v\|_w$. Absorption gives (7.52), with the factor $1-\vartheta$ on the left. For zero pins this gives $c_L$ by Equation (7.21); existence for every datum still uses Proposition 7.8.

b12-lemma-b2|Breakdown.CoerciveWeak.rowM.annotation: Let $I=\mathcal I^+-\mathcal I^-$ and $A=\sum_i\beta_i\langle b_i,\mathsf Mv\rangle$. Then Equation (B.20) says $I+A\le\langle F,\mathsf Mv\rangle-c\|v\|_w^2-c_\mu\|v\|_\mu^2$, while (B.21) says $I+A\ge c\omega^2|\beta|^2-c[F]^2-1000|\ell(v)|^2$, with $c=3/50$. Comparing the bounds eliminates both $I$ and $A$ and leaves the squared norm of the pair with the extra frequency energy.

b12-lemma-finite|Breakdown.CoerciveWeak..annotation: The multiplier theorem gives a finite $\mu$ seminorm even before assuming the density bound. The lemma additionally assumes $\mathcal I^-<\infty$, which makes $\mathcal I^+$ finite by the extended inequality. Only then is the real subtraction in Equation (B.20) legitimate.

b12-lemma-division|Breakdown.CoerciveWea.annotation: Using $P\le a+Q$ and $Q\le\sqrt c[F]+\sqrt t|\ell(v)|$, drop the nonnegative frequency energy from $P^2$ and divide by $\sqrt c$. The coefficient of $[F]$ becomes one by construction; the others become $c_{\mathsf M}/\sqrt c$ and $\sqrt{t/c}$. This is the normalization in Equation (7.18).

ns-b3-purpose|Breakdown.CertCell.rowRest.annotation: The integral in Equation (B.21) measures what is left after the positive energies in Equation (B.20) have been reserved. A lower bound for it is needed, not a bound on its absolute value. The forcing-field pairing has opposite signs in (B.20) and (B.21); its cancellation leaves an estimate for both $v$ and $\beta$, not just for $v$.

ns-b3-quarter-plane|Breakdown.CertCell.m.annotation: Although each $\mathcal I_\iota$ is independent of time and angle, $J$ contains products of different harmonics and must first be averaged. The reduction to $(r,z)$ is exact. In particular neither the Fourier coefficients nor the integrals in Equation (B.23) are values at discretization nodes.

ns-b3-modal-meridian-values|Breakdown.Ce.annotation: By Equation (B.13), moving from $(0,(r,0,z))$ to $(\theta,R_\phi(r,0,z))$ multiplies a mode by a phase and rotates its vector components. The gradient transforms by the rotation on both indices and the Hessian on all three. The Euclidean norms in Equation (B.16) are therefore unchanged.

ns-b3-b3-hypotheses|Breakdown.CertCell.m.annotation: Reflection at $z=0$ changes the harmonic label as in Equation (B.24). The symmetry (B.17) is needed for the coefficients of the five squares to change in the same way. Thus the sum over labels has the required symmetry even if a single modal density does not.

pdf-item-equation-B-23|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The cylindrical change of variables gives $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$, since the time interval has length one. The second factor of two follows by Equation (B.24), after summation over the reflected labels. This accounts for the factor $4\pi$ relating the integrals over the cells to the integral in Equation (B.21).

ns-b3-reflect-stretch|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The rotation $R_*$ is the half-turn about the first coordinate axis and has determinant one. In particular $(R_*a)\times(R_*b)=R_*(a\times b)$, and curl transforms by $R_*$ as well. This is why all three contractions in Equation (B.18) are unchanged; an orientation-reversing reflection would require different curl signs.

ns-b3-three-harmonic-sets|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: The three sets have different uses. Resolved harmonics contribute polynomial coordinates; only the subset with triples $\varphi$ gives explicit tests of the equation. Eliminated harmonics contribute to those estimates without contributing coordinates: their velocity can be expressed through an angular derivative. They, like the other unresolved harmonics, must still pass the residual test after the charges in Equation (B.28) have been deducted.

ns-b3-complex-forms|Breakdown.CertCell.A.annotation: For a real global vector $x$, the local form is $\operatorname{Re}((X_Qx)^*A_QX_Qx)$. It is therefore the real symmetric form with matrix $\operatorname{Re}(X_Q^*(A_Q+A_Q^*)X_Q/2)$. This is how a complex cell matrix contributes to the real form $N$ in Equation (B.38).

ns-b3-leaf-coefficients|Breakdown.CertCe.annotation: The lower bounds $\mathsf I_2>0$ and $\mathsf I'_2\ge0$ apply to different second-derivative squares. A positive Hessian floor supplies the principal reserve in Equation (B.27). If there is also a curl-gradient reserve, it first pays the cost involving the curl of the omitted part; only the excess curl cost has to be paid from the Hessian reserve.

pdf-item-equation-B-26|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The direction of (B.26) is dictated by Equation (B.33): we seek a lower bound for the density integral, so the form of $\mathsf A_{\mathsf Q}$ must be no greater than the sum of the forms obtained from that integral and the permitted pairings. The subtraction of $\mathsf T_{\mathsf Q}$ is essential; it has already spent part of the measured gradient energy on the velocity tail. `residual_value_le` imposes the comparison only on the admitted local vectors.

ns-b3-unresolved-charges|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: The quantities $\mathsf a'_1,\mathsf a_1,\mathsf a_0$ account for the curl, gradient and velocity squares left out of the finite cell form. Inside a cell these are signed coefficient allowances: for instance the velocity allowance contains the cost of the reflected trace in Equation (B.34). On the complement there is no cell form to return a credit, and the three allowances are required to be nonnegative. This ensures $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L\ge\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$ there.

ns-b3-modified-stretch-constant|Breakdow.annotation: In Equation (B.25) the factor $\sqrt{7/2}$ multiplies the mean-gradient product $\mathsf s_2|G||u|$ and the two Young terms with $\mathsf s_3$. Replacing it by $\mathsf c^*$ leaves the curl-square cost $\mathsf s_1$ alone. The larger constant is therefore allowed at the expense of a smaller lower bound for the unresolved density.

ns-b3-rectangle-region|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The rectangle does not introduce a second copy of the trace. Its vector consists of selected axial trace moments already present in the cells along $z=0$. The energy for their estimate comes from the reflected harmonic, which is neither resolved nor eliminated, so that it can be reserved in its velocity charge in Equation (B.28).

ns-b3-region-coefficient-data|Breakdown..annotation: The labels in a regional set must share the enclosures for the multiplier pieces. Membership in $N_p$ and lower bounds on $|\Omega_p(\iota)|$ determine the contributions from Equations (B.14)–(B.16); $|\varkappa\iota_1|\ge k_0$ supplies a separate angular derivative bound. In particular a mode with $\iota_1=0$ and large $|\iota_2|$ can benefit from the multiplier but not from a positive angular gain in Equation (B.35).

ns-b3-charged-coefficients|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: Subtract (B.25) with $\mathsf c^*$ and the three charges in Equation (B.28) from the five lower coefficients of (B.16). No term being subtracted contains a second derivative of the mode, so $\mathsf f_2$ and $\mathsf f'_2$ are unchanged. The sixth coefficient $\mathsf f_{01}$ bounds a loss, not a square, which is why it is an upper bound and enters (B.36) with a minus sign.

ns-b3-effective-coefficients|Breakdown.C.annotation: Put $q=(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2$. For $\mathsf t\ge0$, $\mathsf t|\nabla u|^2\ge q\mathsf t|u|^2$. Transferring this part of the gradient coefficient increases the velocity coefficient by $q\mathsf t$. Taking too much would leave too little of $\mathsf f_1^*$ to bound the mixed term in Equation (B.29).

ns-b3-exterior-shapes|Breakdown.CertCell.annotation: The square exterior is a ray exterior with inner radius $a/\max(r/\rho,z/\rho)$ in the direction $(r,z)/\rho$. Its separate condition exploits the component symmetries of the zero angular mode. The constant $2$ in place of $1/4$ in Equation (B.31) reduces the velocity cost in Equation (B.30) by a factor of eight and the mixed cost by $\sqrt8$.

ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-bounds|Breakd.annotation: The factors $\rho^2$ and $\rho$ remove precisely the powers of radius controlled by Equation (B.31). The velocity loss is bounded by a constant times the integral of $|u/\rho|^2$; the mixed loss is bounded by a constant times the integral of $|\nabla u||u/\rho|$. Any faster decay of the adverse coefficients can be incorporated into smaller upper bounds on the chosen exterior.

pdf-item-equation-B-30|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Use measure $r\,dr\,dz$ on $Z$, and put $D=\int_Z|\nabla u|^2r\,dr\,dz$, $V=\int_Z|u|^2\rho^{-2}r\,dr\,dz$. By Equation (B.31), $V\le D/\Lambda_0$, and Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the mixed integral by $\sqrt{DV}$. Substitution into Equation (B.36) gives a lower bound of $(\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0})D$. Equation (B.30) makes this nonnegative.

pdf-item-theorem-B-4|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The first conclusion of Proposition B.4 precedes any calculation with the finite matrix: it ensures that the density integral can be defined as $\mathcal I^+-\mathcal I^-$. Only in the finite-positive case are the real-valued cell bounds (B.33) and (B.34) needed. The linked theorem establishes the negative-part assertion.

pdf-item-equation-B-33|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: There are two operations still to perform on (B.33): drop the unresolved residual integrals using Equation (B.29), and move $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$ to the right. The resulting signed error is exactly the one in Equation (B.34), which also accounts for the rectangle forms. Neither operation requires the cell form itself to be nonnegative.

ns-b3-b33-absolute-convergence|Breakdown.annotation: The complement of the resolved set is taken separately in each cell. Absolute convergence is asserted for the sum of its residual integrals, not obtained merely by knowing each integral exists. This justifies discarding their nonnegative sum after Equation (B.29), even though infinitely many harmonics have no coordinates.

ns-b3-b34|Breakdown.CertCell.rowSharesOf.annotation: Put $f_k=e_k/\sqrt{\tau_k}$. By Equation (B.11) the $f_k$ are orthonormal, whereas $[F]^2=\sum_k\tau_k|\langle F,f_k\rangle_{\mathcal H}|^2$. The weights are therefore part of the row calculation in Equation (B.34); replacing it by an unweighted projection norm would in general change the coercive estimate.

ns-b3-b34|Breakdown.CertCell.InstancePai.annotation: The actuator term in Equation (B.34) is a gradient pairing. Indeed the modes of $b_i$ have $\operatorname{sgn}_p(\iota)=0$ for all the skew multipliers by the condition in Subsection B.2, so $\langle b_i,\mathsf Mv\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle\nabla b_i,\nabla v\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. The other pairing, $2\zeta\cdot\ell(v)$, has the gradient representation (B.10). Thus both can be estimated by the polynomial gradient data and errors in the cells.

ns-b3-b34|Breakdown.CertCell.creditLeave.annotation: One trace estimate uses the charged velocity square of $\iota^\flat$. The estimate for the conjugate label $-\iota^\flat$ gives the same real form because the underlying perturbation is real. This accounts for the factor $2$ in Equation (B.34); it is not the factor of two from the reduction of the meridian to the quarter plane.

ns-b3-square-final-claim|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: For $\iota_1=0$ the reflected label is the original one. At $z=0$ the axial component changes sign in Equation (B.24), so its trace is zero. On the axis, a smooth axisymmetric vector must be fixed by all axial rotations, hence its transverse components vanish. These are the boundary conditions on the coordinate planes; none is imposed on the two inner sides of the square exterior.

ns-b3-trace-free-contraction|Breakdown.C.annotation: The two mixed terms in Equation (B.18) must be estimated together: the matrix $\mathbb V$ has trace zero because $\operatorname{div}\operatorname{curl}W^{\rm r}=0$. The contraction estimate quoted here uses this restriction to obtain the constant $\sqrt{7/2}$. Since both the mean and the fluctuation have trace zero, the same estimate is available for the diagonal modal pairing and the full fluctuation pairing.

ns-b3-unresolved-absorption|Breakdown.Ce.annotation: The residual in Equation (B.28) is not the original energy of an unresolved mode. The stretching loss and the three extra charges have already been deducted from it. Its nonnegativity therefore leaves the deducted energy available to pay for the products and measurements assigned to that harmonic.

ns-b3-row-and-pairing-errors|Breakdown.C.annotation: The forcing term $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,1}$ is a form of the squared test pairings; $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,2}$ contains the signed actuator and pinning pairings. The latter sign is essential. Replacing that pairing by its absolute value would not recover the cancellation with the multiplier inequality and the pinning expression in Equation (B.44).

ns-b3-remainder-budget|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: There are two parts to the velocity-tail bound. A coefficient outside degree $\mathsf d-1$ is controlled by the derivative in a variable in which its degree is at least $\mathsf d$. That derivative may have a measured component near the top degree, giving $T$, as well as an unmeasured component. In the polynomial norm the bound is $V\le T+G/\min(\Lambda^r_{\mathsf d},\Lambda^z_{\mathsf d})$, where $V,G$ are the squared velocity and gradient remainders. The first cost is included in Equation (B.26), the second in Equation (B.27).

ns-b3-b34-sum|Breakdown.CertCell.rowShar.annotation: For each cell and harmonic group, the pairings with the given triples are normalized by the inverse square root of the Gram matrix in Equation (B.11), then weighted by $\tau_k$ in the squared norm. The groups have disjoint supports or orthogonal harmonics. Adding their contributions gives $[F]^2$; the normalization of (B.33) requires the factor $(3/50)/(4\pi)$.

ns-b3-b34-sum|Breakdown.CertCell.Instanc.annotation: The actuator and pinning pairings reassemble to the global pairings once their cellwise profile errors are included (these terms are needed for the density bound in Equation (B.21)). In particular $n_b|\beta|^2$ bounds the remaining actuator error rather than multiplying the forcing measurement. The $4\pi$ factor is the conversion from the quarter-plane form to the original space-time integral.

ns-b3-b34-sum|Breakdown.CertCell.creditL.annotation: Add the rectangle forms to the sum of the cell forms, moving $\mathsf r_{\mathsf Q,0}$ to the right in Equation (B.33). The resulting right-hand side contains precisely the left-hand side of (B.34), which is bounded by the global row and pairing terms. This is why the rectangle forms are added in Equation (B.38), although they are paid for by energy deducted from unresolved harmonics.

pdf-item-theorem-B-5|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: These derivative inequalities use the spatial transformation law (B.13), at fixed $\theta$. In particular their frequency is the angular wave number, independent of the rates $\nu_p(\alpha)$ used in Equation (B.15). They apply to all the harmonics of $v$, including those not chosen in a cell or acted on by a skew multiplier.

ns-b3-b35|Breakdown.CertCell.TailBand.an.annotation:
For the example in Subsection C.1 the angular order is $19$. The first nonzero angular wave number already gives $|
abla u|^2\ge324|u|^2/r^2$ and $|
abla^2u|^2\ge289|
abla u|^2/r^2$. The zero angular modes have neither gain, irrespective of their time frequency. The lemma also applies to the smaller orders allowed by Equation (B.1).

pdf-item-equation-B-36|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: Equation (B.36) retains all the Hessian gain in $\mathsf f_1^*$ while discarding any positive remainder in the curl square. It has not yet used the bound for $|u|$ in terms of $|\nabla u|$. That last step can be taken pointwise by Equation (B.29) or, on the exterior, in the integrated form (B.31).

In `quad_lower` the exterior expression $\mathsf f_1^\infty|\nabla u|^2-\mathsf f_0^\infty|u|^2/\rho^2-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty|\nabla u||u|/\rho$ is subtracted from the actual form. By the exterior coefficient bounds the resulting lower form has nonnegative effective gradient and velocity coefficients and zero mixed coefficient. It passes the same scalar test with $\mathsf t=0$. This yields the pointwise lower bound used in Lemma B.6, without requiring pointwise nonnegativity of the exterior density.

ns-b3-angular-derivative|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: Let $Jx=\mathbf e_z\times x$. The angular derivative acts on a vector as $ikI+J$, rather than $ikI$: on the axial and circular transverse components its eigenvalues are $ik,i(k+1),i(k-1)$. Each transverse component can lose at most one unit of $|k|$. Keeping the directional derivative in this estimate will also give the extra term in Equation (B.31).
