ns-b3-negative-lower-coefficient|Breakdo.annotation: If $\mathsf f'_2\ge0$, multiplication of the last squared inequality in Equation (B.35) by this coefficient preserves its direction. If $\mathsf f'_2<0$, the proposed lower bound is nonpositive while the actual curl-gradient term is nonnegative by admissibility. This proves the same bound in either case.

pdf-item-theorem-B-6|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The first assertion of Lemma B.6 is an inverse-square inequality for the ray geometry and the angular mode, with no multiplier coefficients in it. The second requires such an inequality and the exterior coefficient test. This separation permits the constant from Proposition B.4 for the square exterior to be used in the same argument.

ns-b3-b6-integrated-claim|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: After Equation (B.31) is available, the shape of $Z$ no longer enters the coefficient calculation. The total negative contribution is bounded by the gradient energy times $\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0+\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$. This also explains why the exterior cover must be assembled by integrals, rather than by testing individual points.

ns-b3-exterior-coefficient-signs|Breakdo.annotation: Set $s=\sqrt{\Lambda_0}$, $G=\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/(2s)$ and $A=\mathsf f_0^\infty+s\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/2$. Equation (B.30) is equivalent to $\Lambda_0G\ge A$; as $A\ge0$, also $G\ge0$. This sign is needed to multiply the gradient lower bound in Equation (B.31) by $G$.

ns-b3-exterior-lower-bound|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: The lower bound from `quad_lower` contains only $|\nabla u|^2$, $|u|^2/\rho^2$ and their geometric mean. The first integral is finite by the perturbation hypothesis and the second by Equation (B.31); Cauchy–Schwarz then gives finiteness of the mixed integral. This is sufficient even if some of the original higher-derivative terms have infinite positive integral.

ns-b3-exterior-integrability-sign|Breakd.annotation: Both terms in the lower bound are integrable with measure $r\,dr\,dz$: the gradient energy is finite and Equation (B.31) bounds the inverse-square integral. If $L$ denotes this lower bound, then $(\mathcal I_\iota^\circ)_-\le L_-$. Thus the signed integral is defined before its nonnegativity is established, including when its positive part is infinite.

With $G,A$ the two coefficients after Young’s inequality, (B.31) gives $\int_Z\mathcal I_\iota^\circ r\,dr\,dz\ge(G-A/\Lambda_0)\int_Z|\nabla u|^2r\,dr\,dz$. Expanding the coefficient gives exactly $\mathsf f_1^\infty-\mathsf f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0}-\mathsf f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0$, nonnegative by Equation (B.30).

ns-b3-tree-data|Breakdown.CertCell.Certi.annotation: The tree works with the sum of the forms attached at a node and the forms supplied by its children. A node keeps its own outgoing form, records positive pivot squares and records negative column squares. The signs of the outgoing forms are immaterial except at the root. Their intermediate contributions cancel when the node estimates (Equation (B.42)) are added.

ns-b3-attached-matrices|Breakdown.CertCe.annotation: Partitioning a cell matrix into blocks does not partition its coordinates into independent problems. Off-diagonal blocks join two coordinate groups, and a block and its adjoint must be kept together to account for the real cross term. The additional matrices attached at two nodes with opposite signs are permitted because their sum in Equation (B.38) is zero.

ns-b3-b38|Breakdown.CertCell.Assembly.Tr.annotation: This identity is a sum of the attached forms, not a new inequality: every cell block is included, the rectangle forms have their factor two, the global form occurs once and the auxiliary pairs cancel. Thus the later tree estimates are estimates of exactly the form used in Equation (B.44).

ns-b3-b39|Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.annotation: Put $S_\xi=N_\xi+\sum_{\xi\prime}V_{\xi\prime}$. Subtracting (B.39) gives a lower bound on $S_\xi-V_\xi$ consisting of $H_\xi-K_\xi$, the positive nonpivot charges, and the negative error form $-(H^\prime_\xi+K^\prime_\xi)$ on $|x|$. The nonpivot charges are exactly those needed to cancel the corresponding diagonal error in Equation (B.40).

ns-b3-b40|Breakdown.CertCell.Certificate.annotation: Write $C=|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime$ for the entrywise error bound in Equation (B.40) and put $a_j=1/\mathsf w_j$. The row test is $(Ca)_i\le m_i a_i$. By symmetry and $2|x_i x_j|\le (a_j/a_i)x_i^2+(a_i/a_j)x_j^2$, it gives $|x|^{\mathsf T}C|x|\le\sum_i m_i x_i^2$. The positive weights redistribute the required diagonal margins: for an error joining only two coordinates, making one margin smaller makes the other larger.

ns-b3-pivot-diagonal-and-slack|Breakdown.annotation: At a pivot the error allowance must be paid out of the proposed positive diagonal: $p_j-m_j\ge p_{\xi,j}>0$. At a nonpivot it is paid by deducting $m_jx_j^2$ from the outgoing form, as in Equation (B.39). Thus a variable need not have a positive margin at every node where it appears; the sum of the node estimates will require one positive pivot somewhere.

ns-b3-complex-residual|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The complex analogue of a real column square is the Hermitian form $yy^*$, whose value is $|y^*z|^2$. Thus $Y^\prime Y^{\prime *}$ contributes nonnegative squares and $-YY^*$ contributes negative squares. The residual, after removing these and the proposed pivot diagonal, is estimated entrywise by moduli in Equation (B.40).

pdf-item-theorem-B-7|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The column-count condition and the pivot condition are used for different conclusions. If there are $f$ free coordinates, the common kernel of the real negative-column pairings has codimension at most $f$. The positive pivot coefficients make the root lower form strictly positive there, and the signed-tree bound transfers this to the total form. Proposition B.8 supplies the additional fact that the kernel meets the free-coordinate subspace only at zero.

ns-b3-column-kernel-positive|Breakdown.C.annotation: For a vector in the common kernel the only surviving terms in Equation (B.41) are the positive pivot squares. Each coordinate has at least one strictly positive coefficient, so the sum can vanish only at zero. The formal positivity assertion is for the root lower form, which bounds the total form from below by the preceding lemma.

ns-b3-weighted-row-proof|Breakdown.CertC.annotation: The row-sum argument controls the residual $B$ and the two enclosure errors together. Their combined contribution to the lower estimate is at least $-|x|^{\mathsf T}(|B|+\mathsf H^\prime+\mathsf K^\prime)|x|$, hence at least $-\sum_jm_j x_j^2$ by Equation (B.40). It is not necessary for either enclosure-error matrix to be positive semidefinite; their entries are nonnegative and the estimate is on $|x|$.

pdf-item-theorem-B-8|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: Proposition B.8 is the passage from finitely represented data and their inequalities to a bound on every admissible perturbation. It supplies (B.21), not yet (7.18); the latter follows by Lemma B.2 together with Equation (B.20). The Lean implication has the cell, region, tree and field-data conditions as hypotheses. Neither the statement nor its proof is an enclosure of the numerical matrices of a particular certificate.

ns-b3-b8-finiteness-proof|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: The negative integral is finite by Proposition B.4. If the positive integral is infinite, the left side of (B.21) is $+\infty$ while its right side is finite for the given $v,\beta,F$. It is therefore enough to prove the remaining inequalities in the case where both contributions are finite.

ns-b3-finite-signed-integrals|Breakdown..annotation: Finiteness of both sign integrals implies summability of the absolute modal integrals and integrability of the stretching term. In particular the quarter-plane expression in Equation (B.23) can now be restricted to the cells and their complement and added back as an ordinary integral. This is the reason for disposing of the infinite-positive case first.

ns-b3-cell-off-modes|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: The finite cover makes the negative-part integral of the unresolved density zero for each unresolved label. The formal cover can use larger regional curl, gradient and velocity charges, with the same stretching constant, than those subtracted in the cell: this only decreases the tested form. The sum of unresolved negative-part integrals is therefore zero (`OffModesVanish`), which leaves the absolutely convergent nonnegative remainder in Equation (B.33).

ns-b3-exterior-loss-comparison|Breakdown.annotation: The original stretching loss uses $\sqrt{7/2}$; Equation (B.28) enlarges it to $\mathsf c^*\ge\sqrt{7/2}$ and subtracts further nonnegative charges on the complement. Consequently $\mathcal I_\iota-\mathcal L_\iota\ge\mathcal I_\iota^\circ$. On bounded regions the latter is nonnegative pointwise by Equation (B.29), whereas on unbounded regions only its integral need be nonnegative. Either estimate suffices to show that the exterior makes no negative contribution after summing the modal integrals.

ns-b3-exterior-sum-positive|Breakdown.Ce.annotation: We are now in the case $\mathcal I^+<\infty$ and $\mathcal I^-<\infty$. By Lemma B.3, the sum of the integrals of $|\mathcal I_\iota|$ is finite. The nonnegative $\mathcal L_\iota$ on the complement has integral at most that of $\mathcal I_\iota$ for each $\iota$, so its sum is integrable as well. This permits (B.32) to be integrated and gives the nonnegative exterior contribution to (B.21).

ns-b3-sum-before-b44|Breakdown.CertCell..annotation: After dropping the nonnegative unresolved residuals, add the cell bounds and move the four error terms to the right. Add the rectangle forms; Equation (B.34) bounds the resulting error by the forcing rows, actuator and pin pairings, and $\mathsf n_b|\beta|^2$. The last term cancels with Equation (B.43). Multiplication by $4\pi$ now puts both the density and the pairings back in their original normalization. The exterior can be included because its integral is nonnegative.

pdf-item-equation-B-44|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: By Equation (B.38) the cell forms, twice the rectangle forms and the global form constitute the same real quadratic form that is bounded by Lemma B.7. The auxiliary matrices used in the tree have zero total contribution. Thus no further matrix approximation is needed between the analytic inequality (B.44) and the signed tree bound.

ns-b3-completed-square|Breakdown.CertCel.annotation: The pinning expression has the exact form $1000|\ell(v)|^2-|\zeta-1000\ell(v)|^2/1000$. Its maximum provides the term in Equation (B.21), but we do not choose $\zeta$ to attain it. Any $\zeta$ gives a sufficient upper bound, including the one selected by the tree argument.

ns-b3-find-free-coordinate|Breakdown.Cer.annotation: The remaining step concerns the affine set $(x_{\rm p},0)+\{(0,x_{\rm f})\}$, not all global vectors at once. We seek a point of this set orthogonal to every negative column. The tree gives positivity on their common kernel (the concluding assertion of Lemma B.7); what remains is to show that this kernel meets every such affine set.

ns-b3-kernel-free-intersection|Breakdown.annotation: If two vectors in $\mathcal Y^\perp$ have the same prescribed coordinates, their difference is purely free. Its form is nonpositive by the zero-input estimate and strictly positive by Lemma B.7 unless the difference vanishes. This proves injectivity of projection onto prescribed coordinates and explains the need for strictly positive pivots.

ns-b3-final-nonnegativity|Breakdown.Cert.annotation: Take the extension in $\mathcal Y^\perp$ with the prescribed $x_{\rm p}$. Its form is nonnegative by Equation (B.41), and by Equation (B.44) the gap in Equation (B.21) is at least $4\pi$ times this form. The extension changed no measured quantity of $v,\beta,F$. Since these were arbitrary and their omitted parts were included in the estimates, (B.21) holds on the full perturbation class.

ns-b4-001|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Cell.annotation: Unlike the estimate of Subsection B.3, the estimates below do not require a cellwise representation of the unknown perturbation. The quadratic and linear adjoint pairings are bounded by a multiple of $\|v\|_w^2$ and of $\|v\|_w$, respectively. It is the known fields in those pairings whose norms must be enclosed. The last estimate, (7.34), involves only the given approximate family.

pdf-item-equation-B-46|Breakdown.CertRed.annotation: Put $a=\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$ and $b=\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}$. The mixed product is bounded by $(a^2+b^2)/2\le |u|_w^2/2$, which gives the third bound. Together with Equation (7.48) it also gives $\|u\|_{L^\infty}^2\le (4\pi\sqrt{w_*})^{-1}|u|_w^2$. The linked result uses the constant weight of Appendix B.

pdf-item-theorem-B-9|Breakdown.CellLayer.annotation: There are two fields associated with the centre of the parameter set: $W_0^{\mathrm a}$ is the member used in Equation (B.9), while $W^{\mathrm r}$ is the field used to prove the inverse estimate in Subsections B.2–B.3. The latter can be chosen for ease of certification and need not be a member of the approximate family. Its difference from the centre is estimated once, and the additional variation from the centre is estimated uniformly on $\mathcal K$.

pdf-item-theorem-B-9|Breakdown.CertReduc.annotation: There are two contributions to the reference convection form. The one in which $W^{\mathrm r}$ differentiates $u$ reduces by incompressibility to a quadratic form in $\nabla u$ with the strain as coefficient. Only its lower bound is needed. The term in which $u$ differentiates $W^{\mathrm r}$ is bounded in absolute value with the $L^3$ norm of the full reference gradient (these two estimates are used for the frozen-time lower bound in Equation (7.22)).

In Equation (7.52) the use of the reference estimate costs $(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r}\|v\|_w$ because the change of forcing is measured in both the norm and the seminorm (7.17). Thus $c_{\mathrm r}<1/(c_1+c_0)$ is needed when $c_1+c_0>0$. The inverse constant for zero constraints is then bounded by $(c_1+c_0)/(1-(c_1+c_0)c_{\mathrm r})$. The first bound of (B.48) must be sufficiently small for the chosen $c_L$ in Equation (7.21).

A bound for the period norm in Equation (7.19) by itself gives no bound on the supremum of the gradient energy over time. For the latter, Proposition 7.9 uses the energy identity and integrates from a phase of minimum energy. The spatial form (7.22) controls the increase between phases, so its estimate is required for each $\theta$, before time integration.

ns-b4-006|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Shif.annotation: The supremum in $\theta$ of the spatial norm is taken separately for each parameter, and the same bound must hold for all parameters in $\mathcal K$. It cannot be replaced by an $L^3$ norm in space-time: the product involving $u$ is to be estimated also for a single time slice in Equation (7.22). For the fixed centre error the parameter quantifier is redundant.

pdf-item-equation-B-48|Breakdown.CellLay.annotation: Group the first budget as $A+B$, where $A=c_w\mathsf n_0^{(2)}$ and $B=(\mathsf n_0^\infty+\mathsf n_1^\infty+2\mathsf n_1^{(3)}/\sqrt3)/\sqrt{w_*}$. The third budget is $A+B/2$. Its terms multiplying $\|\nabla u\|_2\|\Delta u\|_2$ gain the factor $1/2$ from Equation (B.46); the term $\|u\|_\infty\|\Delta u\|_2$ has already used the mixed product in the derivation of $c_w$ and is bounded by $c_w|u|_w^2$.

pdf-item-equation-B-48|Breakdown.CertRed.annotation: The middle budget concerns only $W^{\mathrm r}$. The strain loss is at most $\mathsf s_-\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}^2\le(\mathsf s_-/w_*)|u|_w^2$. The remaining convection term has one gradient and one Laplacian norm, so Equation (B.45) and the product estimate in Equation (B.46) give the coefficient $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-008|Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTra.annotation: At fixed $\alpha$, the reference equation and the approximate-field equation use the same $S(\alpha)$, constraints and forcing fields. Hence the change in the equation is exactly the two convection terms with $W_\alpha^{\mathrm a}-W^{\mathrm r}$. There is no estimate of a time derivative of this difference in Equation (7.19).

ns-b4-009|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Shif.annotation: Here both profiles are evaluated at the same $\theta=s/S(\alpha)$ in period-one coordinates. The centre error $Z_0$ is fixed as a function of these coordinates. By Equation (B.9), $Z_1$ is affine in $\alpha$ inside $B_{r_\chi}$ (and vanishes at $\alpha=0$); outside the ball the radial phase varies as well. The gradient norm in Equation (B.47) must enclose the derivative of that phase, not just the affine coefficient variation.

pdf-item-equation-B-49|Breakdown.CertRed.annotation: To obtain the squared norm bound, apply Hölder to $|\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}^2|u|^2$ with exponents $3/2$ and $3$. The resulting factors are $\||\nabla Z_1|_{\mathrm{op}}\|_{L^3}^2$ and $\|u\|_{L^6}^2$, respectively. The latter gives the constant $4/3$ by Equation (B.45), which becomes $2/\sqrt3$ in Equation (B.49).

ns-b4-012|Breakdown.CertReduction.gapTra.annotation: The bound is for the unprojected difference of the two convection fields. Squaring and integrating over the normalized period gives $\|G\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le c_{\mathrm r}^2\|v\|_w^2$ for $G=(C_\alpha-C_\alpha^{\mathrm r})v$. This also proves $G\in\mathcal H$, so that the reference right-hand side $F-G$ in Equation (7.52) is admissible before any projection onto solenoidal fields.

ns-b4-016|Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftG.annotation: Hölder bounds the second pairing in magnitude by $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}$. Use Equation (B.45), then $2\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla u\|_{L^2}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le|u|_w^2$. Its cost is thus at most $\mathsf n_{\mathrm r}^{(3)}|u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$.

ns-b4-017|Breakdown.CertReduction.frozen.annotation: In Equation (7.22) we may discard $\|\Delta u\|_2^2+\|\nabla u\|_2^2/4$ when obtaining a lower bound. The remaining two terms are the strain contribution and the term estimated by Sobolev. The resulting bound may be negative; Proposition 7.9 controls the increase of the energy over an interval, without requiring the form to be coercive at every phase.

ns-b4-018|Breakdown.CertReduction.shiftG.annotation: The $L^2$ gradient error is bounded using $\|u\|_{L^\infty}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le c_w|u|_w^2$. For the $L^3$ error, apply Equation (B.45) and the third inequality of (B.46) to get $\|u\|_{L^6}\|\Delta u\|_{L^2}\le |u|_w^2/\sqrt{3w_*}$. These give the remaining two terms in the third budget of (B.48).

ns-b4-018|Breakdown.CertReduction.formSh.annotation: Pairing the operator-norm bound (7.19) with $-\Delta u$ at the slice level would give the first budget of (B.48) as a sufficient coefficient. The proof instead keeps the separate terms in Equation (B.49) until multiplying by $\|\Delta u\|_2$. It thereby gains a factor of two in the costs of transport and of the $L^3$ gradient error, but not the $L^2$ gradient error.

ns-b4-019|Breakdown.CertReduction.frozen.annotation: In Equation (7.55), the total $c_3\ge c'_3+c''_3$ contributes $(2S(\alpha)/m)c_3\|v\|_w^2$ to the bound for the squared gradient supremum. At $\|v\|_w\le2\varepsilon$, the cost is at most $8S_{\max}c_3\varepsilon^2/m$, which appears in Equation (7.27). The bound on $c_{\mathrm r}$ is used earlier, to obtain the joint norm estimate in Equation (7.52).

ns-b4-020|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Adjoin.annotation: An exact adjoint field would recover the linear functional $(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j$ by testing the linearized velocity equation. Thus the unknown field would enter this measurement only through the prescribed constraint values. Lemma B.12 quantifies the error of this replacement; it is distinct from the bound on the nonlinear pairing and the offset of the approximate family.

ns-b4-021|Breakdown.CertReduction.Adjoin.annotation: To estimate $(v\cdot\nabla)v$ in $\mathcal H$ one needs the separate supremum in time from Equation (7.27). To estimate its pairing with $\psi_j$ it suffices to control the product of the two velocity factors at each time by $|v|_w^2$. This is why Lemma B.10 uses a spatial norm of the given test field uniformly in time.

pdf-item-theorem-B-10|Breakdown.CertRedu.annotation: The bridge first bounds the integral of $|(v\cdot\nabla)v|\,|\psi_j|$ on the period. This is sufficient both to define the pairing and to bound its absolute value by $\tilde a_j\|v\|_w^2$. In contrast to Lemma B.11 below, the estimate does not use cancellation between angular or temporal modes.

ns-b4-023|Breakdown.CertReduction.adjoin.annotation: There is no smallness hypothesis on $v$ in Lemma B.10. Its coefficient is computed before solving (7.12); only when (7.32) is used in Equation (7.35) does the radius $2\varepsilon$ give a quadratic error of size $4\tilde a_j\varepsilon^2$.

ns-b4-025|Breakdown.CertReduction.adjoin.annotation: Compare Lemma 7.6: the square of the full $L^2$ norm of the quadratic forcing involves the product $\|v(\theta)\|_\infty^2\|\nabla v(\theta)\|_2^2$, for which a supremum bound is needed. Here the pairing is integrated without squaring the spatial estimate. The energy over one period therefore suffices, and the coefficient in Equation (7.35) is $4\tilde a_j\varepsilon^2$.

ns-b4-029|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Azimut.annotation: Here $k$ is the wave number of a scalar Cartesian component, not the label $\iota_1$ in Equation (B.2). Indeed a cylindrical mode of angular number $m$ has $u_1\pm iu_2=e^{\pm i\phi}(u_r\pm iu_\phi)$, hence scalar wave numbers $m\pm1$, and its third component has number $m$. It is these scalar numbers that enter $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}$. For $|k|=1$ the resulting dual norm coefficient is $2/3$ instead of $2$.

pdf-item-theorem-B-11|Breakdown.AdjointD.annotation: For a given decomposition the cost is $\mathsf n'+\mathsf n''$. Orthogonality is available within the represented modal field but need not hold between that field and the ordinary remainder (for the use of this decomposition in the linear adjoint defect bound, see Lemma B.12). The linked bound in fact tests arbitrary weak-gradient slices in $L^6$ with finite period gradient energy, without a solenoidality hypothesis.

ns-b4-031|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.dualBo.annotation: An adjoint residual with dual bound $\mathsf n$ contributes at most $\mathsf n\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}\le (\mathsf n/\sqrt{w_*})\|v\|_w$. This is the estimate used not only for $\mathsf R_{j,\alpha}$ in Equation (B.56) but also for the transposed stretching and time-derivative terms. No $L^2$ bound for $v$ is needed.

ns-b4-032|Breakdown.CertCell.Internal.sl.annotation: In the ray integral, the volume factor $\rho^2$ cancels the inverse-square weight, so Equation (B.37) with $a=0$ gives $\int |U|^2/|y|^2\le4\int|\partial_\rho U|^2$. The radial energy is only part of the full gradient energy; the remaining angular part is what will improve this bound for a nonzero wave number.

ns-b4-035|Breakdown.CertCell.Internal.sl.annotation: At $k=0$ the coefficient in Equation (B.50) is $1/4$, giving $\|U/|y|\|_2\le2\|\nabla U\|_2$. The argument for $k\ne0$ uses the vanishing of a smooth mode on the axis; that vanishing is not available for $k=0$ and is not needed.

ns-b4-044|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsPote.annotation: The auxiliary fields are a way of representing a functional of the perturbation in norms already present in Equation (7.14). A term $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ can be paired with $\Delta v$ by moving two derivatives, whereas $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ can be paired through the gradients by moving one. Thus a potential of size $O(|y|^{-1})$ is allowed for $\mathsf U_j$, even though it need not have finite $L^2$ norm. The remaining defect is measured by Lemma B.11.

pdf-item-equation-B-51|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The bounds $O((1+|y|)^{-2})$ on $\mathsf G_j,\nabla\mathsf U_j,\mathsf F_j,q_j$ give square integrability in space. The common bound on their indicated derivatives is in $L^{6/5}$, both near zero and at infinity, as required in Equation (B.55). The linked condition also bounds $\mathsf U_j=O((1+|y|)^{-1})$ and gives the stronger separate decay estimates for $\Delta\mathsf G_j$ and $\Delta\mathsf U_j$ of orders $-4$ and $-3$. These are regularity requirements, not the smallness requirements in Equation (B.53).

pdf-item-equation-B-52|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The sign of the constraint source follows from $\langle v,-\Delta\tilde\Phi_l\rangle=\langle\nabla v,\nabla\tilde\Phi_l\rangle$. Thus the desired adjoint equation has right side $-\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\tilde\Phi_l$, and moving it to the left gives the plus sign in Equation (B.52). The three auxiliary terms may reduce the dual norm of the remainder, but their own costs must be included in Equation (B.53).

ns-b4-048|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.remain.annotation: The adjoint is chosen to reproduce a constraint, not to be in the kernel of the transposed operator. The advantage is that at the corrected solution the constraint has a prescribed value. Because the matrix field $\Xi_l$ is not generally a gradient, (B.52) uses a divergence-free replacement generator and Equation (B.56) restores the difference from the true constraint.

pdf-item-theorem-B-12|Breakdown.AdjointD.annotation: Lemma B.12 gives a bound for the difference between two linear functionals of $v$, before the constraints are imposed. In Equation (B.56) the first line is the adjoint equation defect with its auxiliary terms, the second changes the operator to the one at the actual parameter, and the third changes the represented constraint back to (7.11). Each is bounded by a multiple of the same energy norm.

The two operator-related costs in Equation (B.53) make up `defectSum`: the first covers the residual of the adjoint about $W_\alpha^0$ with period $S(0)$, and the second covers the remaining changes in the operator. The formal definition also has a sum for individually fitted tangent defects; it is empty for the represented family. The pin error is a separate charge.

pdf-item-equation-B-53|Breakdown.Adjoint.annotation: The number $a_j$ is an upper bound for an operator norm on the perturbation space, uniform over $\alpha\in\mathcal K$. For example, the first square root alone is not sufficient if the inverse period or the tangent fields change appreciably. The other terms in Equation (B.53) restore the full operator and the actual constraint, respectively.

pdf-item-equation-B-53|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: The expression in Equation (B.53) is recovered from the general formal budget by substituting the links of this represented instance. In particular, no tangent direction is fitted by a separate potential, so the sum over fitted directions is zero and the free-direction sum runs over all coordinates. The row of coupling coefficients is the one used in the constraints.

ns-b4-053|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.IsAdjo.annotation: Although $F$ is only specified modulo gradients, its pairing with the divergence-free $\psi$ is independent of the representative: $\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}=\langle PF,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}$. This is why the pressure of the unknown correction is absent from Equations (B.54)–(B.56). The statement still assumes $F\in\mathcal H$.

ns-b4-059|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Intern.annotation: For $A=q_j I$, the right side of (B.55) is $-\int q_j\operatorname{div}v=0$. This removes the auxiliary pressure from the defect bound, not from the definition of the strong residual. In Lemma B.13 the pairing will instead be restricted to a ball, where the same cancellation cannot be made without a boundary condition.

ns-b4-060|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Intern.annotation: The decomposition does not expand the radial phase in powers of $\alpha$. It is exact at the current phase: $W_\alpha^{\rm a}-W_\alpha^0=\sum_i\alpha_iW_\alpha^i$. Hence the difference from the operator in Equation (B.52) consists only of this convection change and the inverse-period change $\varsigma\cdot\alpha$. No term involving $W_\alpha^0-W_0^0$ has to be added to (B.56).

ns-b4-060|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: The base and tangent fields in the adjoint equation and in the offset calculation must come from the same represented family. `centre_eq` and `free_eq` use the phase at $\alpha$; `centrePeriod_eq` and `periodRate_eq` identify the reciprocal period and its affine coefficients with those in Lemma B.13. The matching-ball restriction in B.13, not these links, is what permits evaluating the fields at $\alpha=0$.

ns-b4-061|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Intern.annotation: Solve Equation (B.52) for the first line. The three auxiliary terms to be paired with $v$ are then $-\Delta\mathsf G_j$, $-w_*\Delta\mathsf U_j$ and $+\operatorname{div}\mathsf F_j^{\mathsf T}$. Moving two, one and one spatial derivatives respectively gives the signs $-,+,-$ in the first line of (B.56); the pressure pairing vanishes. The linked slice identity formalizes this part of the calculation.

The inverse-period change contributes $-(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)\iint v\cdot\partial_\theta\psi$ because it is the adjoint of the time derivative. The convection change contributes $\sum_i\alpha_i[(W_\alpha^i\cdot\nabla)v\cdot\psi+v\cdot\sum_k\psi_k\nabla W_{\alpha,k}^i]$ under the integral. These are exact differences of linear operators; there are no products of two direction fields as in Equation (B.57).

ns-b4-062|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjoin.annotation: The three estimates use no norm of the time derivative of $v$. Even the period-change term now pairs $v$ with a derivative of the known field, to which Lemma B.11 applies. Hence the bound for the defect is in $\|v\|_w$, the norm provided by the inverse estimate, rather than the full graph norm of the similarity operator.

ns-b4-063|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.potent.annotation: Put $B=w_*\mathsf n_{\mathsf U}+\mathsf n_{\mathsf F}+\mathsf n_{\mathsf R}$. The bound $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H}+B\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H}$ is the dot product of $(\mathsf n_{\mathsf G},B/\sqrt{w_*})$ with $(\|\Delta v\|_{\mathcal H},\sqrt{w_*}\|\nabla v\|_{\mathcal H})$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives the square root in Equation (B.53), rather than the larger sum $\mathsf n_{\mathsf G}+B/\sqrt{w_*}$.

ns-b4-064|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.freeSh.annotation: At fixed $\alpha$, Cauchy–Schwarz gives $|\sum_i\alpha_i W_\alpha^i|\le(\sum_i\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i)^{1/2}(\sum_i\varpi_i|W_\alpha^i|^2)^{1/2}$. Pair the latter factor times $|\psi|$ with $|\nabla v|$. For the transposed stretching term use Lemma B.11 first, then the same weighted Cauchy–Schwarz on $\sum_i|\alpha_i|\mathsf n_i$. Thus the common radius factor multiplies $\mathsf n_{\rm v}+\mathsf n_{\rm d}$.

ns-b4-067|Breakdown.AdjointDefect.adjoin.annotation: The final inequality has the form $|\langle F,\psi\rangle_{\mathcal H}-(Y(\alpha)\ell(v))_j|\le a_j\|v\|_w$. It has been established for any $v\in\mathcal D_{S(\alpha)}$ with the indicated $F$, not just for a perturbation of size $2\varepsilon$. The size restriction enters only when the inequality is used for the parameter update (the linear error term in the inclusion budget of Equation (7.35)).

ns-b4-068|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: One could try to expand $F_\alpha^{\rm a}$ on the whole space, but a change of period changes the logarithmic radial phase at infinity (Appendix C.4). The phase correction vanishes on $B_{r_\chi}$, where the velocity and inverse period are affine. Therefore the coefficient calculation on that ball is exact and the exterior needs just a norm enclosure, not bounds on the parameter derivatives of the phase.

pdf-item-equation-B-57|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: Collecting the ordered coefficients gives $F^{(ii)}$ once, and gives $F^{(ii')}$ as the sum of the two orders for $i<i'$. For example, the gradient contribution from $\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}$ is then $-\nabla(W_0^i\cdot W_0^{i'})$, not half of it. The resulting coefficient is used once in Equations (B.58) and (B.59).

The constant coefficient of the ball response is $V_j\cdot\beta^0-\langle F^{(0)},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. It includes the centre's prescribed force as well as its residual, even though the desired diagonal response vanishes at $\alpha=0$. The corresponding whole-space constant differs by the exterior pairing, bounded later in Lemma B.13.

ns-b4-072|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: Solenoidality removes a gradient from a pairing on all of space under the indicated integrability hypotheses. On the ball, however, $\int_{B_{r_\chi}}\nabla p\cdot\psi_j=\int_{\partial B_{r_\chi}}p\,\psi_j\cdot\nu$ for smooth fields, and there is no zero-normal condition on $\psi_j$ there. Thus the pressure and kinetic-energy gradients in Equation (B.57) are retained in Equation (B.58). Lean integrates on the closed ball; the sphere has measure zero.

pdf-item-theorem-B-13|Breakdown.CellRedu.annotation: The intervals in Equation (B.58) enclose coefficients of the signed scalar response, not of the norm of the residual. In particular the centre and linear coefficients subtract the residual pairing from the corresponding force coefficient. For the quadratic part the force is affine, so its coefficient is just $-\langle F^{(ii')},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$.

The monomial estimates use an enclosing box of the parameter set. For distinct $i,i'\notin\mathcal J$ one could use $|d_i d_{i'}\alpha_i\alpha_{i'}|\le\varrho_*^2/2$ from the sum of their two squares; Equation (B.59) instead uses the simpler product of the individual radii. Thus the budget is sufficient, not necessarily the supremum of the response error on $\mathcal K$.

Write the ball response as $P_j(\alpha)=V_j\cdot\beta^{\rm a}(\alpha)-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a},\psi_j\rangle_\chi$. Then the quantity to bound in Equation (7.34) is $P_j(\alpha)-d_j\alpha_j-\langle F_\alpha^{\rm a}\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi},\psi_j\mathbf1_{|y|>r_\chi}\rangle_{\mathcal H}$, since $\bar\ell=0$. The polynomial enclosures are used only for the first difference.

pdf-item-equation-B-59|Breakdown.CellRed.annotation: A bound on the absolute response itself would also charge the term $d_j\alpha_j$ needed for the Newton update. Instead the diagonal linear coefficient is centered at $d_j$ and the other coefficients at zero. The sum in Equation (B.59) encloses the remainder after these subtractions, which is the approximate-family part of $-d_j\alpha'_j$ in Equation (7.35).

ns-b4-077|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: Equation (7.34) is an enclosure of the approximate-family contribution to the new scaled coordinate, not the whole coordinate. In Equation (7.35) one still needs the quadratic pairing, the linear adjoint defect, and the difference of the force pairings from $V_j$. The coordinates outside $\mathcal J$ are estimated by Equations (7.36)–(7.37), without the ball polynomial for an adjoint row.

ns-b4-084|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instan.annotation: The adjoint pairing predicts the force with the additional term $-(Y(\alpha)\bar\ell(\alpha))_j$ in Equation (7.34). In Subsection B.1 the constraints for the correction have value zero, so the entire offset is the one just estimated. If nonzero constraints were prescribed, their known contribution would have to be included before testing the parameter inclusion.

ns-b4-085|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Cert.annotation: The remaining inequalities close the analytic argument. In Equation (7.24) the given residual fits the correction budget; Equations (7.25) and (7.27) permit the quadratic correction map to preserve the energy and supremum bounds. The paper imposes (7.26) but does not use it in the proof. Finally, (7.28) ensures nontriviality: if $v=-W_\alpha^{\rm a}$ then $w_*\|\nabla W_\alpha^{\rm a}\|_{\mathcal H}^2\le\|v\|_w^2\le4\varepsilon^2$, contradicting the strict inequality.

ns-b4-087|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isEx.annotation: The conclusion supplies the hypotheses of Theorem 7.1, not its solution. The theorem will solve the constrained correction problem with the certified inverse estimate, choose the parameter using the adjoint and stiff-coordinate enclosures, and use Equation (7.28) to exclude the zero profile. The formal assembly likewise establishes the certificate predicate; the profile construction is a subsequent theorem.

ns-b4-088|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isEx.annotation: Properties such as the allowed harmonics, the symmetries and zero divergence come from the represented form in Subsection B.1 and its compatibility conditions. Bounds such as the size of the residual and coercivity do not follow just from this form. This is why the statement of Proposition B.14 needs both the representation and the inequalities.

ns-b4-089|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Cert.annotation: The required residual is the unprojected representative supplied in Subsection B.1. In Equation (7.23) one measures its full $\mathcal H$ norm and the weighted row pairings of (7.17), not just the Leray projection. Although its gradient part disappears from the whole-space solenoidal adjoint pairings, changing the representative can affect both bounds used in Equation (7.24).

ns-b4-090|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.isEx.annotation: Proposition B.8 and Lemma B.2 give the a priori estimate at the reference field, while Lemma B.9 bounds its change to the approximate field and the growth of the slice gradient energy. Lemmas B.10–B.13 supply the three adjoint bounds for the parameter update. Conditions such as invertibility of $V$, the residual size, and the scalar inclusions (7.35) and (7.37) remain direct hypotheses; they are not consequences of the cell coercivity estimate.

ns-b4-093|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Cell.annotation: Checking the finite matrices alone is insufficient. Their entries must enclose the intended integrals, the polynomial identities must match the global-to-cell map, and the coefficient inequalities must hold throughout the relevant cells and regions. The positive forms are then tested on all allowed coefficient vectors, with the omitted modes controlled by the estimates of Subsection B.3.

ns-b4-094|Breakdown.CellLayerSystem.Cell.annotation: The numerical thresholds at the end of Subsection B.4 are restrictions on any admissible data, not the achieved sizes of the computed error. For example (7.25) bounds $M$ by $(2c_Lc_w)^{-1}$; dropping nonnegative terms in Equation (7.27) gives $2\varepsilon/\sqrt{w_*}\le M$. Combining the two gives the stated restriction on $\varepsilon$. The formal unresolved-mode and exterior estimates permit a stretching constant at least $\sqrt{7/2}$.

ac-033|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantia.annotation: The correction directions may have the same logarithmic tail dependence as the base field, but the phase change in Equation (B.9) is turned off on a ball. There one may form the trial profile and its derivatives by ordinary affine combinations of fixed fields, which is useful for bounding the residual as a function of the parameter.

ac-034|Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase|1.annotation: Since every azimuthal Fourier integer is $19\iota_1$, pure rotation through $2\pi/19$ preserves each scalar component in the rotating frame. The half-period rotation in Equation (B.1) is a stronger relation between time and angle: it permits a rotation through half that angle if time also advances by half a period.

ac-048|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.fie.annotation: Writing $W(\theta,y)=\bar W(\bar S\theta,y)$, the generator identity reads $W(\theta+1/2,R_{\pi/19}y)=R_{\pi/19}W(\theta,y)$. Replacing $y$ by $R_{-\pi/19}y$ and returning to $s=\bar S\theta$ gives the half-period relation in the paper (compare Remark 7.3 for how such a symmetry changes the period of the exact profile). Thus the sign of the rotation in the argument is fixed by the vector symmetry, not by the sense of either individual travelling pattern.

ac-035|Breakdown.CertCell.labelPhase|1.annotation: The two lines $\iota_2=0$ and $\iota_2=\iota_1$ are characterized by phases $\iota_1(19\phi\mp2\pi\theta)$. In similarity time $s=\bar S\theta$ the corresponding angular velocities are $\pm2\pi/(19\bar S)$. Thus in the frame of either pattern its own harmonics have zero frequency. The useful high-frequency test in Subsection C.4 uses the other frame for these harmonics, rather than assuming that every large angular integer oscillates rapidly in either frame.

ac-049|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.log.annotation: For $f(\rho)=A\log(1+\rho/r_c^2)$ one has $\rho^j|f^{(j)}(\rho)|=|A|(j-1)!(\rho/(r_c^2+\rho))^j$ for $j=1,2,3$. These are bounded by $|A|(j-1)!$ since $r_c>0$. Thus the phase grows logarithmically but meets exactly the derivative conditions of Subsection B.1.

ac-037|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.key.annotation: At fixed $x\ne0$, substitute $y=x/\sqrt{T-t}$ and $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ into the square brackets (the change of variables in Equation (1.4)). They become $\log((T-t)+|x|^2/r_c^2)-\log T$, which has a finite limit as $t\to T$. The prefactor of a leading $R^{-1}$ term becomes $|x|^{-1}$ in Eulerian velocity. Thus the logarithmic radial phase compensates the time oscillation for the specified leading coefficient.

ac-038|Breakdown.SimilarityResidual|1.annotation: For a solenoidal smooth field, $-\Delta W=\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W$. Also $(W\cdot\nabla)W=(\operatorname{curl}W)\times W+\nabla(|W|^2/2)$. Substituting both identities into Equation (1.2) gives the curl formulation, with the kinetic-energy gradient absorbed into $H$. `SimilarityResidual` uses the original advection and diffusion form.

ac-038|Breakdown.Coercive.Internal.TestD.annotation: For any smooth vector field, $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}W=\nabla\operatorname{div}W-\Delta W$. In Equation (C.1) the second displayed equation sets the first term on the right to zero. The linked lemma is the solenoidal specialization of this identity; it explains why the diffusion term in the residual of (C.1) is the positive double curl.

ac-053|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.sha.annotation: For a nonzero azimuthal mode the two splines determine the third amplitude via Equation (B.7); for an axisymmetric mode the stream function and swirl determine the velocity via Equation (B.8). The numerical unknowns therefore consist of the independent scalar coefficients and the origin coefficients, with one additional unknown for the period. No separate divergence equation for three independent velocity components is necessary.

ac-054|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsT.annotation: A common partition lets every retained harmonic use the same radial rings and height intervals in quadrature and Newton's method. The general representation does not require this: each spline may have its own partition, provided its own traces agree to the orders in Subsection B.1.

ac-055|Breakdown.CertCell.GivenShape.IsT.annotation: The join conditions are built into the polynomial basis used for the unknowns. For example $\mathsf A$ needs an extra radial derivative and $\mathsf B$ an extra height derivative because of their contributions to $u_2$ in Equation (B.7); $\mathsf S$ needs both because of the two derivatives in Equation (B.8). The resulting velocity has continuous first derivatives, although its second derivatives in the residual are only piecewise continuous.

ac-057|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantia.annotation: The term $\nabla H$ in Equation (C.1) drops out of the weak equations because the tests are solenoidal. For a compactly supported test the identity is immediate by integration by parts; the represented tests in the computation have decay rather than compact support, so removal of a spatial cutoff uses their decay. This pressure elimination does not mean the residual before subtracting a gradient is small.

ac-043|Breakdown.CertCell.CellCalculus.I.annotation: The differential expression in Equation (C.2) is the linearization at the current profile. The formal strong right-hand side also allows the actuator forcing and the gradient of pressure: its diffusion term is minus the Hessian trace, using solenoidality to replace $\operatorname{curl}\operatorname{curl}v$ by $-\Delta v$. In Appendix C the expression is tested in a finite space to find an approximate field; in Appendix B its cellwise pairings are estimated for arbitrary perturbations of the reference field.

ac-045|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantia.annotation: The fields $W^i$ are chosen from a linearized solve with the inverse period, force coefficients and prescribed constraint values included. The equation $F^{(i)}\simeq0$ is the target of that solve, not an exact identity of the represented fields. Even a small first variation modulo gradients does not by itself bound its ball pairing; Equation (B.58) uses the actual residual representative and the adjoint field. The phase is changed only outside the matching ball so that this first variation and the quadratic terms are exact interior coefficients.

ac-046|Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantia.annotation: For a leading term with time integer $j$ and radial index $l=-j$, the change $S^{-1}\mapsto S^{-1}+\varsigma\cdot\alpha$ adds $2\pi i j(\varsigma\cdot\alpha)$ to its similarity transport multiplier. A phase increment $(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)\log R$ adds $il(\mathsf k\cdot\alpha)/2$ through the radial drift. They cancel for $\mathsf k=4\pi\varsigma$. Without such cancellation, the change produces an order-$R^{-1}$ term for a nonzero leading oscillatory coefficient, whose square is not integrable at infinity. The cutoff allows the change to be made only in the exterior (so the interior residual can be expanded polynomially as in Lemma B.13).

ac-059|Breakdown.PieceWeights.frameFreq|.annotation: At $S=\bar S$ the positive rate $2\pi/(19\bar S)$ cancels the term $-2\pi\iota_1/\bar S$ in Equation (B.15), giving $4\pi\iota_2/\bar S$; the negative rate gives $4\pi(\iota_2-\iota_1)/\bar S$. Away from the intersection of the two slow strips at least one modulus is larger than $4\pi j_*/\bar S$. This calculation at the central period motivates the choice of sets; it does not replace the uniform frequency test on $\mathcal K$.

ac-060|Breakdown.PieceWeights.modeTerm|1.annotation: For one selected curl mode and fixed share $d>0$, ignoring the other losses and the weight derivative, the curl-square coefficient gains $a|\Omega|-a^2 b^2/(4d)$ for $a=\lambda_p$, where $b$ bounds relative speed. If $b>0$, completing the square gives the best gain $d|\Omega|^2/b^2$ at $a=2d|\Omega|/b^2$. This explains the proportionality in Subsection C.4 and why the useful frame is chosen by both frequency and relative speed. The actual weights also pay the remaining terms in Equation (B.16).

ac-061|Breakdown.CertCell.Instance.IsWei.annotation: The numerical optimization selects the spline coefficients, not the perturbation being estimated. In particular it must choose weights for whole classes of modes and for the exterior as well as for the finite set of cell interactions. The representation predicate supplies the permissible spline shapes; the inequalities of Subsections B.2 and B.3 must subsequently be checked for those choices.
